N the course of the year 1920 arrangements were [= in Sweden for a scientific expedition to Kamchatka. Its principal purpose was zoological, botanical and ethnographical discovery. It was partly financed by the Swedish Geographical Society, and its members—apart from the Author, who was appointed its chief, and his wife, Mrs Dagny Bergman—were the botanist, Eric Hultén, M.A., and his wife, Elsie Hultén, D.Sc.; the zoologist, René Malaise, M.A., and the taxidermist, Ernst Hedstrém. The Author’s special province was in the field of zoology and ethnography. This book consists of a popular account of two journeys undertaken by members of the expedition: a journey on skis and with dogs from north-eastern Kamchatka down to Petropavlovsk, and a journey of four months on dog-sledges into the central and northern regions of the peninsula. The latter journey was undertaken by the Author and his wife alone. On the former they were accompanied by Mr Hedstrém. For all the help afforded us by the local authorities, business houses and private individuals, I beg to express my warm sense of gratitude. The collections made by the expedition are now contained in the Swedish National Museum (Svenska |
Riksmuseum). The scientific results are under publication, in part in the Transactions of the Royal Swedish Academy of Science, in part in Swedish scientific journals. STEN BERGMAN.

FTER a stay of a month in Japan, during A which we had sought in vain for a steamer to take us to Kamchatka, we at last found a schooner at Hakodate, the northern seaport. It was to go to a place on the north-east coast of Kamchatka, and its owner had no objection to dropping us at Petropavlovsk, the capital. But he wanted such a fabulous price for taking us that we felt we must regard this vessel as out of the question. As, however, nothing else offered, we had to resume negotiations with him later, when we found him more reasonable in his demands.

Accordingly we decided to go on board the schooner and see what she was like. While a Japanese boatman was rowing us out to where she lay at anchor we descried in the midst of all the Japanese vessels out on the roadstead an elegant-looking little craft which flew the Soviet Red Flag. We altered our course at once and let our boatman take us to her instead of to the schooner. Her captain told me that she was bound direct for Petropavlovsk, and that she was the Soviet Government’s armoured steamer Commander
Behring, serving as an “‘ inspection steamer ” in these waters.

On my asking whether our party of six Swedes might accompany him, he was unable to commit himself definitively, but he declared that not only all the berths and bunks were occupied, but also all the benches on board and the whole of the decks. He was friendly enough however to add that there might be sleepingroom under the dining-saloon table and also possibly in one or other of the life-boats.

When he was made to realize that we were extremely anxious to be accommodated, he went on to say that he himself had nothing against it, but that it was an official named Volovnikoff who must decide the matter. Mr Volovnikoff, it seemed, had gone ashore and there was no getting hold of him. When eventually we ran him to earth, he not only gave us permission to come along, but granted us all a free passage and free freightage for as much of our baggage as could be got on board. The vessel was to start at midnight.

We had a tremendous job to manage things in the time. Our entire baggage, about a hundred and fifty packing-cases, was stored in the warehouses of the Customs, and these were closed for the day. Barges had to be hired to take the packing-cases out to the steamer, and gangs of coolies had to be engaged for the carrying of them, Our difficulties may be imagined when I add that our things lay in the innermost recesses of the warehouse, that in front of them bars of pig-iron had been piled up almost to the roof, that we had to od get out our Christmas-tree candles in order to see, as the electric light wasn’t working, and that, on top of all, the coolies struck work at the most critical moment and cleared off home!

All the same, at ten minutes to twelve we had got everything on board that could be found room for. It was just as well, as it turned out, that there was not room for everything. What was left over was to follow by the next boat.
When the Commander Behring raised anchor and steamed off, that lovely moonlit and starlit night, we little imagined that she was starting on her last voyage !

It was a momentous occasion for us Swedes, this departure from Japan. We were saying good-bye to the civilized world for three summers and two winters. I remember I stood for a long time on deck and watched the last lights sink below the horizon. My thoughts travelled alternately to the great unknown region whither we were faring and to those dear to me at home, my mother and father and all my family and my many friends.

We were to get to Petropavlovsk, it was reckoned, in six days. The vessel was armed with two cannon and had fifty-three souls on board, including crew and passengers, all of them Russians except ourselves,

They were a strange collection, these Russians, Most of them had been in the war, and when they told us their adventures we could well believe that they had had narrow escapes from death. Here sat a young soldier with a St George’s Cross on his breast, there an airman in uniform, in a corner an old man surrounded by a lot of dirty-looking bundles. He also was bound for Petropavlovsk, he told us, as he sat there quietly, rolling himself cigarettes and watching the flight of the seagulls round the boat. All had been recently at Vladivostock, where there was still an echo of gun-shots after the last revolution, and all were looking forward to the stillness and peace of Kamchatka.

The days succeeded to each other while we travelled past the snowclad volcanoes of the Curile Islands. We noticed how the cold increased every day. Whales kept us company now and again and sometimes swam along quite near the vessel.

When we had come to one of the last of the Curile Islands a fateful decision was arrived at. The ship, it was settled, instead of continuing direct to Petropavlovsk, should make for the Sea of Okotsk and follow up the west coast of Kamchatka a bit to find out whether any foreign vessels were cruising about in the neighbourhood of the “ tabooed ” Cape Lopatka. The guns were made ready for action and the Commander Behring ploughed her way into the icy Okotsk waters. Lights were put out and a war atmosphere reigned on board. The Russians rubbed their hands with joy at the prospect of capturing some schooner perhaps next day. A cold, raw fog enveloped everything. Darkness came on and we lay down to sleep. But our open life-boat made a somewhat comfortless bed.

At about half-past six in the morning we were awakened by a tremendous crash. It made me jump, and I thought at first that a cannon had been fired. Two more crashes in succession now brought home to me the seriousness of the situation. We had driven on to a submerged rock. All on board came up on deck and there was a scene of great commotion. The steamer had had a hole knocked into her bottom and the water was rushing into the machine-room and the hold. The captain gave orders to the crew to let down the lifeboats. The vessel was filling with water and must be forsaken. ‘To the life-boats!’’ was now the word of command. Everyone made haste to gather together their most valuable possessions and there was a tremendous rushing about on board. Of course, the saving of human lives had to be our first consideration, but it was a bitter thought that we might have to abandon all our equipment for the three years which we were to spend in Kamchatka.

Fortunately we were only a few miles from land— from the south coast of Kamchatka. As soon as the boats had been filled with people, parcels and travelling bags, we made for the shore. The boats were not large and they went hopping about over the waves and we were all drenched to the skin; but at last we reached land and were at our destination—Kamchatka—shipwrecked castaways !

The coast was flat and bare, without a single tree on it. Great snowdrifts reached right down to the waterside although it was the 14th of June. A wooden cross standing out on the tandra—the word used in these regions to describe the expanses of barren land—was evidence that we were not the first visitors to the spot. The life-boats went back to the wrecked vessel and returned with the rest of the passengers. The captain and some of the crew had still to be fetched, so they then made a third journey. Fortunately one of the life-boats was provided with a motor and this one towed the other ; otherwise it would have been very difficult to get out to the steamer, as the wind was unfavourable. When the boats got to land for the third time the captain gave orders for us to go back to the wreck on the one with the motor in order to rescue those portions of our baggage to which we attached most importance. When we reached the Commander Behring the water had risen high in the machine-room and in the few cabins. The picking out of our most valuable packingcases was a very difficult business—what we had on board being a selection of the most important items of our equipment. (As already mentioned, the less important things lay at Hakodate.) _ That thinning-out of our possessions was really tragic. It was a question of choosing ten boxes only ‘and doing so at once. We chose the cases containing the most essential items of our scientific equipment and we managed to get them up on deck, whence they would have to be lowered into the life-boats. When we had got eight of them up on deck, and were busy with the ninth, we were checked by the cry: “‘'To the life-boats! The ship is sinking!’’ We had to drop our burden and make a rush for it. The water had risen to such a degree that the vessel had begun to swing over to one side. At any moment now, so it seemed, she might capsize. It was heart-breaking to have to leave her with only a few of our scientific implements saved—our microscopes, for instance, our meteorological implements, our photographic cameras and two guns. The captain, however, reassured us a little by saying that he thought the steamer would remain stranded on the rock until the following day unless the wind increased.

Evening was now coming on, and on the beach were assembled fifty-three shipwrecked persons, with their bundles, chests and packing-cases. Almost every man possessed a gun also, for guns are indispensable in Kamchatka. All the tents and tarpaulins on board the steamer had been saved, and in a short time the tents were put up and we all made ourselves as comfortable in them as we could. It would be difficult to find a more inhospitable spot in the whole of Kamchatka. Storms, winds and mists seemed indigenous to it.

The fate of our expedition was to be decided by the course things should take that night, so it was in’ * no tranquil state of mind that we laid ourselves “down: on the wet ground and listened to the rain beating upon the roof of the tent. With intense anxiety we noted the behaviour of the wind, how it sometimes seemed to slacken, sometimes to increase. Naturally not one. member of our party was able to sleep. We just lay there awaiting the dawn when we could continue the salving of our property—if there were anything left to salve. I myself went out several times during the night to try to see in the semi-darkness whether the steamer still lay where she had been wrecked, but the fog and the rain prevented me from seeing anything.
When at last daybreak began, we were able to descry the steamer still holding up, though with a slight list. So there was still hope. In a very short while we were ready to get to work.

It was a cold and inclement morning as we motored out to the steamer. When we got to her a tragic sight met our eyes. The whole of her stern had sunk and with it about thirty of our packing-cases. Of these we managed to extricate ten, which had not been damaged as they were zinc-lined and water-tight. The rest of the cases were lost irretrievably. The eight which we had got on deck the previous evening stood where we had left them. There was now nothing for us to do but to get all these eighteen packing-cases down into the life-boat. This accomplished, we returned safely to the shore.

On arriving we were met by one of the Russians with the cheering news that five of the cases which we had given up as lost had floated to land about a mile and a half from our camping place. The wind, it seemed, had blown landwards during the night. We took a walk along the beach, and sure enough there were the five cases with their blue and yellow stripes, and outwardly undamaged. The words stamped on them, “Swedish Scientific Kamchatka Expedition,” were still legible. They had come ashore only a few yards’

distance from each other. They presented a strange appearance where they lay. When we had packed them in Stockholm, we had never imagined that the waves of the Sea of Okotsk would carry them on to the beach of Kamchatka!

On going carefully into the matter, we ascertained that just fifteen cases had been lost. We proceeded to study our inventory of their contents. Now there would be a cry of relief over the discovery that some important thing had been saved, now one of despair over something else of importance that had been lost.

The most important of the things lost were as follows: our medicine-chest, our store of photographic plates—which was very large and carefully chosen—our cinematograph films, three-fourths of our ammunition, a couple of guns, a camera, the greater part of the clothes of two members of the expedition—in addition to any number of smaller things of great value.

There was nothing for us to do now but await rescue. A great beacon fire was lit and we raised a flag as a signal of distress. A schooner showed itself on the horizon, but did not notice us. Next day another schooner was sighted, but this one also proceeded on her course without noticing us. We decided to try to waylay her with the help of the motor-boat. A flag of distress was hoisted on it and off it went full speed, watched by many anxious pairs of eyes. Great was our joy when the schooner suddenly changed her course and came to meet the motor-boat. She proved to be a little Russian two-master, bound for a place called

Kambolnaja, on the west coast of Kamchatka. She was willing to return thence immediately and take on board as many passengers as she could find room for, but no baggage. She reckoned she could get back in three or four days. The fourth day came, then a fifth, sixth and seventh, but no schooner. Afterwards we heard that she also went aground. :

In the meantime our first concern was to procure the necessaries of life. Some sacks of flour had been saved out of the Commander Behring’s store, together with sundry other sorts of food, and our party had with us a box of biscuits and a box of Swedish hard rye bread, as well as some packets of oats and some condensed milk. But there were fifty-three people in the camp! It was the height of ill-luck for us that we were stranded on so wild and barren a spot—quite near Cape Lopatka. There were seals and sea-birds along the shore, and inland there were some marmots, but the seals were difficult to come by when they had been shot, and apart from them the animal life was scanty. We ate with good appetite all the seal-flesh, etc., we could get, and careful rations were distributed of the biscuits and hard rye bread, which, thanks to the excellent soldering of the boxes, were unspoilt and which were highly prized. We managed thus to stave off hunger, but dry boots and clothes were out of the question. A slight improvement in our condition was effected after we had built up a little house out of various boxes and covered it over with moss.

The camp consisted of ten tents, and above the tent of the Bolshevik Commissary Volovnikoff waved the Soviet Red Flag, on which were the words in Russian, “ Long Live the Democratic Republic!’ Our existence was full of interest. We all lived together on excellent terms. We went out on excursions together, paid visits to each other’s tents, and generally made the best of things. The ship’s dog, which had lived on board since she had been launched fifteen years before, and three little pigs—which had been put into a sack and thrown into one of the life-boats, and which now were allowed to run free—contributed a good deal to our amusement. Every tent had its own fire, on which we cooked our food and which helped us to warm ourselves when the weather was too cold—for although it was midsummer the snow still lay on the ground to within a few yards of the camp.

Practically all the Russians were Bolsheviks, and to their credit I must say that I could never have believed that Bolsheviks could be such pleasant people. Among the sailors, it is true, there were some bad specimens, but no one did us any harm apart from some minor nocturnal thefts of ammunition and preserves.

After a few days we espied smoke on the horizon— a steamer evidently, so we exerted ourselves to attract her attention. We lit bonfires of driftwood and moss, but the steamer, which was a long way off, made no response. So we sent out the motor-boat again, with the flag of distress at her bows as before, and again we all watched with the utmost anxiety. The steamer changed her course and, to our delight, we saw the big vessel and the little one meet in the distance. It was a Japanese cargo-steamer. The Japanese were cordial and friendly, but they said they could not take us themselves to Petropavlovsk. They would effect our rescue, however, in another way. They would see whether there was not some Japanese warship somewhere on the Sea of Okotsk with which they could communicate by wireless. If so, they could guarantee that it would come quickly to our help.

And so we resumed our life on the barren shore in the hope that this might come about. Two days later the sounds of a siren came to us from the sea, which was enveloped in fog, and in the course of a few hours, after the fog had cleared, we saw a couple of extremely narrow and elegantly-shaped torpedo-boats lying at anchor near the wreck. The Japanese officers were most kind and friendly, and offered to take us all on board, but with only a small portion of our baggage, as they had very little room. We Swedes, however, were allowed to take all our belongings with us. On the night of Midsummer Day we steered our course for Petropavlovsk. Soon the two torpedoboats were joined by another pair, and all the four proceeded in line along the rocky eastern coast of Kamchatka until, some twenty hours later, we swept into Avatcha Bay.

Soon Petropavlovsk came in sight, the goal of our long pilgrimage. It was a strange sensation for me to see the place which I had so often looked at on the map and which I had always thought of as the world’s end.
It was like entering into Paradise to see the rich, green birch-groves which covered the hillsides and valleys. The snowclad volcanoes were screened from our eyes by the fog.

HUS it was, then, we arrived at the capital of Kamchatka. One of the first things we heard was that the four-masted schooner by which we had been so near travelling had blown up and sunk, all on board being lost. We felt that we had been very lucky in having been merely wrecked on the Commander Behring instead of having been sent sky-high with the schooner !
The Government of the Reds, as represented by the Head of the Police, came on board and gave us permission to land.

We were rowed ashore by Japanese sailors and set foot for the second time on the soil of Kamchatka. We proceeded to stroll down the principal street, in which there were not many people. The houses for the most part were single-storeyed buildings, unpainted, and with roofs of corrugated-iron. Empty-looking shops lined the street. Most of them were Chinese. On all sides we heard the grating sound of the Russian language, mingled with Chinese and Japanese. All the people stood and stared at us and seemed astonished at our appearance. An empty cart rattled past us, drawn by a horse with the typical big Russian wooden bow on the back. The driver had to pull up to gaze at us. We must have presented as strange an appearance to them as a party of Kamchadals would present in the streets of a small town in Europe.

It did not take us long to inspect most of the town. Finally, being very hungry, we resorted to the one and only café—a very low-class establishment. We had seen enough of Petropavlovsk to satisfy ourselves that it was a pleasant little place of three streets with the nucleus of a fourth, and that it was inhabited chiefly by Russians, Chinese, Japanese and Koreans, as well as by other races which it was not easy to identify. Moreover, that its inhabitants were very inquisitive, that no one seemed to be in a hurry, and that slop-pails were often emptied direct through the kitchen door; finally, that pigs went about loose everywhere and that bear-cubs were to be seen walking about in front of many of the houses.

Two hours later we were sitting in the office of a Chinese business man, Sun-in-tun, and negotiating with him about the leasing of a house. We succeeded in securing the only empty house in the town, a house built entirely in European style, with five rooms and kitchen, and situated in Third Street, with a lovely view over Avatcha Bay.

For a payment of fifty thousand roubles—about three pounds at the rate of exchange of that date—a grey-haired old fellow named Sacharoff conveyed our baggage to this house, and after we had drawn lots for the rooms we began to settle down in them as best we might. The largest room was made into a workingroom to be used by us all in common, with a separate place for each of us when busy preserving specimens of flora and fauna; another room was to be our diningroom, and the remaining three to be private rooms to sleep and work in. It was a point of honour with us all to make our own rooms as nice as possible. A number of boards which we managed to get hold of were rapidly
~ made into tables, benches and book-shelves, and our latent gifts for carpentering found great scope. The ladies of the party attended to the esthetic aspect of things.
Meanwhile we made acquaintance with some of the bigwigs of the town.

Of these the most notable was the priest, a welldressed gentleman with long hair, whom we met in the street and who addressed us in the purest Swedish. He was the son of a Swedish mother and a Russian father, and had been brought up in Finland. He became one of our closest friends and associates, and was very useful at first as interpreter and adviser. With characteristically Russian open-heartedness, he at once told us the whole story of his life, which had been full of change and variety. He seemed to regard it as his particular duty to come almost every day and give us a résumé of the latest scandals of the town. He told us much that was enlightening about its inhabitants, who seemed to be a very bad lot indeed. We learned, for instance, that a man in a certain house was given to boasting that he had murdered so many persons, that his neighbour had escaped from Sachalin, that such-and-such a person made his money by fraudulent enterprises, that his brother-in-law was a thief, etc. It amounted to this—that most of the town’s inhabitants were rogues and rascals. Very few of them found favour in his eyes.

The person next in importance was the principal of the chief school in Petropavlovsk, a Kamchadal who had studied at Tomsk. He was an intelligent man and e spoke excellent English. Above all, he was interested in natural history and was a keen botanist, and was able to tell us much about the resources of the country. He rendered us many services on various occasions.

Another man of importance was the veterinary surgeon of the “ district,” an Estlander, who had been living in Kamchatka for more than ten years. His “ district” included the whole of the Kamchatkan peninsula, the region of Anadyr, the Chukchee peninsula, the island of Wrangel, etc. It was so extensive that he had begun from the start to regard it as out of the question for him to achieve anything useful, so he decided instead just to vegetate. He never quitted Petropavlovsk, and he had done no professional work for years, although he was an official and in receipt of a salary. Moreover, he declared that he had forgotten all he had ever known about his job!
These three were the only men of any education whose acquaintance we made during our first summer.
Petropavlovsk lies on the slope of a hill. All the principal shops are in the main street—Pjervi ulitza.
They are for the most part Chinese, but there are also iS

some Japanese shops, one American, and one Russian. The American shop, Seidenberg & Wittenberg, is the best stocked. There you can buy Swedish Primus stoves, preserved fruits from California, matches from Japan, and everything else you can reasonably desire in such a place as Petropavlovsk. In the same street are the post and telegraph office » (in which about fifteen persons are employed, although, as a rule, only two or three mail-boats arrive in the whole year), the church and, a little farther on, the People’s House, in which stormy political meetings alternate with social entertainments—such as cinema shows, dances, etc. Apart from a Japanese barber’s shop, I think I may say that there is nothing else of importance in the centre of the town. At the eastern end are the Government buildings, all constructed in the same style— grey-hued, two-storey houses with corrugated-iron roofs. Among them is the dwelling of the former Governor, in front of which lie a pair of rusty cannon. A little way farther on, outside the town, is the wireless station, the only connecting link with the outer world in the long winter. Immediately beyond, the wilderness confronts you in a really remarkable way. You come suddenly to a full-stop if you want to continue your promenade, for here begins the alschovnik (Alnus maximowiczi), the dense jungle, curse of Kamchatka, through which it is possible to creep if you have nothing to carry, but which otherwise you must cut your way through. Petropavlovsk externally may be described as a blend of a typical small Russian town and a hastily built mining town in Alaska. The collection of grey, wooden houses of which it consists look as though they had been dumped down more or less anyhow along the three streets. Except in the main street, which has a certain touch of civilization about it, you come now and again upon huts and hovels which are constructed of odds and ends—iron pots, pieces of boarding, old trousers and the most incredible ingredients. They adjoin refuse heaps and potato patches. If you enter one of these dwellings in the dusk you are as likely as not to stumble over a fat pig. The pigs in Petropavlovsk are so numerous that they give the town a certain character. Everywhere they go loose, and for the most part they forage for themselves among refuse heaps and cabbage patches.

The water-supply consists of some pleasant rivulets coming down from the fijells, the water of which is beautifully fresh. They have been made to ramify into a great number of little channels, which flow down to the various houses. The clear water is sullied here and there, by some pig which takes it into its head to wallow in it in the warmth of the morning sun, or by some inconsiderate neighbour washing clothes in—or rinsing out a cask of salt salmon in—one of the streams farther up.

The population of this unique little town is in number little more than a thousand. As already indicated, most of these are Russians, but the Japanese, Chinese and Koreans combine to make a good third,

The Chinese and Koreans cut wood, fetch water and do all the other forms of hard work in the town. The Russians in Petropavlovsk are disinclined for hard work of any sort, and every self-respecting Russian employs a Chinaman to do it for him. ‘The Japanese in Petropavlovsk are mostly business men, apart from the officers and soldiers belonging to the Japanese men-of-war.

In addition to these, and to a sprinkling of Kamchadals, there are the specimens, already mentioned, of races difficult to identify, Aleuts, Tartars, Jakuts, etc., a mixture of white men and yellow men, of Europeans and Asiatics.

In contrast with the gold-mining cities of Alaska, where energy and feverish industry give their stamp to the life, the atmosphere of Petropavlovsk is marked by lethargy and sloth. Time has no value. What is not done to-day can be equally well done to-morrow, or next year. Herein lies the great danger for the European. Slowly but surely he becomes more and more apathetic every year. I believe that a man who has lived for ten years in Petropavlovsk is lost for civilization and incapable of any well-ordered kind of work.

The Russian population of the town is of a very mixed kind. The priest’s account of them was, I think, well founded. I soon came to realize that it was better not to question them as to what they were before coming to Kamchatka. One could always be sure that they had not been born in the country, but had come from some far-off corner of the Russian Empire. One met men from the Crimea and Astrakhan, from Archangel and Jakutsk, from Petrograd and Moscow, and from all the towns and villages of Siberia. _ But, whatever their place of origin, they all bore the same stamp— the same optimism in regard to the morrow, the same nitchevo—“ it doesn’t matter ”’—attitude in regard to all their undertakings. Were one to try to separate the sheep from the goats, I am afraid the latter would be in the majority, for it is not the best types that are _ drawn to these regions, including many criminals from Sachalin and Siberia.

Petropavlovsk, being the capital of Kamchatka, is the seat of the Government of the country. In the good old times—i.e. before the Russian Revolution—supreme ' authority rested with the Governor. When, gradually, the waves of the revolution swept over Kamchatka the Governor was deposed, and the country was placed under the control of a Bolshevik Committee. This Committee was in existence at the time of our arrival. It bore the haughty title “The Revolutionary Committee of Kamchatka,”’ but its attitude towards us was most amicable. In the service of the Reds there were about a couple of hundred officials of all kinds. A regular bureaucratic system had been installed, with commissioners and departments for everything, and any number of typewriters.

To maintain order in the town there was a police force of about a dozen men. Some of these were posted always in the main street. They looked not a little imposing, with their big sabres and revolvers and red

bands. Their principal duty would seem to have been the confiscation for their own benefit of spirits on the Russian steamers which arrived. Occasionally there may be hundreds of gallons to be confiscated on a single boat, so, as may be imagined, the post of policeman in Petropavlovsk is much sought after.
TO THE MOUTH OF THE KAMCHATKA RIVER

URING the remainder of the summer we D-=: expeditions in various directions in the districts around Petropavlovsk, studying the fauna and flora and making collections. As each of the party had his special task, we divided ourselves into various groups during these journeys, and thus it happened that my wife, Mr Hedstrém and I left Petropavlovsk in the autumn on a steamer to study the fauna for four or five weeks—as we then intended —in the deltaland of the River Kamchatka, north of Petropavlovsk.

We were to have made our way up to Ust-Kamchatsk on the Russian war cruiser Magnet, which had been lying for some time in the harbour of Petropavlovsk, but the day before we were to start the captain sent a sailor round to tell us that his orders had been modified and that he was to go only as far as the Commander Islands, and from there direct to Vladivostock. The real reason of the change was quite different. A great many of the crew had deserted while at Petropavlovsk and a good number of those who remained were threatening to do likewise unless the captain agreed to go where they wished—namely, to the Commander Islands first

and then to Vladivostock. He had acquiesced rather than lose all his men. A fine specimen of a war cruiser ! The great attraction for sailors calling at the Commander Islands, by the way, is that spirits can be bartered for blue-fox skins.

The Magner having failed us, our only hope lay in the very last steamer of the year going to the north, the Yana, also Russian. It was some time in the middle of September that I interviewed her captain and told him that we wanted to go with him as far as Ust- Kamchatsk on the understanding that he should pick us up there again on his return journey and take us down to the capital. To this he agreed, pledging his word with a handshake.

The appearance and condition of a Russian steamer on this coast have to be seen to be believed in! Her hull will not have had a coat of paint for years. Her deck is simply crammed with every imaginable kind of cargo, from barrels of fish to great piles of cabbages and boxes full of onions—no Russian can thrive for long without onions and cabbages. Cattle stand about among the confused mass of objects, some of the poor beasts being brought along by intending settlers, others just to be killed and eaten on the voyage. The former are the worse off, for there are no stalls for them, even if they have to spend the winter on the Arctic coast. There are pigs too on board, often let quite loose and not adding to the general cleanliness !
As for the passengers, their slovenliness and dirt are appalling. There is no limit to their number, and

this state of things will continue as long as there are so few steamers available. Now and again the captain makes an effort to prevent some of them from coming on board. Then there is a tremendous commotion. Women utter piercing screams, men curse and swear, and it ends by the whole crowd being allowed to squeeze on to the vessel, each individual as a rule carrying his possessions in some sealskin bags. They all have to shift for themselves on board as best they may. Those who can manage it settle down in the hold. The lifeboats are next in favour. After them there is only the deck.

On the vessels coming from the north the passengers usually have reindeer hides or else some kind of tattered bearskins to lie on, but those on vessels from the south have to put up as a rule with sacking. When it rains all try to get under tarpaulins. The general discomfort is simply indescribable !

It may be thought that the problem of provisioning must be a difficult one in such conditions, but as a matter of fact it is quite easily solved with the help of the tea-kettle. When going north from Vladivostock there is always a supply of coarse loaves. Travelling south, sun-dried salmon is the stock food. Onions are always to be had if you keep on good terms with the Chinese cooks on board. Nothing else is felt to be really indispensable.
Such is the life on the Russian steamers which visit these parts in the summer, starting out from Vladivostock. The terrible suffering which results when a
vessel of this kind runs aground somewhere in a storm or mist, as often happens upon this rocky coast, may easily be imagined.

And such a vessel was the Fama. She was on her way up to Baron Korffs Bay, picking up passengers and cargoes of fish at a number of places as she went. Petropavlovsk was her first halt from Vladivostock, so she was not so overcrowded but that we were able to find room in the hold. On other occasions we had to adapt ourselves to life inside the life-boats, contriving as best we could, and comforting ourselves with the reflection that at all events we were well off in case of shipwreck. In the hold we ensconced ourselves on a kind of shelf about three feet in height, and with an iron top to it, of which we had painful reminders every time we tried to emerge from it in a hurry.

Ror company we had a number of Russians and a gang of Chinese coolies. The latter worked as wharfmen in the ports, getting the cargo on and off. It was very interesting to study the ways of these dissimilar racial types during the three days of our voyage.
The Russians drank tea, smoked cigarettes, talked politics and abused Kamchatka as a country fit only for savages and not for civilized human beings. They slept most of the day.

The Chinese were the more numerous below. When not called on to work, they squatted about and played cards by candlelight, using small tubs for tables. We were struck by their grave demeanour while playing, the first time we saw them there.. A company of Swedish

sailors when playing cards gets excited, and shouts and swears, whereas these Chinamen sat there, playing so seriously. They used matches as markers. They kept up a conversation in low tones. Most of them smoked small-bowled pipes, continually relighting them from the candle.

After half-an-hour or so there was an exchange of angry words between a couple of players. Although we did not understand what they said there could be no mistake about their feelings! In another second there was a babel of vehement cries—none of them could hear what the others were saying. Presently one of them snatched up all the cards and flung them about in every direction. The lighted candle he flung into the hold, hitting a Russian on the head with it, and the din was now redoubled, the Russian trying to find out which of all the chattering Chinese was the culprit. At last the skipper intervened and things quieted down, but there were no more cards that evening.

It was interesting also to watch the Chinese eating. One of the company acted as a kind of foreman for the others, fetching two big dishes twice a day from - the kitchen—one dish containing rice, the other some kind of soup. Then the others would produce their bowls and chopsticks and begin their meal. The sound they made as they all gobbled down their food’ was exactly like that of so many pigs at a trough!
In the mornings all the Chinese washed themselves thoroughly, and most of them brushed their teeth. During the daytime they were often to be seen sitting
about, mending their clothes and talking—not politics» probably. They looked happy and pleased with things and laughed continually.

During the voyage up to Ust-Kamchatsk, our destination at the mouth of the Kamchatka river, we kept well out to sea, but near enough to land to descry the volcanoes and snowclad mountains along the coast.

After thus progressing for a day and a night we reached Semljatschik, a fishing place, off which the Russian steamer Tomsk was anchored, taking on board a cargo of fish. Semljatschik is known for its hot spring, which is reputed to cure syphilis. People come thither all the year round to bathe.

It seems impossible for two Russian steamers to meet out in this distant latitude without getting to close quarters. The Russians are a sociable race. All | the Russians on the Yana had acquaintances on the Tomsk, so we had to exchange greetings. Accordingly we dropped anchor alongside her and there was a lively va et vient of small boats between the two vessels. Our captain and a lot of the passengers made their way over to the Tomsk to drink tea. Never could I have believed that a steamer could be so crammed with people as the Tomsk was. They were packed together on deck as close as sardines in a box.

Not until the chattering had continued for six hours did the Yana hoist anchor again. Time is not of much account here in the wild East, whereas on the Swedish steamer which brought us to Japan every minute spent
at a seaport was noted, and everything was done at an almost feverish rate of speed.
Next day we experienced the great sensation of setting eyes on the gigantic and wonderfully beautiful volcano Klutchefskaja. But it was at least a hundred miles off, and was screened in mist.

At last, on the morning of the third day, we dropped anchor a mile and a half outside the mouth of the great Kamchatka river. The expanse of country comprised in the delta of the river was flat and treeless. With my field-glasses I could make out some clusters of houses. At two points a couple of factory chimneys were to be seen. These were the Japanese canneries.

E had had thirty-six hours or so of tossing ‘ } : about by the waves beyond the mouth of the river before the sea calmed down enough to let us think of trying to land. To effect a landing in Ust-Kamchatsk is always a very precarious undertaking. The whole coast is quite open and without any kind of harbour. The gigantic river, which, after its meandering course through the country, moves forward in great breadth and strength as it discharges itself into the Behring Sea, provides the only possible landingplaces, so we had to penetrate up its mouth. Where the waters of the sea and the river meet and war with each other the effect makes one think of some monstrous witches’ cauldron. When motor-boats are drawn into the centre of this maelstrom it often happens that they refuse to obey the rudder, and consequently capsize, and they and all aboard go down into the depths. Evening was at hand when at last, together with all the passengers and baggage to be disembarked, we found ourselves on a great barge, which, towed by the Jana’s motor-boat, directed its course up the turbid stream. Every individual had been provided with a life-belt for the passage. Anxiously we passed the dangerous point. The waves were short and high, and 46 the force of the stream was very great. The heavy barge made such a strain upon the tug that it could only creep. It was a ghastly experience, this upstream progress. Had the engine stopped we should in all probability have been done for! But everything turned out all right, and we drew a sigh of relief when at last we were well up the river. Never in all my life, by the way, have I ever seen such a number of seals as in this river-mouth. They kept raising their heads in every direction and gazed at us wonderingly.
The big Russian village of Ust-Kamtchatsk is situated on the southern bank of the river. It consists of an agglomeration of grey houses and huts and hovels.

The whole made an unpleasant impression, and this was deepened by the appearance of the villagers who hastened down to the shore to meet us. We had intended to encamp on this side of the river, but the appearance of the people whom we should have had as neighbours caused us to decide at once to proceed to the other bank. And we soon found that this was a wise precaution.

As soon as the barge had been emptied of its cargo we crossed over in the motor-boat to the northern bank, where the great canneries are situated. Darkness was coming on and it was beginning to rain, and altogether it was a very unpleasant autumn evening. We disembarked our things, and went up the bank to find a suitable spot to pitch our camp. Some inquisitive persons collected round us, among them a big powerfully built man, dressed in blue clothes, and carrying a spanner. A bull was approaching and seemed to threaten us. ‘‘ Look out for the bull, madam!” the big man called out to my wife. While we were giving the animal a wide berth, my wife and I exchanged some remarks. ‘‘ What the hell do I hear?” exclaimed the big man, in our own language. “ Blessed if you’re not talking Swedish!” And he went on to say that he himself was a Norwegian from Christiania, and that his name was Anderson. This was, indeed, a pleasant surprise for us, and the beginning also of an acquaintanceship from which we were to derive much profit as well as pleasure.

Anderson now ordered forward some Chinamen, who began to see to the installing of our baggage in safe quarters for the night, and he then invited us to supper in his house. And here we were at once introduced to Mrs Anderson, a good-natured little Japanese woman, whom he told to produce everything the house contained in the way of food, and that proved to be not a little, although our host and his wife were starting for Japan the next morning and had just finished packing up.

When introducing his wife, Anderson remarked, as though apologetically: ‘‘ You see, I got tired of going to restaurants for my meals, so I decided to get married. She is a first-rate cook!’ And so we found her to be.

The Andersons spent the summers here in Ust- Kamtchatsk and the winters in Japan. Anderson had been connected with the factories from the start, and was responsible for all the machinery being kept in good order. He was some sort of over-machinist, and by dint of long and faithful service had, he told us, won himself a good salary and a post of confidence. He declared that now all he had to do was to wander round with his spanner and shout occasionally at his Japanese underlings.

Anderson proved to be a great wag, and in the course of the evening he entertained us with the story of his experiences and adventures. He had had a varied career. Among other things he had served as a machinist for three years on Russian steamers, but he then gave it up, having found the Russians bad seamen, altogether too much addicted to “‘ anchoring with their keel.”’ He found, he said, that the two mottoes of the Russians here in Kamchatka were, “‘ There’s no hurry,” and, “It doesn’t matter.” We were to learn for ourselves later how true this was.

Anderson kept us laughing the whole evening over his stories and jokes. Presently he began to declaim bits from Frizjof’s Saga, which he knew by heart from beginning to end, and finally he sang a number of Swedish popular songs for us. It seemed a pity that poor little Mrs Anderson could not understand them.
Our host, who claimed us as compatriots, put us up for the night, and gave orders that two rooms should be at our disposal as long as we remained at Ust- Kamchatsk.
Fortunately for us the Andersons’ departure for Japan was delayed for a couple of days through the outbreak of a storm, and we had two more evenings in which to enjoy his company.
But when the storm ceased Anderson and his wife went on board a barge, and were towed out to the Japanese ship by which they were to travel, and we saw them no more.

Mrs Anderson was nervous about the sea-voyage, and it was to prove a more alarming one than she could ever have imagined. Some days later the vessel was caught in a typhoon and wrecked against the rocky shore of one of the Curile Islands with all her passengers—more than five hundred in number. They had the good luck, however, to be stranded on an island upon which the Japanese had just established a wireless station, and with the help of this a steamer was summoned which saved them after a fortnight of keen anxiety.

The canneries, which lie on the north bank of the river, belong to the Russo-Japanese firm of Denbigh & Co. They consist of two blocks, standing at a distance of a mile-and-a-half apart alongside the river. They afford employment to a couple of thousand Japanese workmen in the summer, and they are run upon ultra-modern lines. South of the river, at a distance from each other of about ten miles, there are two other large canneries, which now belong to the Japanese firm known as “ The Nichiro Company,” and which also employs a couple of thousand workmen. During the winter both canneries are idle.

Within a radius of twenty miles or so from the mouth of the river there are no trees of any kind. The region consists of swampy marshland intersected by countless arms of the river. A great deal of it is open tundra, the rest nothing but willows and osier-beds, but with no real woods. The great lake of Nerpitche Osero, which is as big as Avatcha Bay, extends over a large portion of the lowlands. But in every direction except seawards this marshy region is bounded by mountains at a distance of twenty or thirty miles, and in clear weather one can see the volcano of Klutchefskaja—eighty miles away.

Close to the Denbigh canneries stands an extremely up-to-date and very powerful Japanese wireless station, _which had been erected only a few weeks before our arrival. Its purpose is to enable these Japanese canneries, in case of a threatened attack by Bolsheviks in the winter, to notify the Japanese warships which lie on guard at Petropavlovsk. During the previous winter there had been some looting by the Russians, but now the Japanese were armed to the teeth in case of the recurrence of anything of the kind.

In this connexion it may be mentioned that the _ Japanese, after the Russo-Japanese War, assumed salmon-fishing rights along the coasts of Kamchatka. On the other hand, they do not possess fishing rights on any of the rivers.

Through Anderson’s good nature, as I have mentioned, we were provided with excellent quarters. We began our excursions and our collecting at once. We were already at the end of September, and the stamp of autumn was on everything. On the /undra the crakeberries and red whortle-berries were ripe, and flocks of migrating birds came sweeping along from the north.

Out on the tundra one saw golden plovers and curlews. Small waders of different kinds were to be seen along the river banks and the seashore. Divers and different kinds of ducks, together with sea-gulls, were, however, the birds most characteristic of the region. Among ‘the ducks the beautiful harlequin duck was among the most numerous.

Bears were to be found by the shores of Nerpitche Osero, a couple of hours’ journey from our home. We explored the zundras in every direction, journeying by boat and canoe along the innumerable branches of the river. The results were satisfactory and we were glad to feel that we could continue for a time our studies of this peculiar neighbourhood and its denizens.

Then suddenly, at the end of a fortnight, came the notification to us from the captain of the Fana—which had been taking on its cargo meanwhile—that we must go aboard at once as the vessel would probably not be able to take in Ust-Kamchatsk on its return from the north. A motor-boat was to be available at once to take passengers out to the steamer. ‘To pack up our collections in a couple of minutes, so to speak, was quite impossible. Instead, I went out on the motorboat and asked the captain what he meant by breaking his word of honour. He did his best to excuse himself, but it came to this, that he could not keep his promise, and that if the weather were stormy he would have to start during the night, if it were calm he would remain two more days continuing to cargo. We were indignant at having been let in, but we had perforce to try to get ready to be off. We ordered a motor-boat for six o’clock next morning, and spent the whole night packing up all our belongings.

That was an exciting night for us. We knew that we should be cut off from the return to Petropavlovsk unless we travelled by the Faxa—which was the last boat of the year. It would mean wintering in Ust- Kamchatsk, for the only possible way to Petropavlovsk through the interior was one of about five hundred miles, and we had no winter equipment.

Towards midnight the storm began. It came thundering in from the sea, which in a few minutes was all foaming white. At least twice every hour I went out to see if the steamer were still at anchor. Throughout the night her lights could be seen in the darkness. They rose and fell, disappeared and reappeared, as the vessel tossed about on the big waves. But there she still lay. The situation bore a certain resemblance to that on the night of the shipwreck at Cape Lopatka.

At last daylight came, and then it became clear to us that it was out of the question to try to get out to the Fana. ‘The entire sea seethed with white foam, and at the river-mouth gigantic waves were rising to tremendous heights. The scene was a terrible one, At six o’clock came the Japanese machinist who was to have motored us out, but who now declared that to attempt it would be to court destruction.

But why was the Jana still delaying? Was it for us? Had the captain’s conscience been pricking him? Would he wait until we could get on board?... No, towards eight o’clock the steamer began to move off, and to our dismay we saw her disappear in a northerly direction.

There we were, five hundred miles from Petropavlovsk, shut off from the possibility of return. A wild mountainous region and an Arctic winter stood between us and our headquarters. But we made up our minds to put forth all our resources to overcome them both,

There had been one other chance of a passage for us to Petropavlovsk a little earlier, but for bad luck. This was the fine little three-masted merchant-schooner Avatcha. ‘The day after our arrival at Ust-Kamchatsk I had watched a schooner battling with the storm out to sea. I thought no more about the matter then, but next day she was thrown upon the beach. She came from the Chukchee peninsula and Alaska, and was to have called for a lot of cargo at Ust-Kamchatsk, and then proceeded to Petropavlovsk.

The situation was a very awkward one. We had our skis and all our other winter equipment at Petropaylovsk. We were now in October, and the Kamchatkan Winter was approaching. ‘The house in which we were lodged was one built for summer use in the Japanese style, with sliding windows. Snow was beginning to fall and to clothe the zundra in its white mantle. It did not fall softly and pleasantly, but in whirling storms ; and it worked its way in through the loosely-fitting windows in our dwelling, and lay in drifts on the floor. The temperature inside the house sank to that outside the moment the fire became extinguished. The water in our jugs was always frozen in the morning.
Some months were to pass before we succeeded in fashioning fur sleeping-sacks for ourselves.

However, we made the best of things. One of our longest and most interesting excursions was to the northern shore of Lake Nerpitche Osero, where we had our camp for a week. Here we made several new and interesting acquaintances in the animal world.

It was there that I came for the first time upon the white hawk of Kamchatka. It is an imposing-looking bird. It is entirely white in colouring, and is of the size of a goshawk. I remember well the occasion when I saw him first. It was a rainy October morning. I was wandering on the tundra. A ptarmigan flew up here; a golden plover there. Suddenly I saw a flock of ptarmigans come flying along. They alighted, terrorstricken, in a clump of bushes. Then I perceived a large white bird coming swiftly in pursuit, but he could not follow them into the bushes, so he raised himself again and described some circles in the air while keeping his eye on his prey. Presently he gave up the chase and steered his course in my direction. I crept into a bush. He kept on making direct for me. I fired and he fell. I subsequently saw the white hawk chasing ptarmigan on several other occasions, but he is a rare bird at all times.

A little later I met with an adventure of a curious kind quite near that same spot. It was late in the evening and as dark as is possible where the ground is under snow. I was on my way home after a long day of it, and very tired. I was in a grove of small trees, walking along pensively with my gun slung behind me. Suddenly I all but stumbled against a large animal, which rose up from the ground, emitting a kind of bellow, and nearly frightened the life out of me, I was so unprepared for it. I withdrew quickly a few steps, raised my gun and discharged its contents—namely, two cartridges of bird-shot——at the beast without knowing what it could be. There was a flash in the darkness and the animal remained quiet. With two new cartridges in my gun I approached it cautiously. A big black object became visible in the snow, but it remained motionless when I came within three yards of it. I lit a match in order to see it better. To my astonishment it was a big seal.

The mystery was to be thus explained. The great Lake Nerpitche Osero is connected with the sea by a stream about seven miles long, and seals often swim up this river to the lake, hence its name, which means the Seals’ Lake. But it sometimes happens that the stream is frozen while there still remain large openings in the ice on the lake; so the seals remain on there until it also is completely frozen over. Then they are in a fix. They hear the sound of the sea in the distance, and the stretch of land in between is not great, so they are tempted to flounder their way to the coast through the intervening brushwood and over the tundra. It was one of these frozen-out seals that I had come upon. He had got only a short distance on his way and he was not finding his job an easy one.
Animal life, generally speaking, was scarce in these

tundras. Some small red mice managed to keep alive under the snow. Occasionally they would come up on the surface, where they would sometimes lose track of their hole and go wandering about, an easy prey for the snowy owl or the gyrfalcon—both of which birds, together with the white hawk, hold sway over the tundras, the former at night, both the latter by day. The first specimen of this stately-looking white gyrfalcon I shot was on the mast-top of the wrecked schooner.

Some ravens used to come flying every day along the coast and the river banks, keenly on the alert for any food that might offer. Sea-gulls, northern divers and solitary ducks were also among the regular frequenters of the region, but apart from these one might wander all over it without seeing anything.

We remained on in our summer house the whole of October and part of November, but soon the weather conditions became too severe. When one woke in the morning one had to begin by shovelling out the snow from the room and breaking the ice in our water-pails. At last we succeeded in getting somewhat more habitable quarters in the Japanese Radio Station, in which two rooms were unoccupied. These also were intended for summer use, and there was a fireplace in only one of them.

Here we had as neighbours four Japanese wireless operators and their servants. Among the former, Masahiko Koike became our special friend. In addition there lived in the same house a Russian, named Arcadi Michailovitch, and his wife. He was in every way a s8 Our Enforced Wintering in typical Russian with a singularly varied past—police, gold-digging, trading in skins, doctoring.

In the Russian village on the other side of the river lived our most distinguished acquaintances, a Norwegian named Hansen and his young Russian wife, as well as another Russian, named N. P. Sokolnikoff, at one time Governor of Chukchee peninsula and the region of Anadyr, and later of the Commander Islands. Now the Bolsheviks had deprived him of his post. He was the most cultured and sympathetic Russian that I made acquaintance with during the entire expedition. Hansen, also, was a very nice man and showed us much friendliness. He had earned enough to retire on as a business man but had lost all his money—having placed it in Russian banks.

One day in November a wireless official came rushing in to us breathlessly to announce that signals of distress had just been received to the following effect : “*S.0.S.—Jana helpless, rudder lost.” The scene of the wreck was also named, and we noted that it was on one of the northern Curile Islands where typhoons are at their worst. Long afterwards we heard that the vessel had drifted about rudderless for eleven days, until an American steamer came along and took her in tow. ‘‘ That is what the captain got for playing you false!” the Japanese added.
One day soon after this we had our first sight of a dog-sledge. This was a great sensation and we all rushed out to look at it. But we were too late—it had sped past like an arrow.

Ust-Kamchatsk, from the standpoint of climate, is a dreadful place—like Cape Lopatka and the whole of the western coast. From October to April there are almost daily snowstorms—Kamchatka’s dreaded purga. Sometimes the snow comes down in such dense masses that you cannot see more than a yard in front of you, and the storm is so violent that you cannot breathe when facing it, or hold yourself upright. Sometimes the snow is extraordinarily fine and then it works its way in everywhere, sometimes it feels like sharp needles so that one cannot keep one’s eyes open. Usually the temperature during a snowstorm is not very low, but the wet purga is almost worse, when the temperature stands at about freezing-point. Luckily this does not occur often. Woe to the man who ventures far afield from human habitation during a wet purga. All his clothes are drenched through with the wet snow—he feels that the damp has penetrated into his very bones, When the snowstorm is over the extreme cold returns, and how icy that is cannot be described.

The snowstorms often prevented us for days together from undertaking any excursions or expeditions. ‘The wireless station became surrounded by such high snowdrifts that the dogs often made their way right up on the roof. At times a whole side of the house would be absolutely snowed up, and much exertion was needed to extricate the doors.

We occupied ourselves all the time with plans to attempt to proceed to Petropavlovsk while winter was on, but as long as we had snowstorms every other day our chances of effecting this were very small. We decided, therefore, to wait until later on in the winter, when the days would be longer and the snowstorms —so we were assured—less frequent.

We kept our first Christmas in Kamchatka all alone. I had to go quite a long way on skis before I succeeded in coming upon the little osier-tree which did duty for a Christmas tree. We decorated it with wool and a number of candles which we managed to get hold of. My wife contrived some Christmas cakes out of the scanty material she had at her command. We were provided with rice for our rice-porridge, but the Swedish Christmas fish had to be replaced by salmon. Anyhow, we succeeded in creating the right Christmas spirit for ourselves. It was a stange experience, however, celebrating Christmas in a Japanese wireless station on the shore of the Behring Sea! Our thoughts flew home, and also to our comrades at Petropavlovsk—the latter were at least able to boast a veritable Christmas tree. Thanks to the courtesy of the Japanese we were able to talk with them by means of the wireless in our house and the cruiser /wami in Avatcha Bay. We wished each other a Happy Christmas from our different extremities of the land, while expressing regret that we could not celebrate it together.

New Year’s Day—which is the great Japanese festivity—was celebrated by a great banquet, at which were present about sixty members of the Japanese colony who were stationed here for the winter. To this most of the Russians in the village were invited, and a great many of them came, all travelling in their dogsledges. The festival consisted mostly in eating and drinking and cheering, and it ended by almost all the celebrants having to crawl or reel out to where their dog-sledges were awaiting them. That there were few if any casualties on the way home was a marvel, and reflected great honour on the dogs!

New Year’s Day over, we began to make preparations for our long journey to Petropavlovsk, which we decided to accomplish on skis. On a dog-sledge, with a team of dogs, we proposed to take all our baggage— a tent, sleeping-sacks, scientific equipment, weapons, provisions, etc. But it was no easy matter to supply ourselves with all the things that were essential for the expedition.

Our skis we had left at Petropavlovsk, so we were obliged to manufacture new ones for ourselves, and we were at a loss at first as to how to get the material. There were no trees anywhere near, the wood of which could serve our purpose. At last I discovered in the wrecked schooner a pair of dilapidated cabin doors, and managed to get out of them several pieces which we could use. Fortunately it was not necessary to have very long bits, as we were going to make skis of the Kamchatka pattern, which seemed most suitable for our needs.

These skis are about two yards long and eight inches wide, and underneath they are covered with sealskin with the hair lying back. They have this advantage over Swedish skis—that they do not slip backwards when going uphill, even if one is not using staffs. They have the further advantage that they do not get clammy in a thaw, and the fact that they do not slip backwards " makes them particularly suitable when one has to push a dog-sledge. They are more effective still when it is a question of making a road for the dogs in loose snow. They are an essential accessory to a dog-sledge and, thanks to their moderate length, they do not take up much room. ‘Thus on a dog-sledge journey they are decidedly superior to Swedish skis. On the other hand, when it is merely a question of getting from one place to another the Swedish skis are certainly more suitable.

With the most primitive tools we now fashioned three pairs of skis. It was not an easy job, especially for me, as I had two pairs to make—one for myself and one for my wife. But when at last we had them ready we felt that the results were quite good. Now, however, came the considerably more troublesome job of making the dog-sledge.

We revisited the wreck of the schooner and carried away with us all the best bits of wood obtainable, with the sanction of the vessel’s owner, who gave us carte blanche. ‘This he could, indeed, afford to do, for after the ice-bombardment the vessel had been undergoing it was almost in splinters and was entirely valueless.

We then borrowed a dog-sledge as a model—for we proposed to keep rigidly to the Kamchatka type. The narta, as it is called, is contrived with wonderful ingenuity. It is a typical woodland sledge, as distinguished from those of the Koryaks or the Lamuts—which are tundra sledges, It is elongated and narrow and very low, and thus well qualified to move swiftly along over untrodden ways through forests. But the most remarkable thing about it is that there is not a single nail or screw in it. Instead, all the joints are fixed together by strips of raw sealskin, and this makes them pliable in every direction. On the two long runners there are on each side four short vertical stanchions, on which the bottom of the sledge and the framework rest. The front bow, which holds together both the runners in front, is constructed so as to push aside bushes and the like, as well as to act as a buffer, diminishing the shock when coming up against trees and other solid objects; the other bow, which connects the first pair of stanchions over the sledge, is simply the sledge’s handle. This is the conveyance which copes with all the winter trafic of Kamchatka, except for the reindeer-sledges of the nomad races.
It took us several days to make the sledge, but the winter days were not of much account in that snowstorin-ridden place.
Then came the most difficult matter of all—the securing of the dogs to draw the sledge. An ordinary team would have cost between fifty and one hundred pounds in Ust-Kamchatsk just then.

A short time previously we had made a very pleasant and valuable acquaintanceship. That was with the Japanese director of one of the big Japanese factories south of the river. His name was Minoru Hatasawa. He often wrote us the most touchingly friendly little letters in a mixture of English, Russian and Japanese, inviting us to his quarters, and he would send his dogsledge—his ‘‘dog-express,” as he called it—to fetch us. We accepted gladly and sometimes paid him visits of several days. We agreed that he was “‘ the world’s nicest and kindest host.” He did not know how kind he was. He would offer us the most delightful preserves, and if we expressed our delight over any one particular kind would immediately present us with a large quantity of it. If we evinced interest in anything in his room, he wanted us immediately to accept it as a gift. He wanted to give us everything he possessed ! At last we became almost afraid to look or point at anything, and we had to go home lest he should bestow the entire factory on us.

I had told him of our decision to try to accomplish the journey to Petropavlovsk on skis. He was alarmed over the project and declared it would be suicidal, especially for ““ Madame.” He did everything he could to dissuade us. We should stay the whole winter in his factory. We should have everything we could want— food, firewood, attendance. He had only to send a wireless message to his chief in Japan and the thing would be settled. He wanted to sit down and compose the telegram then and there. I thanked him heartily for his friendliness but made him see that our resolution was unshakable. I comforted him, however, by saying that we should not start for some weeks. When he saw that it was useless to try to turn us from our purpose he realized that he would be rendering us the ssa *
he Kamchadals keep a few horses and cows.

In the autumn the owners cut a little h which is carrie ay, d home on dog-sleds. KAMCHATKAN PRIEST ON AN OFFICIAL TOUR he sled (pavoska), drawn by fifteen to twenty dogs, is w ell protected from storms by a cover, and require s two drivers, greatest possible service by assisting us in our equipment. He now set himself to searching for dogs for our sledge, and it was not very long before he had got together half-a-dozen, which he presented to us. This
_was a very valuable service indeed. But for it we might not have been able to start at all.

With the greatest difficulty I succeeded in providing Sleeping-sacks, furs, gloves of reindeer-skin, and the various other things necessary for a winter journey in Kamchatka. The collections we had got together during the autumn and winter were packed in boxes and deposited in a warehouse.

Then I telegraphed to our companions that we proposed to start on skis for Petropavlovsk. The evening before our departure Hatasawa mobilized all our Japanese friends, and a deputation of Japanese came to our rooms to make one more final effort to dissuade us from our project. ‘They promised us everything if only we would stay on. Both Hatasawa and Koike had tears in their eyes, and it was moving to note their unselfish sympathy and friendliness. They really believed that we were certain either to perish in a snowstorm, or _be eaten up by wild beasts, or become the victims of wild men. And they were horrified when they heard that we should have to sleep out in the snow. Hatasawa wanted to furnish us with everything that would help to make us comfortable on the journey. Among other things he wanted to give us three camp beds, and he suggested that his carpenter should make us a longlegged table, for use in the deep snow, for our meals.
N the last day of February we packed our () and took farewell of all our friends in

Ust-Kamchatsk. The Japanese believed that we were going straight into the jaws of death, the Russians shook their heads, but some of the Kamchadals who were present thought that we should get through all right. At noon the dogs were harnessed to the sledge, and we put on our skis and started on our journey. We were to make our way over roadless regions without native guides, and to have dealings with natives whose language we should find it hard to understand ; we should have to control a team of dogs with whose ways we were not yet familiar ; above all, we should have to hold out against the icy snowstorms of the Kamchatka winter. While we were making our start, therefore, it was not difficult to understand the general view taken by our friends as to our foolhardiness, but I said to myself that decision and energy ought to yield good results.

Hatasawa was more solicitous than ever during these last moments. If we were attacked by wild men, he urged, I must send a message to him by the swiftest of the dogs, and he would immediately dispatch all his Japanese, strongly armed, to our support.

As we made our course across the frozen river we waved our adieux to our friends. Koike, the wireless operator, signalled to us the message “‘ Bon Voyage!” Our long and enforced wintering in Ust-Kamchatsk was at an end. New experiences and adventures awaited us.

The weather had been bad for a long time all along the coast, but the day on which we started the sun was shining splendidly, and it was not excessively cold. We were to see the last of the sea for a long time. Icebergs gleamed in their whiteness in the distance. Across the frozen river were the tracks of another dog-sledge and. these we followed.

At this point I must beg to introduce to the reader our four-footed travelling companions. There were eight of them altogether, but two of these did not belong to us, and were to be left at a village through which we should be passing—later, however, they came into our possession. As leader of the team we had “‘ Captain,” a dark-hued, serious-looking dog who clearly hailed from some more southerly land than Kamchatka, for he had drooping ears and quite short hair. He resembled a Swedish mastiff. Then we had Griza, an unhappy blend of dachshund and Kamchatka dog, who combined the dachshund’s stubbornness with phenomenal strength—a combination so valuable that it atoned in our eyes afterwards for the shortness of his legs. Next came Sera, an old veteran, who had been badly looked after and was worn out. He was nervous and a bad worker. Paired off with him was Muschika, the finest dog of all, big and powerful, with his whole heart in his task. He never bungled and was always exuberantly willing. Then there was Tommik, a dog of fragile build, with no special characteristics. Number five was an animal of whom we felt ashamed always when we met any other dog-sledge, for he was only half the size of the others and he also had dachshund legs. He always wore a reproachful expression when the harness was put on him, which, indeed, was not so surprising. He was the greediest of all the dogs and gobbled down in an instant all the food we gave him. He got entangled with the harness more than any of the others and caused many stoppages and much bad language. When this happened, and when he had had a touch of the whip for his clumsiness, the leaderdog would almost always go for him and give him a bite or two to teach him better manners, and I would | have to defend him. ‘ Captain ” would not stand any nonsense. Number six was a coal-black, worn-out dog of singularly bad character, who had often changed masters. He was always trying to wriggle away, and worked only when he knew we were watching him. He did not hesitate, moreover, to steal his comrades’ food whenever he had a chance, and whenever he could steal anything out of the sledge he did so unhesitatingly. When one came across him after one of these incidents he would wag his tail and be demonstratively amiable. He always had a bad conscience, and was of the regular criminal type. Had he been human he would have been well known to the police. The dogs
_were harnessed to the sledge in Kamchatka fashion— that is to say, two abreast with one trace in between. Both the trace and the harness are made of undressed sealskin.

We had not intended to journey farther, the first day, than the Russian village of Tjorni Jarr (Black Bank), situated ten miles from Ust-Kamchatsk. For the greater part of the way we travelled over the snowcovered ice of the river. To guide us we had in front of us the Klutchefskaja volcano, to the foot of which we should be coming presently.

The sledge was a trifle too heavy and the dogs were not yet trained to their work, so things did not go very brilliantly the first day, but in the evening we came without mishap to the little village which is inhabited exclusively by staroveri—i.e. ‘‘old believers.” ‘These are Russians belonging to a sect who, in addition to religious opinions at variance with those of the Orthodox religion, have many strange habits. For instance, they never shake hands when greeting people, they never smoke or allow others to smoke in their houses. Although Russians, they never drink tea and they never eat in company with others or out of vessels that others have used. Dogs may not enter their houses. On the other hand, cattle and cats are allowed in, and the first thing I met when I opened the door of one house was a calf, while there were about half-a-dozen cats to be seen in the same house. ‘The village had a very bad reputation. According to report its population comprised a number of notorious malefactors. But of this we had no evidence ourselves, and we were received in a very friendly and hospitable way, and slept excellently on the floor, together with our host and hostess and their children and the calf and the cats. But for our protection we carried our Brownings loaded in our hip-pockets !

No one travelling in Kamchatka, whether he be a native or a foreigner, a European or an Asiatic, need have any fear about not finding night-quarters in a village. Even though he be entirely unknown in the village, he may enter any house, haphazard, and propose to stay there until the morrow, and it is unthinkable that he could meet with a refusal so long as the house be not already full of visitors. But we must remember that visits of this kind do not involve much trouble for the hosts. Every traveller carries his bed with him— i.e. his sleeping-sack. ‘This is constructed in oblong form out of three tanned reindeer-skins sewn together. Sleeping-sacks made out of the skins of mountain sheep are still warmer. Wolf-skins are also used, but they are more expensive; the skins of young bears are also used. The hairy side is put inwards, of course. The reason why reindeer-skins are most used is that they are most easily come by, the nomads having large herds of reindeer. In such sacks you can hope to sleep comfortably even when the temperature is down to seventy degrees of frost. Sleeping-sacks are the most essential item in the traveller’s equipment on a winter’s journey in Kamchatka. Without one you are lost should you encounter a snowstorm, and your progress be barred, and you be obliged to spend the night in the most uninviting place possible.

Were the owner of a house to refuse lodging to a stranger he would create a regular scandal—it would be considered a shocking thing, and there would be talk of it all over the neighbourhood. When a snowstorm breaks out while you are staying in a house, you remain on till it has blown over, even if it should last _a fortnight. You are bidden to the meals and have your sleeping-place on the floor with the people of the house. When you start again on your journey you express your thanks and take farewell. As a rule your hosts will accept no payment. But if you buy any little article, or if you have any piece of work to be done, they know how to charge with a vengeance. The Kamchadals and the Russians often restrict themselves to saying adieu when they leave, even if they have paid a visit of a fortnight. They think it unnecessary to say thanks for anything so much to be taken for granted.

Such is the hospitality of Kamchatka. It is one of the finest characteristics of the people there—indeed, I think I may say their only fine characteristic. The explanation of their boundless hospitality lies in the fact that your host knows that next time it will be he who will be travelling and needing harbourage.
