Of course there is also the humane instinct not to drive away a stranger who comes to you half-frozen in a snowstorm seeking a refuge.

The food offered you in such a home is always the same. For breakfast, dinner and supper you get salmon, either sun-dried or salted or half putrid, and in this case either boiled or fried in bear’s fat. Sometimes it is possible to have fresh fish also in the winter at places where there is a river not ice-bound hard by, or if you are willing to fare out to a distant river for the purpose of getting some. Occasionally you have meat also, although seldom in the winter, unless the village should lie near the abode of the reindeer-breeding natives.

All the Kamchatka natives drink tea, usually the simplest form of brick-tea, which cannot be called exactly palatable even if it does not consist of the sweepings from the tea-shops of Russia and China as is declared by the salesmen of other brands. This tea, which is pressed down into hard cakes of the size of a brick, though much thinner, is the only kind in request by the Kamchadals. It is a very important article of commerce, and from the depots of the merchants it is carried all over the country on dog-sledges, motorboats and canoes. A cake of brick-tea constitutes a unit which is in general use as an item of barter throughout a large section of Kamchatka. Tea is drunk in tremendous quantities. You usually can get bread to soak in it, especially on the eastern side of the country. On the western side you must put up with dried salmon. In the houses of the more prosperous you generally are given sugar with your tea, but the majority of the inhabitants of Kamchatka do not use it or care for it. It is regarded as a luxury.

We took farewell of our hosts next morning and started on our second day’s journey. In return for the hospitality shown us I photographed the family outside the house and promised to send them copies of the photographs later. This was a mistake on my part. News of what I had done spread like wildfire the whole way to Petropavlovsk, and in every village we came to I was beset by natives begging to be photographed with their children and their dogs. My plates and films were very limited in number, and I could not afford to waste any. Apart from the people in whose houses we stayed, only those aspirants were photographed who had done something to earn the privilege —either by collecting some zoological specimens, or furnishing us with some ethnographical material, or supplying us with food for our dogs. A few, indeed, earned it just by their personal appearance. That they were not to receive the photographs for a year did not matter in the least. Time is a thing of no value in these regions, as I have said before. The natives are always accustomed to waiting a year for things they order from a merchant when he has not got them in stock. Should he prove then to have made any mistake about the article ordered, they have to wait for it another year. But that never matters in the least.

The next stage of our journey was to be to the very ancient village of Nischne Kamchatsk, which formerly was the capital of Kamchatka; but now our difficulties were to begin. When we awoke in the morning it was snowing a little and there was a slight breeze, but nothing would induce us to allow ourselves to be held up at this early stage of our travels, and we did not give a moment’s consideration to our host’s kindly advice that we should remain on with them until the snow had ceased. Instead, we started off in the con-. fident hope of reaching Nischne Kamchatsk before the tracks of other dog-sledges should be covered over— for several other sledges had journeyed thither since the last fall of snow. We had not covered more than two miles, however, before the snow began to fall more thickly and the wind to rise. It was obvious that we were in for a snowstorm. The sledge-tracks, which the day before had been clear and distinct, were now invisible under the snow, already a foot deep, and deepening every moment. The dogs panted and worked their hardest, but they were evidently becoming tired out, and continually they showed their desire to stand still and rest. It was Hedstrém’s turn to drive them—he and I drove on alternate days. Matters improved a bit when my wife and I went ahead on our skis, making tracks for the dogs to follow. Now neither they nor the sledge sank so deep in the snow. But when half the day had gone we had covered only half the way, and the snowstorm was raging with undiminished violence. As already mentioned, we had now no tracks to guide us, but we knew that the village lay on the Kamchatka river, so we followed its course, and, fortunately, we had got away from the region of the depressing marshland and were in the midst of birch-woods—birch-woods of the same gnarled and knotted order as those round Petropavlovsk.
There was no fear of our missing the way, but dark-

ness was coming on and the snowstorm continued. As yet no village was to be heard—in Kamchatka one always hears a village before one sees it. All three of us looked like snow-men. The prospects seemed hope-
_less, and it appeared as though Petropavlovsk would
be a quite unattainable goal. But we were prepared for hardships and set-backs, and we were determined not to lose courage.

So we urged the dogs along, trying the effect alternately of encouraging words and the whip. The former served no purpose: the dogs had not yet become attached to us. The little dachshund bothered us most —it was useless either to be kind to him or to be down on him! |

At last the dogs could continue no more. They just lay down and tried to sleep. We let them rest for a good while, then livened them up a little by giving them each a morsel of fish. Then we drove on again. My wife went first to provide tracks. Hedstrém and I looked to the sledge, shouting and yelling at the dogs. After we had progressed a hundred yards or so we had to give them another rest. It was now almost dark and the snow was deepening every minute, so we had to make a fresh start and proceed another hundred yards The dogs were now up to their shoulders in the snow and we ourselves had to exert all our strength to help shove along the sledge. It was a question whether we should have to spend the night out in the snow or whether we should reach the village in time. When we had almost given up hope we suddenly heard the barking of a dog. We listened as well as we could in the snowstorm and for a while heard nothing more; but our dogs also had heard the sound and that was the important thing. They realized as well as we did that it meant food and rest and companionship, and they began now to exert themselves again more than ever; but without our help they were unable to pull the sledge forward—it was like pulling a snow-plough. Both we and they were thoroughly exhausted when at last we saw the lights of the village. A hundred or so of other sledge-dogs began barking out a welcome to us and, putting out all the energy we had left, we at last reached our destination.

Feeling almost dead with fatigue we sought out the home of an Esthonian named Norrit, and found refuge in his well-built house. Only on a few other subsequent occasions have I enjoyed tea so much as I did that evening. We emptied one glass after another, and I still remember the taste of the delightful wheaten rolls which Mrs Norrit baked in our honour.

Norrit was a big rough fellow who had been a sailor at one time and had sailed round the coasts of Sweden and been shipwrecked outside Helsingborg. He had enjoyed himself thoroughly there and had left behind him a pair of sweethearts. ‘The Swedes had been most hospitable to him and he was anxious now to make returns. He had the opportunity to do so as the snowstorm continued for three days, during which he fed us and our dogs in a fashion beyond criticism,

During our stay in the village we paid a visit to the native Kamchatka priest—an octogenarian who had much to tell us about the old times. The white-haired old man had a gramophone with which to entertain himself, and he told us with satisfaction that he had some Swedish discs. We were a little dubious about this, but sat down to listen, wondering what we should hear. When they began it was as much as we could do not to burst into roars of laughter, for they turned out to be vulgar comic songs. The good old priest listened to them pensively, evidently imagining that they were something very fine. We allowed him to remain under this illusion. A Dane who had been a mechanician in one of the big salmon canneries at Ust-Kamchatsk had given them to the priest.

It was not until the snowstorm had been raging for a couple of days that we were able to see what the village looked like. It was in no respects different from other Kamchatkan villages. It was a conglomeration of grey wooden huts, erected unsymmetrically all round a small hillock. In the centre was the church. To one side, in a group by themselves along the river bank, were the balagans—that is to say, the houses for drying the salmon. The sledge-dogs were chained up everywhere and some long-haired cows and horses wandered about freely.

The church is a survival from the great days of the village and contains a great number of gilded statues and sacred pictures, etc. ‘There was a feast-day during our visit and the priest held a service. It was very curious to see the inhabitants of the village—for the most part only the women and children indeed—all dressed in their furs, standing and listening to the sermon, if so it could be called. The priest, who wore a very showy cape, embroidered in gold and silver, read out some old Russian text from a book with extraordinary haste, stumbling over the words. At intervals, while he took breath, an assistant—the so-called psalomchik—sang some monotonous hymns. Then the priest would start off afresh as rapidly as before. Occasionally he would make a brief halt and sprinkle a little incense over the congregation. Then he would make the sign of the cross and bow down his head. Some of the people would then go down on their knees. After a little more than an hour the service came to an end and the people streamed out of the church and rejoined their dogs, who were waiting outside. There they seemed more in their element. I am convinced that neither the priest himself nor any of his listeners understood anything of what he read. The Kamchadals are nominally Greek Catholics, and it was a Greek Catholic service that we had witnessed. Of the other two local races, the Koryaks and the Lamuts, the former are heathens and the latter also are nominally Greek Catholics, although they retain a good deal of their Shamanism. (The word “‘ Shamanism”’ is explained in the chapters dealing with the Koryaks and Lamuts.)

In the village there lived also some Koreans and, naturally, a couple of Chinamen. The Chinese, wonderful people that they are, seem to thrive equally under the Equator and in the Polar Circle. I have never been to any village of any size in Kamchatka where there was no Chinaman.
NLY on the fourth day was it possible for us (): continue our journey with the village of

Kamaki, twenty-six miles distant, as our goal. Both we ourselves and the dogs were rested. A Korean had gone on ahead of us and had left sledge-tracks which we followed. Between Nischne Kamchatsk and Kamaki flows the great Kamchatka river, here broad and slow, through the low-lying land, there, through a long and narrow pass in a high mountain chain. This reach of the river is swift and does not freeze over until late, and many were those who warned us against traversing it alone. The sides of the mountain rise steep on either bank, and avalanches are apt to come sweeping down them, clearing off heavy trees and overwhelming any dog-sledges that may be passing at the time. We had been hearing all this ad nauseam, and we therefore kept respectfully out in the middle of the river while we made our way through the pass.

About midday we made a halt for tea. The dogs at once formed themselves into a ring and settled down for a sleep, while we got together some wood and lit a warming fire. For our tea water we melted some snow. That is one of the advantages of winter journeys in this

country—you need never give a thought to the question of water wherever you may encamp. The bag in which one keeps the tea, the enamel mugs, the biscuits and the sugar is always at hand, firmly packed on the top of the sledge so as to avoid having to unfasten and fasten when a halt for tea is made. The tea-kettle ({jajnik) always has its own place, hanging at the back of the sledge. I have not mentioned the fact that all the baggage in the sledge is firmly lashed together so that nothing can break loose when the sledge is tilted up, or when it turns a couple of somersaults on a steep incline. This will happen several times a day, but does no harm either to the sledge or to the dogs. As for oneself, one merely gets a snow-bath if one does not jump off in time.

The halt for tea in the middle of the day is one of the pleasantest breaks on one’s journey. After you have drunk two or three big mugfuls of tea, as hot as you can stand it, you feel yourself a new man. Even when you have been frozen to the skin, and utterly worn out, you grow warm and comfortable. Our friendly hostess at our last stopping-place had given us a freshly baked wheaten loaf to take with us. It was now frozen and like a block of ice, and so hard that you could have killed an ox with it. Hedstrém and I, however, were good hands at cutting it up into elegant slices with an axe, and we held the slices in front of the fire, and when ready they tasted just as though they were newly baked—in fact, like hot rolls. If you have room in your sledge you can take with you loaves

baked in November, and they will taste like fresh, newly baked bread until April, when the thaw begins. When darkness began to fall we had got only halfway to Kamaki and the dogs were worn out, so there was nothing for it but to look for a suitable place for putting up our tent. We hunted about and soon found what we wanted. We dug down into the snow with our wooden spades and thought we should reach the ground, but with the help of a ski-stick we discovered that the snow was more than seven feet deep, so, as there was no good continuing, we had to get the tent up on the snow surface—having first cut some stakes to support it. We then set up the tent stove— a small one which we had made ourselves, and which weighed two pounds. It was made in the style of those used by the sable-hunters in these regions during the winter; it was provided with a chimney which could be taken to pieces. ‘This chimney, which could be packed away inside the stove, could be so placed when in use as to extend upwards and stick out through a hole in the roof of the tent. Some twigs were strewn upon the snow inside the tent and on them were placed the sleeping-sacks. As soon as enough wood had been collected for the stove, and the dogs tethered to trees close by, we crept into our large and excellent tent. We then lit a candle and carefully secured a stick cloven at the top, which was fixed into the frozen snow. This improvised candlestick never tumbled over and could — be fixed in any part of the tent. The stove became red-hot and sank deeper and deeper in the snow, until we placed a couple of cross-bars underneath it. Soon we had the inside of the tent as warm as any room, and we took off our overcoats. Outside, the temperature was 5° Fahrenheit. We congratulated ourselves that we had escaped very hard frost the first night.

On the stove, which served also as a cooker, my wife made coffee—good strong coffee, for it was our first encampment on the long journey to Petropavlovsk, and at the same time our first winter encampment. Coffee we regarded always as a drink for great occasions. It was the first time we had used the tent as a winter tent. Previously we had used our Japanese rawsilk tent, but we were afraid that it would not stand up under a snowstorm and therefore we took the Swedish tent with us on this journey.

It was warm and delightful now in our tent, and we could sit about in our ordinary clothes, post up our day-book, etc. Only the canvas covering stood between us and the keen frost outside, but we were quite all right so long as we kept up the fire. When the fire burnt down it was as cold inside the tent as outside.

After some hours it was time to go and feed the dogs. Sledge dogs in Kamchatka are fed only once a day, and that usually in the evening. They must never be fed until at least two hours after their day’s work is done. If they are given food immediately after they have a journey, while they are still tired and out of breath, they gobble it down, indeed, just as greedily as they would do later, but as a rule they throw it up again. They are given the same food all the year round —namely, salmon. It is remarkable that they can thrive on so monotonous a diet. In winter, for the most part, they get nothing at all except salmon and snow—the salmon usually dried or else putrid. In summer they may chance now and then on a rat, or something else, if they happen to be let loose for a while, but that is seldom. While working, every dog gets a whole salmon a day.

We had with us in the sledge fish enough for some days, for one must always be prepared for snowstorms. When I went out to the sledge and the dogs saw me taking out the jwkko/a there was tremendous excitement. They were all as hungry as wolves and they began barking furiously and tugging at their chains. It isa very pleasant task to go and feed them, for more grateful guests cannot be imagined. The usual practice is to take up one’s position in the midst of them and to throw a salmon to each dog. Generally he catches it in the air and devours it in a phenomenally short space of time, bones and all. He leaves absolutely nothing. Should a dog leave any bit of his ration uneaten it means that he is sick. One must, of course, always tether them out of reach of each other or else there would be bloody fights over their food.

After we had finished our meal of coffee and newly baked bread and jukko/a we crept into our sleeping-sacks. As already intimated, this was our first experience of a winter night in such circumstances, and we bade each other good-night not without a certain feeling of curiosity and anxiety as to whether we should wake in the morning feeling frozen or not. We had pitched our tent just where, according to the Kamchadals, there was most danger from avalanches, and we could only hope and trust that we should not be swept away during the night. I need not add that we kept all our clothes on and added thereto any other garments we happened to have handy.

The Fates were kind to us and we woke to life again, although feeling extremely cold. The thermometer inside the tent was at 4° F. One of us got out of the sleeping-sack and lit the stove with the help of the twigs and wood collected the day before, and in twenty minutes we had the tent back to the ordinary warmth of a room, and were able to enjoy some warm tea and the last of the newly baked bread.

Then we packed up all our household utensils and sleeping-sacks, and put the red-hot stove into the snow outside, where the thin sheet-metal cooled down in five minutes; the tent was taken down and rolled up and everything was made fast on the sledge. Then the dogs were harnessed and we put on our skis. When the dogs are in good form and rested they always bark with eagerness when they are led to the sledge. When harnessed they bark and tug with such energy that it is necessary to tether the sledge very securely until all is ready for a start. The dachshund and Sera showed no enthusiasm on this occasion, but the others were all keen when the word to start—Nuké !—was given.

It had snowed a little during the night, but not enough to impede our progress much, so at first we went ahead quite well, but here and there the snow had been blown up into drifts through which it was difficult to get a heavy sledge.

The scenery was wild and beautiful. The lofty mountains on both sides of the river were clad with dwarf birch. A gigantic white-shouldered sea-eagle came flying past and settled on a big tree up on the heights above and studied us. From his lofty perch we must have looked like small ants creeping on the snow.

We had frequently to help the dogs to draw the sledge at the points where the snow had been blown into drives. We took our usual rest for tea in the middle of the day. Towards dusk I descried in the far distance behind us four small black spots which were moving in our direction. With my field-glasses I was able to see that they were dog-sledges. I guessed that they must be bringing along four Japanese officers from the Jwami cruiser, who had journeyed from Petropavlovsk up country to Ust-Kamchatsk and who were now on their return. They were nearing us very rapidly, thanks to their first-class dogs, and in half-an-hour’s time they had overtaken us. The party consisted just of the Japanese officers in question, and their native guides. We had met at Ust-Kamchatsk so we all made a halt. The Japanese were clad in such an abundance of furs that they could move only with the greatest difficulty. They had seen our tracks and had been hoping to come up with us. With Japanese friendliness they expressed their admiration for our bold decision to cross Kamchatka on skis—they had thought we were only joking when they had first heard about it, but now they saw that we were serious. They admired ‘‘ Madame” especially, and declared that a Japanese woman would never face such hardships. As to this, I think they were right, for the Japanese women have little inclination towards sport of any kind, although the younger generation may be taught to take some interest in it.

The Japanese officers courteously invited my wife to go on ahead in one of their sledges, but although she was tired, she declined the invitation. Instead, we transferred a part of our baggage to their sledges and thus lightened the burden for our dogs, and made it possible to drive faster. And so we parted, after agreeing to meet later in the evening at the house of the Kamchadal, Stephan ee which we proposed to invade in force.

At last we got to the end of the pass and out into the wooded region beyond. We now got away for a while also from the river. At this point it describes a great curve, which we avoided by driving through the woodland. Now we had the freshly made tracks of the Japanese to guide us. When we parted from them we guessed that we must be about six miles from Kamaki, but we went on and on, hour after hour, without seeing a sign of the place. The dogs were tired out and wanted to lie down and rest. Things began to look black, in both meanings of the word. Suddenly a light shone out far ahead, and we thought with joy of the tea and warmth awaiting us. But for all our endeavours we seemed to get no nearer the light. It kept shining out continually above the tree-tops. At last, to our boundless disappointment, we discovered that it was a star! At last we had almost decided to sleep out another night, when suddenly the distant bark of a dog rang out. It was already eleven o’clock when we reached our destination, to be welcomed as usual by the barking of all the village dogs.
We made our way to Stephan’s home and found him a friendly and hospitable fellow, and we were bidden both to tea and to a regular meat meal.

The Japanese had just laid themselves down on the floor in one of the rooms to sleep. They all had their revolvers lying under their pillows. As they would be arriving at Petropavlovsk a good deal sooner than we I availed myself of the opportunity to send a letter by them to my comrades.

Kamaki was the first genuine Kamchatkan village we came to, and we remained there for the following day in order to make better acquaintance with it. From the village you have an open view of the great Klutchefskaja volcano, which, now that we had got so much nearer to it, took on an imposing appearance, seeming to dominate the whole landscape. It was clad in snow from top to bottom, and the smoke rising from it stood out against the sky like a stone-pine. The other great sight was the great extinct volcano, Schiveljutch. It abies

has not the same nobility of form as its lofty neighbour, but it stands there in all its uncouth massiveness, a weird-looking monument in lava over a giant’s grave.

I shall not waste many words on the village itself. It was very like Nischne Kamchatsk and the other villages, with badly built huts, balagans, long-haired cows and countless wild dogs. In a village of from fifteen to twenty huts there are, as a rule, from two to three hundred of these dogs. Every male, from about fifteen years of age, has his regular team of ten.

As a rule, most of the male inhabitants of the villages are away sable-hunting in the forests during the winter. Apart from the women and children, only the old men remain at home. They help a little in all kinds of work, but as little as possible, for they are generally very lazy. Often their share in the work is restricted to bringing home wood and hay. The women, on the other hand, cannot indulge in laziness. ‘They cook, fetch water, look after the animals, and, in fact, undertake all the hard work. On them falls all the burden of hospitality. To provide meals in a house which is constantly full of visitors—visitors who may stay a fortnight or more at a stretch—is no fun. And if the visitors are not well looked after the whole of Kamchatka will soon know about it. But it is the proudest boast of a Kamchadal that his house is sought out by visitors. He will often hold forth on the subject in some such words as the following: ‘‘I have visitors without a break all the winter. They lie as thick as salmon on my floor at night, and all round the house there are dogs. I don’t go To Kamaki & Klutchi know why they all come to me. You seldom see any dogs round the other houses.” He knows well enough, of course, that people go to his house because he treats them well and because he has plenty of room. Or he may say: “Ah, yes, I have visitors every day now since I have been back from hunting, and have been able to give them mountain mutton every evening. At Andrej’s they get nothing to eat but fish.”

The Kamchadals really were flattered when we put up in their houses. They took it as a compliment to their larder and housekeeping methods that the “ Expedizia,” as we were always called, should patronize them. And it was a very serious matter if on any occasion we put up first in one house and then on a second visit to the same place went to another, for our first host would be so much put out that one preferred not to meet him. “ What fault can Expedizia have found with me?” he would ask. “I had a fresh bear joint for them and salmon trout and potatoes as a second course, And I fed their dogs well. Why should they go and stay at Gregorij’s? He has only fish to eat as a rule, and there are more black beetles in his house than in mine, I don’t understand what the matter can be.”

It is possible to devise some adequate excuse for changing one’s quarters when one returns to a place, but to change them during one’s first visit is unthinkable. One’s hosts would die of chagrin. We did not often change our quarters, and never without some good reason, But when we were repeatedly given tea with lice and black beetles in it we would begin to talk
To Kamaki & Klutchi gi of a move; so, also, when almost all the occupants of the hut bore on their faces the stamp of syphilis, or when the women were brandy-drinkers.

The dalagans in Kamaki were of a different type from the specimens I had seen before. They belonged to a type which I found to be the most common in the valley of the Kamchatka river, but strongly differentiated from that of the west coast. The noteworthy thing about them is that the warehouses take up only a part of the upper floor, and not the whole building as on the west coast.

From Kamaki to Klutchi, the big village at the foot of the volcano, it was a journey of about forty miles. Naturally we could not accomplish it in a single day with the dogs and baggage we had. The quickest way thither is not by the river—which forms big loops— but over the marshes and through birch-woods. Two small shanties have been constructed between the two villages as refuges in case of snowstorms.

Shanties of this kind, to be met with occasionally between Kamchatkan villages lying far apart, consist sometimes of earth-huts, which, doubtless, are not very unlike the half-underground so-called jurt dwellings in which the natives here used to live in olden times. The name jurt is still given them even when they are regular wooden huts. Before the Russian Revolution, when a Governor and his staff looked after the country, every village had to keep certain of these jurt huts in repair, and at certain points, where they were specially designed as a refuge against snowstorms, to keep them

supplied with firewood and jukkola. Since then, there being no longer any punishment to fear, no one bothers about these huts, although they are just as much needed as before. Some of them have fallen into decay, others have bit by bit been pulled to pieces and used as firewood. A few villages, however, have shown their good sense by looking after some of these huts, and we hoped to find it was so with those on the way to Klutchi.

In radiant sunshine we left Kamaki with three days’ food for the dogs. Our way lay at first over marshes and frozen morasses. ‘Time after time we were plunged into deep snow. Hedstrém and I helped the dogs to draw the sledge along, and my wife went on ahead and made tracks for us to follow. We were much struck by the convenience of the Kamchatkan skis when we had to push the sledge: they never slipped backwards. In the course of the day we met two dog-sledges coming from Klutchi. That was great luck, as it meant that we had good tracks to follow. When sledges meet in this way out in the waste land it is, of course, out of the question to drive past and continue on one’s journey. Anyone who did so would be thought mad. No; both sledges halt and the drivers talk together for awhile. They may have much of interest to say to each other. First of all come the questions, ‘‘ Kuda?” and “ Otkuda?”’ (““ Whither?”’ and ‘“‘Whence?”’), It is out of the question to drive on without knowing the destination of the other sledge—whether its owner is out sable-hunting, whether he has come upon a bear’s lair, whether he is driving somewhere to lay in a store of meal or to buy a gun. The two teams’ dogs always go for each other unless one threatens them with the ironshod brake (oszo/) just at the moment of meeting. While one stops and talks one places one’s sledge far enough away to separate the dogs. Both the men we met were Kamchadals and were rather wild-looking fellows with weather-beaten features and wearing shaggy furs.

Towards evening, when it began to darken, we found ourselves in the midst of a great expanse of marshland. Dark clouds were rising in the sky, and it was time for us to look for a suitable camping-ground. Where we were we could get no wood, so we had to get on a bit. In the distance we descried a dark speck which, examined through field-glasses, was seen to be an alder-grove. Thither we steered our course.

But it was difficult for the dogs to make any progress. The dachshund and Sera put our tempers very much to the proof, as they did on many occasions during this journey. Sera, the old worn-out dog, worked well for at most ten minutes each time he got a stroke of the whip, then he began to shirk again, but so artfully that it was not always easy to detect it. He was sly enough to move along with his bit of the trace quite taut and yet not pulling any harder than was necessary to keep it so. And not merely that! He was so clever an actor that he would lean over on one side as a dog does when. he is working really hard. But when we called a halt, and all the other dogs were out of breath and panting, with their tongues hanging out, he would be breathing as easily as after an ordinary walk. About the dachshund the less said the better! We made up our minds to shoot both animals as soon as we got to Klutchi and to get a better pair in their place. They had entirely exhausted our patience, and my wife declared that she would never have believed I could use so many bad words as I did every day I was driving those dogs. I can only take comfort in the reflection that it has remained until this day undecided which excelled in this direction, Hedstrém or I.

In the alder-grove we went through the same operations as in the mountain-pass and spent the night there. We awoke, however, to the discovery that there had been a fall of more than a foot of snow, which did away with all hope of reaching Klutchi that evening. When I went out of the tent there was no sign of the dogs. They had all disappeared; but I knew where they were, and when I called to them up they popped all right and began shaking their coats free of the snow. The dogs always dig themselves a hole before they lie down to sleep. Not a great fall of snow, therefore, is needed to cover them completely. They find it nice and warm in their snowy bed, in which they are protected from the icy winds.

Soon we had everything stowed away on the sledge and we put on our skis, but the dogs had a hard job of it to make any headway in the deep snow. It was Hedstrém’s turn to drive. The reader may perhaps imagine that the driver’s task was the easiest. On the contrary, the driver had more work to do than the others. He could never sit in the sledge, which was already too heavily weighted; he had always to be shoving it now this way, now that, and he had always to be on the alert to prevent it from overturning, besides having to keep the dogs in hand and up to their mettle, shouting himself hoarse all the while. There are few things so trying to the temper as driving a sledge with unsatisfactory dogs. Well, we had quite made up our minds to get a good pair of dogs at Klutchi. The excellent Hatasawa had done his best for us, but he had been thoroughly swindled by his Russian acquaintances. Indeed, the purchasing of good sledge-dogs is one of the most difficult jobs a man can undertake. If you buy them one by one you are almost certain to be deceived. Naturally you have palmed off on you the worst specimens the vendor has to dispose of. On the other hand, if you buy a whole team together, there is always some prospect of your getting a good many satisfactory dogs. No sledgedriver can afford to work with a bad team of dogs, and if he sells a whole team at once he cannot hope to swindle the purchaser with the whole lot.

The country we passed through consisted mostly of marshes, alternating with small groves of alders and willows. Suddenly the silence was broken by a sound which one might have least expected to hear in such a region—the cry of a swan, a hooper. It came from up above. Soon I could make out a flock of eight descending on the marsh. That they did not alight on snow I was certain, so evidently there was some open water there. I made my way on skis to the spot and found an open arm of the Kamchatka river. On it were at least fifty swans. It was really strange to see these white birds in the snowy landscape. They looked very well with the snow all round them. When they noticed me their necks grew as stiff as sticks, and they went swimming this way and that. I drew still nearer to them and one by one they began to rise from the — water, whipping the surface for a long time with their wings before they succeeded in raising their heavy bodies. At last all but the boldest of them were in full flight. The latter swam away. There is a tremendous commotion when about fifty swans fly up like that. They kept flying round and round over the marsh and the river with long beats of their wings, and eventually sank down again on the water, a mile or so farther on.

But swans were not the only frequenters of the river. There were golden-eyes and mallards. These birds, as well as one other, the small, red-breasted merganser, winter in Kamchatka in open rivers of this kind. They do not mind the bitter cold and they spend the whole winter here. The fact that the water does not freeze is to be explained by the warm springs which rise from below into the river. The river does not freeze here even when the temperature is 80° F.
Two eagles were perched on a couple of immense poplars near the river, and a snowy owl floated away from the spot. They have their good reasons for haunting rivers of this kind.

My wife and Hedstrom by now had got some distance away, for I had told them not to wait for me. I used often to go on such small expeditions by myself when there was something interesting to see and when my help was not needed. Soon, however, I caught them up. We had decided to make our halt for tea as soon as we should have got to the end of the marsh, (on which there was no fuel of any kind. The wood ‘was always in sight on the horizon, but the marsh proved to be, as always, more extensive than one imagined. It was not until the afternoon that we reached the longed-for wood. Woods are often the saving of travellers in Kamchatka. Once you have got to a wood you have won half the battle. In a snowstorm woods are always a refuge. The strength of the storm is broken by them and the frost is never so keen within them. And, above all, they make it possible for you to light a warming fire.

We had only just reached the outskirts of the wood when we came upon a little open stream, by the bank of which we made our halt for tea. It was pleasant to have our tea water at once, for a change, and not to have to melt the snow for it.

When we set out again, the dogs were in better fettle than usual. Even the dachshund and Sera, the two unhanged rascals, took it into their heads to pull properly. We almost dared to hope that they had decided to start a new life of work and performance of their duty, and assuredly it was time they did. But that was to be over-sanguine. ‘The reason for their behaviour was quite different. They had scented
comrades and putrid salmon close at hand. After a ten-minutes’ advance through the wood we heard quite unexpectedly the barking of dogs, and we came upon a little wooden hut.

Out of it stepped a weather-beaten old fellow wearing boots of reindeer hide and with his head encased in a shaggy cap of fox-skin. It was the old hunter, Vasilij, who had lived more than twenty winters in that jurta. He is known throughout the valley of the Kamchatka river as the cleverest hunter of foxes in the country. He has specialized in foxes and never goes after sable. He spends the entire winter in this jurta, which is particularly well-placed for his purposes, for it stands right in the midst of a system of open rivers and canals on which ducks and swans are plentiful. Reynard spends his winters in this region stalking these birds. But old Vasilij beats Reynard at his own game. The old man’s eyes are as knowing as any fox’s, but with a glint of humour and kindliness in them. We became good friends at once. It was very pleasant and cosy inside his little cottage, and the tea-kettle was boiling on a stove, which was precisely like our own but a little bigger. It was delightful to be sitting in a warm room, and the old man seemed glad to have us there. Apparently he always had tea ready for chance visitors and a welcome for everyone. The circumstance that we had just been having tea did not prevent each of us from emptying a couple more of big mugfuls. In Kamchatka you can drink as much tea as you like. If you enter a cottage for some purpose, even for a moment, and make as if to leave at once, the owner will exclaim: “ Bess tjaj nilsja !”’ (‘ Impossible without having tea!”’) The tea-kettle makes its way on to the fire almost automatically as soon as you open the door, if it does not. happen to be on the fire already.

Well, there we sat tea-drinking and talking with our old host. (By the way, I ought to mention that it is the thing in Kamchatka to drink tea as hot as possible. Kamchatkan people are phenomenal in this respect.) After we had chatted with him for a time he began to wonder what race we belonged to. He could tell by our Russian that we were not Russians. Were we Americans, he asked. When he heard that we were not, he remarked, half to himself, as it were, that we were not Chinese or Japanese or Koreans. He wanted to set us down as Tartars—and he did not mean this to be as uncomplimentary as it sounds—and with this effort he had exhausted his range of knowledge of the races of the world.

When I told him that we came from a country called Sweden, he did not show much interest until I went on to say that we had foxes there also. Then he became all attention and curiosity, and I was led on into a detailed account of Reynard’s life at home with us and of our modes of hunting him. When I mentioned that I myself had actually shot foxes I rose considerably in his estimation, and this set him telling us about his own methods. He never shot foxes, he told us, but always trapped them. So as to avoid leaving any tracks in the snow when setting his traps he always used his canoe, which was constructed out of a hollowedout poplar trunk, and paddled around the adjoining branches of the river, setting his traps along their banks at the points to which the foxes make when after the birds. He even let us into a lot of his secret dodges for blinding the eyes of Master Reynard to his wiles. By the time he had finished I was congratulating myself that I was not a fox in that particular neighbourhood. The old hunter had two young sons, and while we were sitting there they came in carrying a couple of hares. They had just been out clearing traps, but, like their father, they devoted themselves to fox-trapping in the main.

We decided to stay on in the old man’s cottage until the following day, and it was a fortunate decision, for very soon after dark we heard the sounds—sounds grown very familiar to us—of a coming snowstorm.

Later in the evening I succeeded in enriching my collection with about ten small rodents and four shrewmice. When I placed them in their spirit-bottles, old Vasilij could not keep back his feeling of disapproval at the misuse to which I was putting good liquor.

‘When the time came for sleep we all lay down on the floor, and the stove was crammed full with wood. Before the old man spread out his sleeping-sack he went through some form of devotions before a little ikon high up in the corner of the room, making the sign of the Cross repeatedly, bending his head and repeating a number of unintelligible words. I was awakened several times in the night by shrew-mice
running over my face. They are very much more sympathetic things, however, than bugs, which sometimes—though not so often as might be supposed— disturbed our slumbers elsewhere.

In the morning the weather proved to be as comfortless as ever. If one put one’s face outside the door of the hut one received a veritable slap from the raging wind. But before midday it improved, and I had just got ready to go on a little hunting trip in Vasilij’s canoe, with his two sons to paddle me, when suddenly all the dogs began to bark and three dog-sledges came rushing along towards the hut from the same direction from which we ourselves had come. The occupants were a couple of Chinamen and a Tartar, three luckless wights who looked in a most pitiful condition. They were from Ust-Kamchatsk and had left Kamaki the previous morning, and hoped to reach the hut that evening, but the snowstorm had overtaken them in the middle of the marshland, and they had missed their way and found themselves snowbound. ‘The worst of the matter for them was that they had no sleepingsacks. They had a tent, but they had not been able to put it up owing to the wind, and they had had to spend the night lying in a heap on the snow with the tent spread out over them and with their sledges as a screen against the storm. It was a wonder that they had not been frozen to death. As things were there was not much life in the two Chinamen. They seemed chilled to the bone and they had grown so hoarse that they could hardly utter a word. We looked after their dogs and they themselves made straight for the stove, where the tea-kettle came in very handy. They soon revived after drinking several mugfuls of boiling hot tea, and as soon as I had satisfied myself that they were out of danger I set out on my hunting expedition with the two boys.

With expert hands they paddled the long, narrow canoe noiselessly along the winding crystal-clear streams and arms of the river. From the water one realized better how tremendous was the mantle of snow which covered the ground. It was more than two yards deep and it bent forward in the softest outlines over the winding canals. When the river made a bend we would come suddenly upon a few merganser, which would fly up screeching, and I brought down some with my gun. In the course of a few hours we glided soundlessly into the main stream. We started the songs again, and the eagles flew away from the tree-tops.

We were a very tight fit in the little hut that evening, I can tell you! There were nine of us in all, but although we represented four different races, we got on very well together. While we were eating our supper, which consisted of dried bear’s-flesh and jukkola, the two Chinamen told us all about their previous misadventures while in Kamchatka, how on one occasion, for instance, when overtaken by a snowstorm, they had to kill and eat some of their own dogs. They laughed like children now over the recollection, displaying all their thirty-two teeth as they did so. The Chinese are a unique race. They go all over the world and are always happy so long as they can work. I admire and esteem them. The night we spent lying as closely packed together as sardines in a box.

Next morning the weather was beautiful. It was still bitterly cold, indeed, but the sky was blue and there was no wind. That was all one could desire. We were all agreed that we ought to make a start after our morning tea. It was about twelve miles to Klutchi from the hut and the whole way lay through forestland. We who were travelling on skis could not think, naturally, of keeping up with the Chinese and the Tartar ; but we had the tracks of their thirty dogs to follow, and I rejoiced over this, for otherwise we should have had to plough a new road for ourselves through the deep snow.

In among the woods we made a new bird ac- _ quaintance. This was the hawk-owl (Surnia ulula). I heard his mating-cry from several directions in the woods, and we succeeded in adding two specimens of them to our collections. A little woodpecker of the smallest species (Dryobates minor immaculatus), notably whiter than the ordinary little woodpecker, and peculiar to Kamchatka, was secured also, to keep the owls company on the long journey to the Natural History Museum in Stockholm.

Among the birch-trees we saw for the first time single larches (Larix dahurica), a foretaste of the dense larch-woods we were later to reach. Here we came upon small nuthatches (Sita europea albifrons), and a splendid capercailzie (Tetrao parvirostris kamchaticus)

clattered off with a great noise. All the dogs wanted to be after him, forgetting altogether their duty as beasts of burden. Fortunately, the sledge collided with a tree and turned over. There were other occasions we had mishaps through the dogs sighting some quarry. If, out on the open marshland, they suddenly espied a hare at a moment when I was away from the sledge, looking after something, off they would tear with the sledge behind them, deaf to all shouts. Our pursuit would sometimes continue until they had become a mere speck in the dim distance, and then we could only hope that the sledge would turn over. Occasionally, but very seldom, they will return with the sledge after a lapse of this kind, but when one has to walk a long distance after them, clad in one’s heavy furs, it is no joke.
We boiled our tea-kettle on the still glowing embers of the fires lit by the Chinese.

Here and there from the woods we caught glimpses of Klutchefskaja, which had been hidden from us during the previous days by the falling snow and the clouds. It raised itself now to an incredible height. The smoke rose from it quite vertically.

Later on in the day we met a Kamchadal who came driving along in an empty sledge. He was out to get wood; therefore we guessed we must be near the village. And so we were—we soon began to hear it. Now that we knew we could count on getting there, we decided definitively to dispatch our two worst dogs to happier hunting-grounds. They had not earned

their feed since we had left Ust-Kamchatsk; they had, indeed, retarded rather than helped our progress. Hedstrém unharnessed them and I drove the other dogs on. Some minutes later, two revolver-shots rang out in the air; and both animals sank dead in the deep snow. Sera was a genuine Kamchatka sledge-dog and had worn himself out in harness. The dachshund was a square peg ina round hole. Peace to their memory !

It was not long before we began to see the houses in the village. We were to put up with a Russian named Griboff. His house was one of the first in the village and we were very cordially welcomed there. We were treated to coffee instead of tea, and freshly baked loaves instead of dried salmon to soak in it. His wife had undertaken a lot of extra baking in our honour, for our arrival had been awaited some days.

When we had finished our coffee we hastened out to look at the world’s greatest volcanic cone through our field-glasses. It lies surrounded by a row of mountain heights and volcanoes, each of them imposing in itself, though sinking into insignificance beside Klutchefskaja. I shall not attempt to describe its beauty. I can give only a faint impression of it. When once you have seen it from Klutchi, bathed in sunshine in all its snow-white loveliness, you can never forget the picture as long as you live.

We decided to stay several days in Klutchi. Hedstrém had several birds to prepare and I had a lot of preparations to make for the summer, for we proposed to have our headquarters here during a portion of it.

Klutchi is one of Kamchatka’s largest villages. It has about five hundred inhabitants, most of them mixed specimens of Kamchadals, but some Russians, Chinese and Koreans also among them. Some Tartars and Aleuts live there too. It has quite a large church, and it is beautifully situated at the foot of the volcano. The Kamchatka river remains unfrozen outside the village all the year round, so that you can fish all through the winter.

Klutchi is the most important business centre in the interior of the country. It is the seat of the Kamchatkan fur trade, and several fur-trading firms have their depots here. ‘The biggest of them are the Hudson Bay Company and the Olaf Swenson Company—the latter is the concern of a Swedish American of that name. His name is known and esteemed in every dwelling throughout the entire peninsula. Every spring Swenson comes over from Seattle with his steamer, which is laden with everything imaginable that Kamchatka can stand in need of. Part of the steamer constitutes a veritable emporium in which you can buy anything, and when the natives go on board they are tempted to buy everything they see—as long as their furs hold out. Furs—sable, fox, otter, bear, etc.—are valued by Swenson and then the hunters begin purchasing as in a regular shop. They have a great tendency to go beyond their means when they see all the fine things which Swenson has brought over from America, and which are not confined to guns, cartridges and traps. In this great floating store you can buy everything from a motor-boat to a sewing needle, from chewinggum to mowing-machines. Chewing-gum is a thing in great request in Kamchatka. Any customer with any credit at all is trusted to an astonishing extent. They are very apt to sell their bear’s skin before they have shot their bear !

In this way Swenson goes from place to place round the coast. News of his coming spreads swiftly in advance. In the bigger places—like Ust-Kamchatsk —he unloads large portions of his cargo, which are distributed among his local agents and sold by them for furs. When in this very honourable way he has skinned Kamchatka, he proceeds on to Anadyr and the Chukchee peninsula. Should time permit, he swings over to the Arctic coast and returns in the late autumn to Seattle, with his American goods replaced by furs to the value of millions of dollars. Throughout his whole journey he keeps himself posted up as to the fluctuating prices on the world’s fur markets by means of his own wireless.

Returning after this little digression to Klutchi, let us look at the motor-boat which brings Swenson’s goods to the village. It lies enveloped in snow, side by side with another motor-boat, a rival concern, but our host, who is machinist on one of them, says that both are equipped with Swedish motors. In this connexion I may add that the motor-boats used by the great canning factories at Ust-Kamchatsk are to a great extent provided with Swedish motors.

In so large a village as Klutchi there is always much going on. Dog-sledges come and go in all directions. Here a trader is starting out on a long journey with a sledge full of wares, there a Kamchadal is returning home with a supply of firewood from the forest, or with a big load of hay drawn by ten dogs. Hunters are to be seen on their way back from expeditions after bears or mountain sheep with their sledges full of meat and of hides. On the walls of the houses huge bear hides are hung out to dry.

While paying a visit to a Russian family in the village I came upon one more proof that the world is smaller than is generally believed. I was sitting and idly turning over the leaves of a photograph album, when suddenly, to my amazement, I came upon a portrait of one of my oldest friends—a Stockholm schoolfellow. The explanation of its being there was that the lady of the house came from Finland and was a relative of his.

In the foregoing pages I have been careful to avoid talking about politics as I feel that politics are an evil out of place in Kamchatka. But here in Klutchi, as in all the other big villages, the Russians have given to the time-honoured village council, with its elders, the title, ‘* The Klutchi Revolutionary Committee ”’ ; whilst forcing the Kamchadals, who do not even know what a revolution means, to hoist red flags over their huts. The day after our arrival in the village was a feast-day and the red flags were flying. They flamed out strikingly against the background of the great snow-white volcano.

During our stay in Klutchi I added to my collections a curious blue hawk. But we also acquired a new companion of a quite unusual kind. The day before we left the place some Kamchadals had returned from a bearhunting expedition. They had shot a huge brown shebear and had found in its lair two tiny bear-cubs, which they took home with them. One of them had frozen to death on the way, but the other still lived. A Chinaman, who scented an opportunity of earning some extra payment, came and reported this to us, declaring himself to be the agent of the bear-hunter. I bought the jolly little animal, who was still a little unsteady on his legs. No wonder, since he had arrived only that very day from his native wilds, travelling on a sledge. He was still so small that he only drank milk. He learnt at once how to drink out of a bottle. I decided to try to take him with me alive to Petropavlovsk, and I prepared a little reindeer-sack into which he was put, despite his forcibly-expressed protests. When I asked the Kamchadals who were looking on whether they believed he would get on all right during a whole month’s journey in these uncomfortable conditions they answered in chorus, “‘ Yes,” in the most convincing manner. And, indeed, he proved himself to be the most unkillable little beast you could possibly imagine.
N Klutchi, as in all the other villages which we | Fe most of the men were sable-hunters.
Before I proceed to deal with our journey from Klutchi to Petropavlovsk perhaps I may tell something” about the way in which sable-hunting is carried on.
The Kamchadals depend mainly for their livelihood on hunting and fishing. Of late cattle-farming has in some measure become of importance.

The hunting includes sable, bears, foxes, otters, ermine, as well as wild reindeer and mountain sheep. Marmots and hares are hunted also, but more as a sport. Wolves and wolverines are hunted when they are met with.

Of all these animals the sable is the most important. The bear comes next. Sable and salmon are Kamchatka’s alpha and omega. But for them the country would be inhabited only by the nomad races which live by keeping the reindeer. It is the sable and the salmon that have attracted so many Russians and people of other nationalities to Kamchatka and that have reconciled them to its inhospitable climate. It is the sable that brought hither Swenson’s steamer and those of the other dealers in furs, and it is for the sake of the sable

hat the motor-boats tug the barges, laden with all cinds of goods, up the Kamchatka river. _It is a wonderful thing to think that an entire ountry’s economic life should depend upon this little animal, whose fur is an article de luxe. Throughout he winter there is talk of nothing in Kamchatka but the sable. Innumerable small traders travel about the country in their dog-sledges in every direction, with supplies of the most incongruous articles—gramophones, pocket-mirrors, ladies’ high-heeled shoes, tobacco, spirits, sweets, sugar, chewing-gum and clothes. Sometimes they are so numerous that every house in one of the smaller villages will harbour one. A large percentage of them are Chinese, who thrive in all business matters and who succeed in securing a great many skins from the hunters. A great number of these small traders are agents for the big companies, but many of them are “ out on their own.”

The sable may be said to be the financial unit of Kamchatka. All business is transacted in furs—the only orm of currency known to the natives. At first it used o sound quite comical to me when the Kamchadals sked how many sables our guns and field-glasses cost, ut later I became so used to this that I never gave it a hought. Once I was looking on while one Kamchadal ought a canoe from another. He paid a sable-skin and ot a fox-skin back in change. Ina school in one village, the payment for a year’s education for a boy was one able-skin and that for a girl one fox-skin. Practically Il the business is done thus in skins.

It may be interesting, therefore, to note how the Kamchadals get their money—that is to say, the valuable skins which afterwards are sent all over thewo eventually to appear in the drawing-rooms of the ~~ monde in the great capitals.

I shall begin with the most valuable of all, the ahi. It belongs to the family of the marten and is of about the same size as the ordinary marten, and is to be found both in pine-woods and in birch-woods. The Kamchadals hunt the sable from the late autumn—that is to say, after the first snowfalls in October—down to some time in March. The autumn hunting, which takes place before the fall of heavy snow, is done with horses —at least in the valley of the Kamchatka river. The hunters set out equipped with everything they need— guns, skis, tent, food, traps, etc.—strapped on to the back of the one horse, who has to carry the hunter too!. A Kamchadal thinks nothing of putting as much as a hundredweight and a half, in addition to himself, on the back of his horse, which is not much stronger than an Iceland pony. He takes one or two sable-hounds. He makes for a region always several days’ journey— sometimes a week’s or a fortnight’s journey—from the village. On arrival, he puts up his tent in a suitable place, unless he has a little hut there already made of earth, or prefers to put one up quickly. The hunting party consists always of at least two persons, often of several. The results of the hunting are equally divided, no matter who may catch most. ‘Thus, if you ask the. question, ‘‘ Flow many sables have you caught this

After a stay of about a month in the woods the snow becomes so deep that the horses can move in it only with difficulty, so the hunter returns to his village to enjoy a spree on the strength of the sables already caught, and in order to equip himself for the regular winter’s hunting, for which he sets out on a dog-sledge. As a rule, he will take a week or two for this. When at last he makes a fresh start, his sledge is heavily laden with jukkola for himself and his dogs, over and above all the other things needed. Throughout the winter jukkola and tea are the hunter’s principal food and drink. When he returns to his tent or hut—the exact situation of which he often tries to keep secret from the other hunters of his village—he settles down in it for a long stay. The little stove is installed in its place, the dogs are chained to the neighbouring trees, the jukkola is put away in a hastily constructed store-place where the dogs shall not be able to get at it if they should happen to get loose. And now he is ready to begin his hunting, which he sets about in this fashion.

He puts on his sealskin-covered skis—a blend of skis and snowshoes—having first donned his reindeer boots. His kamlejka (a sort of warm overall) is drawn on over his other clothes, he slings his gun over his iishoulders, attached by a sealskin strap, and he carries a wooden spade with a long shaft in his hand. He has ! some sable traps with him and some bits of hare-flesh to bait them with. Now he unleashes one or two of the

dogs, and they bark wildly with delight. They are not ordinary sledge-dogs—although they can sometimes be used as such—they are specially trained sable-hounds. The best of them are of the Lamut race. They have a harness put on them exactly like that put on the sledgedogs, and a curiously shaped long case made of sealskin, with a number of small sticks protruding out from it, is attached by a strap to the harness. This case contains the sable-net.

The two hunters set out very early in the morning, as soon as it is light. The sable is a nocturnal animal and has finished his night’s chase of hares, rats and birds. The first thing to do is to find his tracks. Sometimes the hunters may go for days together without coming upon them, but with luck the sable’s large, foxlike footprints may be discovered quite soon. Then the dogs become tremendously excited. Hitherto they have had to drag along the sable-net: now they are set free from it and disappear with a whisk of their tails in search of the sable. The hunters, after standing and speculating as to where the sable can have gone to, hasten after the dogs.

Suddenly the dogs will set up a violent barking in the distance. The hunters listen a moment, then make straight in the direction of the sound. They find the dogs scraping away and still barking furiously in the neighbourhood of some old tree which has been blown to the ground. They are wagging their tails unceas- | ingly, which means that they are working con amore. The case containing the sable-net is unlaced and the net is taken out. The short sticks which have been brought along with it are fixed in the snow at a short distance all round the tree, and in a moment this is encircled by the net, which is a little more than a yard wn depth.

One of the hunters now gets his gun ready while the other, with the dogs beside him, begins digging in the snow with his wooden spade. Now and again he will hit with his spade against the tree-trunk. Suddenly the sable will dart out, and with two long bounds he is off, with the dogs after him; but the daylight dazzles his eyes, he does not see the net and dashes right into it, and the dogs have him. If they were ordinary sledge-dogs they would tear off with their booty and devour it, but these dogs are trained to kill it only, and to drop it as soon as they have performed their duty.
The net is now taken up again and the hunters set out in search of fresh tracks, unless it be too late in the day.

But things do not often happen quite so conveniently as this. ‘The sable is no ordinary prize—if it were, its coat would not be worth anything from twenty-five to fifty pounds, according to its quality. Often one may dig and dig all day without any result. When evening comes the hunters leave behind them one dog, which remains on the watch all night. If the hunter has luck the dog may, in the middle of the night, make his way to the tent—many miles off, perhaps—with the sable in his mouth. But often the hunter discovers a hole in
the snow through which the sable has slipped out, then clambered up a tree and disappeared.

When the sable has taken up its position in a hollow standing tree, as often happens, the hunter’s task, of course, is to get him out of it, so as to have a shot at him. He keeps hitting the trunk of the tree with his axe, and sometimes the little animal will make a bolt for it. At other times, however, the sable will sit tight. Then the hunter proceeds to extremes. He sets fire to the tree. When the smoke becomes too dense inside it the luckless sable has to make a move. The hunter is sitting hard by with his gun ready, and the moment the sable shows himself a shot rings out.

When the hunter comes upon tracks which he cannot follow up he sets some traps of the same type as common fox-traps, but considerably smaller. As a bait bits of hare or of capercailzie serve very well. To set these sable-traps effectively is an art not to be learnt in a moment, it needs a thorough knowledge of the little animals’ habits—but many of these Kamchatkan hunters are past-masters at it.
The above is the usual way of hunting sables: but very often the hunter has no sable-hound and has to do all the work himself—this applies especially to the Russian sable-hunters.

It is possible also to catch sables by means of snares instead of traps. The snares have to be laid in the late autumn before the rivulets are frozen over. A tree is cut down and the trunk is laid across the stream as a bridge. The snare is so constructed that the sable gets
Sable-Hunting Bi caught in it when he attempts to get over from one side to the other. He wriggles about with the snare wound about his neck, tumbles into, the water, and is drowned.

_ Before the Kamchatkan hunters learned the use of steel traps they made use of a primitive kind of trap of their own contrivance. They fixed a heavy stick in such a position that, when the sable touched the bait underneath, he disturbed it and it came down on him and killed him. This method is now forbidden, but it is still used.
A sable-hunter who is diligent, and who keeps at it most of the winter, will secure from five to fifteen animals in the course of the season if he be efficient and have any luck.

At Christmas all the hunters return home to indulge in festivities. Often the first sable is turned into spirits. It is felt that they would not be keeping Christmas properly without that—often, indeed, it is not the first sable only that is thus disposed of. After some weeks have been thus spent at home the hunters get back to their task.

When they return again at the close of the winter they have nearly always other booty with them in addition to the sable. Usually they have killed some foxes, which are generally taken in traps. Most of these are of the red kind, but they include the black and silver and the cross-marked. In the northern regions of the country one meets the white polar fox. Blue foxes are not found on the Kamchatkan peninsula itself, but they are numerous on Copper Island and Behring Island off the eastern coast.
Almost always the hunter will have killed some otters. They frequent practically all the rivers of Kamchatka and they are caught in traps.
The ermine is also trapped, while hares are usually caught in snares laid close by the camping-places. The latter are very numerous as a rule, and leave regular paths behind them in the snow.

Wolves and wolverines are scarcer. The latter beast is an object of peculiar abhorrence to the Kamchadals. If one ever has to leave any game about to be fetched away next morning, one may be almost certain that a wolverine will get at it during the night and make a clean sweep of it. When the Kamchadals espy its broad tracks in the snow they exclaim at once: “* Proklataja rasamacha!” (‘That infernal animal !”’) The wolverine’s skin 1s worth just a little more than the ordinary red fox’s. It does not find its way out into the world’s markets, but it is in request with the local traders, who barter it for better skins with Koryaks, Lamuts and Chukchees. These people have a preference for it as material for their clothes, etc. They will _ gladly take it in exchange for a sable-skin.

When mountain sheep and wild reindeer are met with anywhere near the hunting district chosen, the sable-hunter will gladly go after them in order to get some fresh meat, as a change from jukkola and as food for his sledge-dogs. These have very little to do while the sable-hunting is in progress, and are tethered to trees most of the time. They need, however, only a minimum of food, and often they are not given their regular ration, which in these conditions is half-asalmon a day.

Finally, it occurs not infrequently that while exploring the woodland with his dogs the hunter will suddenly come upon a bear’s den. Bruin is stirred up at once and forced to émerge from his winter quarters, and is dispatched without delay. But the regular season for bear-hunting is the spring and the late autumn.

Throughout the winter months, which the hunters spend in the woodland, they have a hard life of it. Those who are wise enough to build themselves an earth-cabin have at least the benefit of being able to attain some degree of warmth; but the building of one means at the least some days of hard work, and as hard work is not to the taste of the Kamchadals most of them prefer, out of sheer laziness, to live in tents. Generally speaking, they have with them the little stove already described, but there are many who prefer to shiver the whole winter through rather than bother about procuring such a thing for themselves, although all are agreed that it is a great advantage to have one, It was only about twenty years ago that these stoves first came into use and now they are spread over the whole land.

It often happens during the winter that the hunter will have to spend an entire week or more in his tent while a snowstorm is raging. It is essential, then, to have the tent firmly fixed and to have laid up a sufficient store of firewood, so as not to have to go out to get some. For a European it would be a rather dismal business to have to spend a week or two in a small tent with no means of killing time. But the Kamchadals enjoy idling and are not the least depressed by having to lie in a sleeping-sack for a whole week at a stretch. Usually they are at least two together in the tent. Meals are so simple a matter that they can be managed without getting out of the sack. All that has to be done is to put the kettle on the stove—having filled it first with snow from the ground. The jukkola is always within reach. The hunters sleep most of the time. When they awake, they bite off a bit of the iukkola, drink a couple of mugfuls of tea, and go to sleep again. When they awake again they take note of the weather, and, if it be still the same, they utter a curse or two, turn over on the other side and doze off once more. The unfortunate sledge-dogs, which are tied up to their trees out in the storm, without any other way of protecting themselves than that of letting themselves be buried in the snow, often have to remain several days without food.
During these winter months the hunters all become victims to rheumatism. There can hardly be a single grown-up Kamchadal who does not suffer from this malady.
