N 17th March we left Klutchi. Our team (): dogs was now considerably improved. I | had come by two excellent new dogs in this incredible fashion. After the natives had done their utmost to pass off on me one shocking specimen after another I asked an old Russian, whom I had seen once before, whether he had a couple of good sledge-dogs to sell me. ‘‘ No,” he replied, ‘‘ but you can have them gratis\”’ I thought at first he was cracked, but we went with him to look at his dogs. Ten of them, powerfully built sledge-dogs, rather above the ordinary size, greeted me with angry barks. The old man went in among his dogs, with whom, apparently, he was on the best of terms to judge by the wagging of their tails, and unchained one white animal and one black. He proceeded to hand them over to me leashed, with the remark: “ They are at your disposal. No payment, please. With them you will get quicker to Petropavlovsk.” He was not cracked, nor was he jesting. He was moved by sheer friendliness! I accepted the dogs, but it was with great difficulty I succeeded in leading them when they wanted to go a different way. I tied them up in front of the old Russian’s house while my wife and I went in to have a chat with him. His name was Nikolaj Ivanovitch Boltenko, and he was a most kind and most interesting man. Born among the gardens of the Black Sea, he had grown up in the Government of Jakutsk, in North Eastern Siberia. For a number of years he had been a merchant in a big way of business in those parts, and subsequently at the head of several gold-mining expeditions in Eastern Siberia. He had been living for some years in Klutchi as head of a great Russian fur-trading company. He had, himself, made many long caravan-journeys with dog-sledges and reindeer-sledges, and he knew what it meant to travel with a bad team of dogs, therefore he took pleasure in coming to our aid. He said he feared that, next to the snowstorms, our worst hindrance on the way to Petropavlovsk would be the difficulty of getting food for the dogs in the villages. ‘“‘ Should nothing else help, give the Kamchadals a handful of this for a supply of fodder,” he said, and presented me with a big packet of Circassian tobacco. “They are mad about it. But don’t give them more than a handful at a time!”

Although we had a live bear as passenger, in addition to the rest of our baggage, our sledge now went notably better than before. The two new dogs, one of which was made a leader, worked in first-rate style. The former leader was degraded to the ranks, manifestly to his great chagrin, for he hung his head for a while: he had not obeyed the word of command properly. His greatest merit was that he always noticed and punished the misdemeanours of his fellow-workers— when they got caught in the trace or did anything else that impeded our advance.

The night after our start from Klutchi we slept in an alder-grove. The wood was so rotten that it was with difficulty that we lit a fire to make our tea. We had had a hard day of it with deep and soft snow, and but for the two new dogs we should not have achieved the twenty miles which we had now covered. The little bear was growling away softly in his sack and evoked the keenest interest on the part of all the dogs, which kept twisting round their heads to listen while they worked. None of them had as yet seen him, for I was afraid that if they did they might become so preoccupied with him that they might give up pulling. As food for him we had brought with us quite a big supply of milk —that is, frozen milk. He would not take it frozen however, that would have been to expect too much— he was not a polar bear. Instead, we chopped a bit off with an axe and melted it in a pot over the fire. If we gave him the milk either too hot or too cold, he would be displeased and not drink a drop, but when it was the right temperature he would polish off his ration at one draught and begin to make a contented purring sound. Then, always to his violently expressed disapproval, he was stuffed back into his skin-sack and made fast in the sledge, and in this little travelling lair he remained until we pulled up for the night.

In the village of Uschki, which we reached some days later, just before a snowstorm broke out, we encountered for the first time some of Kamchatka’s nomads, Koryaks and Lamuts. They had come down from the mountains to sell some otter- and sable-skins. They were clad in skins from top to toe and looked veritable children of the wild. They asked us for spirits and for fly-bane—and used the latter also as an intoxicant! They invited us to accompany them back up the mountains and to stay in their huts. But on this occasion we had no time. We promised to do so in the following winter instead.

In the company of some of these wild-looking fellows I met a man with whom I became very friendly indeed, and who was later to prove most useful and most pleasant company. When I first set eyes on him I was struck by his curious appearance. He had coalblack hair, large, very dark eyes, a big, round, potatoshaped nose and an extraordinarily thick black beard, close-cropped. In addition, he was always smiling. If my life depended on it, I could not have said what race he came of. He talked the most comical bastard Russian. When I made his acquaintance, and had been talking with him a while, he declared his origin in the words: “ Maja ni russki. Maja japonski.” A very strange specimen of a Japanese, he seemed to me, while we continued to talk. Suddenly he remarked: “Maja ni japonski. Maja ainski.”” So that was the explanation—he was an Ainu, one of that curious, moribund race that dwells in Northern Japan and Sachalin. They used always to wear their hair and beards long, but he had taken to shaving. He was known always by the name ‘“ Malenki Savonoh” (“Little Savonoh”’), to distinguish him from his elder brother, “‘ Balschoj Savonoh”’ (‘‘ Big Savonoh”’). These two brothers are the only Ainus in Kamchatka. Never in my life have I met a greater jester than this “ Little Savonoh.”’ He had only to open his mouth to have his listeners, whoever they might be, laughing. He always had something funny to say, and gave it out in the most ridiculous Russian. During the winter he traded with the natives, especially with the Koryaks and the Lamuts, with whom he was on particularly friendly terms. He always succeeded in getting hold of more sable-skins than any other trader, and he was very proud of this. I detected him as being the right man to accompany us on our journey among the Koryaks and Lamuts the following winter, and I suggested to him that we should go there together. He took to the idea at once and promised to place himself at our service. We had now reached the region of pine-forests. ‘The next village, Kosyrevsk, lay embedded in a high larchgrove on the bank of the Kamchatka river. There is a telephone station in a little hovel in this village, which is a terminus for telegraph and telephone lines from Petropavlovsk. I went into the house to examine it and found an appallingly garrulous Russian inside, who poured out the entire story of his life before I could escape. Later he came and called on us, dressed in a threadbare old Russian post office employee’s uniform with white buttons on it. He wanted to show that he _ was a Russian official, and he went on to tell us all about his achievements in this capacity in various Russian villages before the revolution. I asked him to go and ring up Petropavlovsk for me and show us what he could do now instead of recording all he had done in the past. He went off, promising to come back and let us know as soon as he had established connexion. But he never showed himself again.

We had a very difficult bit of the journey before us now. It was no less than fifty-two miles to the next village, Tolbatchik. ‘There was one jurta on the way. This was a long stage for us, who could not make any great speed with our heavily laden sledge. We calculated that we must have a week’s supply of food for the dogs, and this made our sledge heavier still.

But it seemed impossible to get the food’ in the village. Nobody had any to sell. They had run short of it in every house. That was the answer I was given everywhere at first. ‘The fact is, that in Kamchatka, one must be acquainted with the people one wants to do business with, otherwise there is “‘ nothing doing.” I was obliged to fall back on both my camera and the Circassian tobacco in order to drag forth the fifty salmon which I wanted. But after I had succeeded in laying in this store the black-haired natives began coming to us one after another to “become acquainted,” as they put it (to pasnakomitsa). ‘They sat around and fumbled their fur-caps, but at last they asked: ‘ Will the Expedition not ‘take off’ [i.e. photograph] the whole family?” If I would, I should have as. much jukkola as liked. “ But how,” I asked, ‘‘ can you have so much jukkola in the village to-day when there was none at all yesterday, when I wanted to buy some?” “Oh, well,” they replied, ‘we weren’t acquainted then.”

We set forth with our heavily burdened sledge, having first obtained some detailed information about our route, which lay alternately between larch-forests and over marshlands. After a violent snowstorm the day before, the weather had now become clear and splendid, with a temperature of 13° F. It was twenty miles to the jurta. We hoped to be able to get there in time to spend the night in it. We had good dogsledge tracks to guide us and all went well from the start. When we had covered about four miles we saw some other sledge-tracks going towards the west. If we had followed them for three days up into the mountains we would have reached the huts of the Koryaks and Lamuts. But we pursued our intended route, though we were sorely tempted to break away from it.

The animal life in the larch-forests was a little different from that among the birches. On the treetops were often to be seen the handsome red-breasted pine grosbeaks (Pinicola enucleator kamchatkensis). Nuthatches and woodpeckers were more numerous than in the birch-woods, and capercailzie flew up quite often and sometimes fell to our guns. ‘The nut-cracker (Nucifraga caryocatactes kamchatkensis) was to be heard now and again, and on one or two occasions we saw wax-wings. We had our guns handy on the sledge and alwaysloaded. With this help we added every day to our collection, and now and again we were able to provide ourselves with a good meal of ptarmigan or capercailzie or hare. The bigger forms of game—mountain sheep, reindeer, etc.—kept up in the mountain districts, which one avoids when travelling with a heavy sledge. Bears were sleeping soundly in their winter quarters.

Tracks of foxes and sables were very rare that winter. During the previous year there had been an epidemic among these animals and it had reduced their numbers to an incredible extent. The foxes, which used to be extremely numerous here, had now almost entirely disappeared. In every village one heard complaints of the poor hunting.

We met a number of dog-sledges, most of them driven by Kamchadals, but one of them by a Chinaman. He was a trader of the ordinary type and had his stock of various sorts of goods with him on his sledge. Hedstrém and I had run short of tobacco, and the Chinaman opened his shop, so to speak, there in the wilds—that is to say, he loosened a couple of straps and removed the covering over his wares, which, as usual, included, among many other things, pocketmirrors, sweets, chewing-gum and tobacco. I got into conversation with him and learned that until a year ago he had always lived in Shanghai. At that time he did not even know the very name of Kamchatka, but he had fallen out with his companion at Shanghai and had jumped on toa Russian steamer in the harbour. A couple of weeks later he had disembarked at Petropavlovsk at a venture, and now he sat there, a full-blown trader, in his dog-sledge, clad in furs and driving his own dogs. He had only a few Russian words at his command, whether dealing with the dogs or with men, but among them were charasché and nitchevé, and he managed to get along quite well. When words gave out, he had resort to the language of signs.

In the middle of the day we came upon an old man who was faring along all by himself. He was afoot and conducting a sledge drawn by three dogs. The sledge was laden with jukkola, a tent, a sleeping-sack, an axe, tea and a tea-kettle. The poor dogs were pulling it wearily, with their tongues hanging out of their mouths, and were panting from their labours. The old man pulled up alongside us. He was a Russian and not a native of Kamchatka. The victim of some kind of misfortune I guessed him to be. Almost every single Russian one meets in Kamchatka has some strange and sad story to tell.

We met about tea-time, so we lit up a fire together. The Russians like to tell the whole tale of their troubles to anyone who will listen, so before the water had boiled he was well under way with his. For some years he had been living happily at Nikolajevsk, on the Amur river, but during the revolution the Japanese came along and occupied the town. In the course of the general disorder which ensued, his wife and child were murdered and he had lost all he possessed. In his despair he tried to hang himself, but the rope broke. He then made up his mind to shoot himself, but the Japanese had taken off all available weapons. Then he

met with a fellow in misfortune, who cheered him up and made him come to Kamchatka, but he had led a dog’s life and suffered terribly from the cold and from lack of food. Now with his three dogs—the only friends he had left—he was making for a warm spring which lay about one hundred miles from Kosyrevsk. There he would lie and bathe for a time in order to get rid of his rheumatism, which racked his whole body. He was going to live in his tent alongside the spring.

When it grew dark, we had covered only half the way to the jurta, but the full moon rose and spread its cold radiance over the waste. It became a bitterly cold night. We felt no desire to sleep in our tent, so we pushed on, hoping to reach our destination. It looked as though the dogs shared our feelings, for they worked with redoubled energy. Later I discovered that sledge-dogs always work twice as well in the moonlight.

When, late in the night, we did at last reach the hut, we were so tired out that it was with difficulty we got together enough wood to warm us and boil the water for our tea. Very soon all three of us were in our sleeping-sacks.

The following evening found us sitting round the stove in our tent and listening to the most unpleasant of all the winter music to be heard in Kamchatka—the sound of the snowstorm; but the evening after that we arrived safely at Tolbatchik. We had overstrained our energies, however, and were not feeling worth much. Weariness seemed to have made its way into our very bones. The sledge had turned over at least twenty times in the deep snow and the dogs had been manifestly dispirited by these mishaps, for they had been hanging their heads all the day. We blessed Ivan Viktorevitch’s floor on which we slept the night.

In the morning our limbs were so stiff that we decided we must remain on another day, although it was fine weather. The inhabitants of the village streamed up to the house to look at us. And they all marvelled that ‘‘ Madame” should be able to go through such hardships. The little bear had a happy day in the village. He was set free for the whole day and went through regular acrobatic performances in his delight over escaping from the darkness of his sack. Our host’s cow had just calved, so little Mischka— as we called him—vwas relieved from his frozen milk and able to drink as much fresh milk as he liked. The calf—as in all the other houses in which cattle were kept—was a member of the family. The Kamchadals never build stables for their cows. At the most they have some kind of shed for them which cannot be kept warm. Therefore, when the cows are about to calve in the early spring, while it is still very cold out of doors, the owner must be on the alert day and night to carry the calf into his own house the moment it is born. If this is not done there is nothing to be found in the morning but a lump of ice. When the calf is carried into the hut it is tied up in a corner and is given a little straw to lie on. When it has to fulfil its needs, whoever is nearest at hand springs forward with an empty preserve pot. In one house in which we lodged there were no fewer than four calves in the dining-room. Not a single meal passed without someone suddenly calling out and rushing forward with a preserve pot in the utmost haste.

Tolbatchik looked more or less like all the other villages we passed. One house in the village stood empty with the windows and doors wide open. The family had moved into the house next door to stay a week with their neighbours so that the cockroaches which had been infesting their own home might freeze to death. They had become absolutely unbearable. “Tf this cold weather continues,” the owner of the house remarked, “ they will freeze to death all right.” It seemed to us a strange experience to be driven outof-doors in this way by vermin in the depth of winter, but to the Kamchadals it all seemed quite natural and they wondered what I saw to laugh at in it.

On our way to the next village, T’chapina, thirty-one miles off, we passed for the first time through one of the Kamchatkan spruce-forests. It was a fine big forest, almost like those in Sweden, although the trees were of a different species (Picea ajanensis). We enjoyed a pleasant, homelike feeling as we made our way through it, even if the ground was very rough and uneven to travel over. ‘he whole landscape, indeed, was astonishingly like Sweden, and when tea-time arrived we took out our last remaining coffee beans and celebrated the occasion in Swedish fashion. And a small bird, a coaltit (Parus ater)—a true child of the spruce-forests—now showed itself for the first time.

Never had we found the business of putting up the tent so pleasant as on that evening. Within the tent we spread out a thick layer of spruce branches over the snow, and the scent of them was delightful. We made a regular festival of it, and took out all the simple delicacies we could muster. My wife made some cakes of flour with water and salt, stirred together into a paste and then fried with a plentiful supply of lard. I can assure you that they tasted better than the most delicious cakes ever made anywhere! As if to intensify the festival atmosphere the heavens displayed all their stars, which glistened as they only can on a cold and frosty winter night. That evening our thoughts travelled to our own land of pines.

In the village of Tchapina the sledge-dogs are fed on something which is called kis/a. It consists of almost putrid salmon, which is dealt with in the following convenient—and to Kamchadals acceptable—fashion. You dig a deep pit and throw into it a couple of thousand salmon exactly as they are when caught. Often they are still alive. When the pit is full it is covered up with earth. The contents of the pit now go through a process of fermentation and decomposition, and the result of this is a sort of gruel-like substance which may be smelt miles away when the pit is opened in the winter. The his/a is taken up out of the pit with a pitchfork of the kind used for manuring. Our dogs had not previously tasted this delicacy and at first refused energetically to eat it. They went like cats round their portion, sniffing at it. But at last their hunger became too great and they began to eat a little, and so, gradually, some of them got actually to like it. Formerly the Kamchadals used to eat this kind of food themselves, but now, for the most part, they have ceased to do so, but one still comes across it in out-ofthe-way villages along the west coast, and during the following winter my wife and I were more than once invited to partake of it.

In such villages, when the river hard by remains unfrozen in the winter, the dogs are fed usually on fresh fish frozen. The frozen salmon are preserved in provision-sheds, heaped up in stacks just like firewood. They are handled like firewood in this respect also, that you use an axe to cut them with. I remember one occasion during the following winter when the temperature had been under 40° F. for nearly a week —it was, in fact, the coldest spell we had had during the entire expedition. I had to*cut some salmon for my dogs, but they were frozen so hard that the axe would not bite into them. They were almost like stones, and when at last I managed to break them in two, and gave each of the dogs his half-fish, the older animals, having bad teeth, could make no way with them at all. I had to hack away at the half-salmons until I got them into small bits before the dogs could tackle them.

In Tchapina we met an unfortunate Russian who in some wonderful manner had become possessed of a very fine camera. He had plates, paper and all the ingredients required for developing, but he bemoaned his inability to get good results when he photographed. The poor man possessed also a book about photography, but that is not much help when one is illiterate! He begged us to give him some instruction in the art and we discovered that he had always been trying to develop his negatives in the fixing-bath and to fix them in the developing-bath. In these circumstances it was difficult to produce good pictures,

In Tchapina, also, we came upon something quite unexpected. At the instance of our friend Novograblenoff, in Petropavlovsk, the chief Bolshevik Commissary in that town had sent a telegram to all the villages on the way thither, worded as follows :—

““Three members of the Swedish Scientific Expedition are on their way to Petropavlovsk along the Kamchatka river. As the purpose of the Expedition is to explore Kamchatka, it is the wish of the Revolutionary Committee of Petropavlovsk that all villages which are visited by the Expedition shall give it help and place dog-sledges at its disposal free of cost.
‘* LaRIN, “ Chairman of The Revolutionary Committee.”

That was an excellent Revolutionary Committee! It would be well if there were many such. But now the question was whether the local representatives of the Committee in the villages would pay attention to the telegram.

In Tchapina we did not trouble to ask for any dogsledges because the way to the next village, Maschura, thirty-four miles off, lay through spruce-forests, and we wanted to study them and make the most of our stay in them; but in Maschura I called on the chief official and asked him to have two sledges ready for us next morning, and he had nothing for it but to agree to do so. In order to ensure his keeping of his promise I let his entire family, mother-in-law and grandchildren take up their position in front of the house, and sacrificed a 12x28 inches film to photographing them. This attention he repaid by presenting me with a mammoth’s tooth which he had found.

Then we drove off at a fine pace in our three sledges on our way to Kirganik, the next village, where we made acquaintance with Kamchatka’s swiftest sledgedriver—the old Kamchadal, Tjurkin. Rumours of his exploits had reached us long before. For him and his dogs one hundred miles a day were a bagatelle. He had some secret way of looking after his dogs which he would not impart to anyone. When we started out the following day from his village for the big village of Milkova, my wife took pleasure in travelling in Tyurkin’s sledge behind his famous dogs, and with himself as driver. When Hedstrém and I were halfway there we met him returning from Milkova. His dogs simply flew over the ground.

In the big and prosperous village of Milkova, with its five hundred inhabitants, there were many horses and cows, and any number of sledge-dogs. In the house of the rich Kamchadal, Korschunoff, in which we were most hospitably welcomed, we made acquaintance with a white-haired Russian octogenarian—a fine old fellow who knew only one Swedish word and that was filbunke (a bowlful of curdled milk). He had learned it from a Swede who used to live in Petropavlovsk, named Sandelin. For this Swede all that is comprised in love of one’s mother country was summed up in the word fi/bunke—which was the best thing he remembered of Sweden. He partook of it every day in his new abode.

While we walked about, looking at the village, making ethnographic collections in the huts, and becoming acquainted with the inhabitants, we were followed by a long queue of Kamchadals curiously studying us as queer specimens of humanity. Suddenly a man came rushing up breathlessly and calling out “‘mister,’? which seemed to be the only word at his command. I thought that at the very least his wife was dying, but all that he had to intimate was that he had shot a big mountain sheep, the head of which, with fine horns, he offered me.

In Milkova I came upon a bird which I did not expect to meet with in the interior of the peninsula. This was an ivory gull (Pagophila eburnea), an absolutely snow-white bird and a visitor from the Arctic, which had been driven hither by the wind.

Scharomsk we came upon a reach of the Kamchatka river which remains unfrozen all the year through. We had to get across it with three sledges and twentyeight dogs. A canoe was moored at either side of the river. The Kamchadals who were with us answered for it that we should all get across without having to swim. In the one canoe they crossed the river themselves and then returned with the other. When they got back they lashed the two boats together. On the boats were pushed two of the sledges, fixed athwart them, with the twenty dogs belonging to them. Our own dogs, who were not accustomed to the crossing of rivers, barked furiously, and we had to use force to get them into the boats.

The punting of the boats across the river was a difficult business. Their bows had to be kept against the stream as far as possible, to prevent them from being carried away. When we came near the opposite bank the dogs wanted to jump out on to the land, but this had to be prevented at all costs or we should have capsized. Strange to say, there are comparatively few accidents on these crossings. To us it seemed in the nature of a lucky fluke that all went well.

We now passed one small village after another. Some of the Revolutionary Committees placed sledges at our disposal, others did not. But we did not trouble much over that, for the weather was now very much better, and it was a pleasure to travel on our skis through the forests. The hunting season was now over and there was quite a lot of traffic between the villages, so that we generally had no need to supply tracks for our sledge. The Kamchadals were all making for the larger villages or Petropavlovsk to sell their furs and buy all they needed for the coming winter. One day we met a party of twenty-two dog-sledges, all of them laden with goods, for the most part flour.

Presently we crossed the extensive marshland of Ganalska—a region feared for its snowstorms — the shortest way over, which is staked out for the benefit of travellers. Then, by narrow passes, we traversed the stately mountain ranges on the other side. The sun was shining on the precipitous peaks, on whose sides mountain sheep and wild reindeer could be seen wandering.

Suddenly we found ourselves in front of a shallow stream on which the ice had just broken up, and which now was rushing along like a torrent. We were now right in the centre of a waste land, and naturally there was no sign of a canoe. After exploring the reach for some kind of ice bridge there remained nothing for it but either to turn back or to go into the water. But how could we get the sledge and the dogs over? We sought out the shallowest point and unloaded the sledge close by the bank. Then we took off our fur stockings and reindeer-hide boots and drew on our ordinary leather boots. Hedstrém and I then shouldered each his burden, and with a ski-stick in one hand waded out into the river. The water was so icy cold that we almost bit our tongues. The stream scarcely reached our middles, but it was hard to keep our balance owing to the volume and force of the current and the slippery stones. We got across, but ugh! it was a horrible experience! Having placed our burdens on the opposite bank we now had to return to get over the sledge and the dogs—no easy matter, for the dogs were all mortally afraid of the water. We forced them in, however, and they swam across, while the empty sledge followed after. When we got up again on the opposite bank the dogs went in for a tremendous shaking of themselves. Our legs felt like icicles and we had to jump about awhile before we could venture into the river once again. I spared my wife the icy-cold wading by carrying her over, but this time I very nearly slipped—that would have meant a fine state of things. As soon as I got her over my wife lit a fire, and after Hedstrém and I had made two more crossings, in order to fetch over the rest of our things, I felt that there could never have been a more comforting fire. We let the dogs come up to it also, and they evidently enjoyed the warmth.

After all these exertions we had little energy left, and it was with difficulty that we managed to get as far as the village of Malka that evening. Here we stayed in the house of a man from the Caucasus, named Afaj Alexandrovitch. He gave us coffee, which was delightful after our ice-bath. It was in his house, by the way, that we found the four calves all living as inmates. That evening the dogs were treated to a somewhat bigger ration than usual, so that they should not lose heart. The little bear, who had been unusually querulous during the day, but who had been got across the river dryshod, was given his ordinary freedom in the evening, and walked about the room and made friends with the calves. They stood and nosed at each other a bit, after which the little bear withdrew respectfully. He seemed to think them uncannily big creatures, and he transferred his attention to a cat which was wandering about the room; but he got on still worse with her.

Ever since we had come upon the telephone station at Kosyrevsk I had tried, in almost every village, to ring up Petropavlovsk in order to have a talk with my colleagues, but it was not until we reached Ganala— about ninety miles from the town—that I succeeded in doing so. It was eight months since we had met our comrades, so we had much to say to each other. All was well with them at Petropavlovsk.

There were fewer dog-sledges placed at our disposal the nearer we got to Petropavlovsk, so we went back to our skis. One day we met a Russian who had a strange-looking cargo on his sledge. It was an ordinary sleeping-sack of reindeer hide which bulged out at one end and which evidently contained something. It was potatoes! He had put the potatoes in the sack in a warm room and had carefully closed up the opening, and had been able to drive a long way in very severe cold without the potatoes getting frozen. An original experiment! ‘This is certainly the only way in which potatoes can be transported from one village to another in the winter.

The nearer we got to our goal the more we increased our day’s march, and on the last day of all we started at seven o’clock from the village of Korjaka. From here it was about thirty miles to Petropavlovsk, but we were resolved not to encamp for another night but to continue right on. It was a radiantly sunshiny day, and in the evening there was a bright moon. We had scarcely any feeling of weariness during that last stage.

At ten in the evening, when we still had three or four miles to cover, we heard the sound of skis on the crisp snow. We stopped and listened. Suddenly three figures came gliding forward out of the forest. They could be no others than our comrades, Malaise, Hultén and his wife, and we exchanged mutual shouts of welcome in the moonlight. In a moment we were all together, and after our eight months’ separation the delight of the happy reunion was great. Hedstrém and I were offered cigars, which we enjoyed, and my wife was presented with some cakes. Our dogs came in for notice and also the little bear in his sack. We then continued our advance in a leisurely way between the snowclad mountains and hills, and soon we saw the lights of the town. At eleven p.m. that night, 16th April, we tied up the dogs outside our own house in Petropavlovsk, and went inside. ‘Thus fortunately, we concluded our five hundred miles’ journey in a month and a half. We had had a hard time of it—but an extremely interesting time—and my studies had benefited much.

As the result of this journey, I decided to devote myself that summer to the valley of the Kamchatka river, and more especially to investigations of the animal life in the forests of birch, larch and pine; but as this book is to deal only with my winter adventures we shall now take a big jump over that summer expedition and find ourselves in Petropavlovsk again in the late autumn.
OUR SLEDGE JOURNEY TO NORTHERN KAMCHATKA:

HAD it in mind, with the help of my wife, to devote this winter to the study of the nomad races in northern and central Kamchatka—the Koryaks and the Lamuts, who live by breeding reindeer. I was anxious also to get to know the Kamchadals of the west coast, where a little sprinkling of them are still to be found not completely Russianized as they are elsewhere in the peninsula, and where, for instance, they continue to talk their own language. It was my intention, of course, to proceed at the same time with my studies of animal life.

Of the two nomad races in question the Lamuts are much the least known—they area branch of the Tungus race—and about the Lamuts of Kamchatka not much is to be read in books. The chief reason for this is that it is so extremely difficult to make one’s way up to their dwelling-places. ‘They live in mountainous districts in central and northern Kamchatka. If one tries to get up there in the summer one encounters torrential streams, morasses and dense thickets through which one has to cut one’s way. In the winter the streams and morasses are frozen over, but there are snowstorms

Nor has much been written about the Koryaks of Kamchatka, but they do not seem to differ much from those who dwell to the north of the peninsula, and who have been exhaustively studied by the Russian explorer, Jochelson, and dealt with by him in his valuable works.

I thought it best, therefore, to devote most of my time to the Lamuts, to whose method of looking after the reindeer Professor K. B. Wiklund, of Upsala, urged me to devote special attention, nd precise description of this having yet been published.

The most essential thing for the carrying out of this winter programme was a first-class team of sledgedogs, for without one it is impossible to get over great distances in the winter. I placed my trust in the dogs which I had bought in Klutchi. The route which I planned out extended over one thousand three hundred miles—a figure which, however, had to be considerably increased.

Now here arose the question whether I should undertake this long sledge journey with or without a native attendant. If I were to take a Kamchadal with me, I would have to have a second team of dogs—for there is never room for more than two persons in a sledge in addition to the equipment when it is a question of a long journey. This would have increased expenses

seriously, for a team of dogs at that time cost about fifty-five pounds, and a native would not come with me for less than twenty or twenty-five pounds a month. In addition there would be the food for the extra dogs, and that was a costly item. Altogether my expenses would have been increased by a hundred and fifty or two hundred pounds. I could not afford that, so my wife and I decided that we should go alone—although I must admit that we did not altogether relish the prospect of the frequent snowstorms or the length of the journey, especially in view of the circumstance that no trustworthy maps were to be had. But the fascination of new discoveries and adventures tempted us strongly and overcame all doubts as to a successful issue to our enterprise.

We waited only for the snow to begin falling. It was later than usual this autumn—indeed it was later than anyone could remember it to have been ever before. The days were bright and cold, without any rain. The ground for a long time past had been frozen hard and the lakes were covered with ice. The dogs remained idle, and they also were evidently eager for the snow to fall.

One day we exercised them on the ice on the lake hard by. We had first to make our way through the town. The moment we got out the sledge the dogs saw what was in question and became wild with delight. They barked violently and began tugging away at their chains. We had our work cut out to prevent them from breaking loose in their excitement while we were harnessing them. When at last I gave the word of command to start they set off at such a pace that it was quite impossible to make the brake felt, although we were on bare ground and there were three of us in the sledge. We tore down the street at a breakneck pace. Suddenly we saw a luckless pig promenading a little way in front of us. The whole team plunged forward more violently than ever, and before the poor animal knew where he was they were on him like a pack of wolves, each trying to get a mouthful out of him. Had not the sledge come up against a telephone pole, and thus been anchored, we should not have been able to rescue him, but as it was we forced our way into the struggling mass and succeeded in kicking away the dogs, and their victim made off squealing pitifully. Two of the dogs broke their straps and were after him, but they were recaptured. An indignant old woman came hurrying out of the house into which the pig had fled, and at once demanded compensation for the damage done to it; but the spectators testified that the pig’s injuries were relatively slight, and that he was not much the worse for his adventure, so she quieted down, and withdrew after a while. Next day I saw the same pig nosing about busily in a rubbish-heap, so apparently he was all right.

_ Shortly before, one of the dogs had done for a pig all by himself and, what was worse, had devoured it entire, but it had been a small pig and the old man who owned it had been given a tin of biscuits in its place and we had parted friends.

Our equipment had long been got together, but the snow still tarried. At last we heard that snow had fallen near the village of Savoiko—only seventeen miles from Petropavlovsk—and that it was now possible to drive sledges there. So as not to lose any more time I decided to transport the sledge, with its contents, on a cart to Savoiko, to which there is quite a good road. Accordingly, I hired a horse and cart and driver, and we put the sledge and everything on the cart, to the back of which were fixed two long poles to which the dogs were tied—five on each side.
We then took farewell of our colleagues, who, however, accompanied us a part of the way, together with a number of Japanese officers who had come to say good-bye, and the cart rattled off.

The dogs—who had been tied up all summer and autumn—were immensely delighted to be able to use their legs. They could not, however, understand their position behind the cart. Surely it was their business to be pulling it! When we had got half-way to our destination it began to snow quite heavily.

After darkness had set in we reached Savoiko. The river which we had to get over was frozen, and our Russian driver wanted to drive across in the dark without first making sure that the ice would hold. But we would not allow this, and it was lucky we did not, for near the opposite bank there was an unfrozen stream, and I had to explore a good way before I found a spot where we could cross with the sledge and the dogs. The horse and cart we left behind on the southern bank.
When we awoke in the morning the ground was white with snow and we were able to make an early Start.

But at this point I must beg to introduce our new team of sledge-dogs, who were to be our companions—and often our salvation—during the months that followed. ~ Only three of them had belonged to our team of the previous winter—namely, Muschika, the best of them all; Captain, the dog who had been leader at the beginning of our winter journey; and Bjela, one of the dogs I was given at Klutchi. The remaining seven were new. The leader—called Tjernogubka—was a quiet but very intelligent dog, who answered the words of command properly, and who possessed moreover a great faculty for finding tracks even when they were all but obliterated. Coupled with him was Bussi, a swift and very industrious dog, who, however, had the fault of over-exerting himself at the beginning of the day and therefore could not pull so well later.

The second couple consisted of Muschika and Bjela —the dogs already mentioned. After them came Laska and Maschnaschka. The former was a quarrelsome animal on whom we could never quite rely. He often tried to scamp his work when he thought he was not being watched. Maschnaschka was one of the best members of the team, but he had quicksilver in his veins and could never remain still. In addition to that he was overpoweringly friendly, and when we approached him he would always jump up and want to lick our faces. The moment he caught sight of my wife or me in the distance he would begin to jump about with delight. He worked very energetically and never shirked, but owing to his liveliness he would often get entangled in the trace. Another fault of his was that he had no scruples about stealing the fish from the sledge when he got a chance. He evidently saw nothing immoral in this proceeding, for he would do it whether he was alone or whether there was somebody looking on— which was a sympathetic trait in his character.

The next couple were Topchik and Opala. Topchik was, perhaps, the strongest of all the dogs. His legs were almost twice as thick as those of the others. He worked like a horse. For him work was everything. He put his whole soul into the pulling of the sledge and had no inclination for any capers or antics. He never got entangled in the trace and he took not the slightest interest in any of the game-tracks that crossed our path. On the other hand, he would not stand being disturbed by any of his comrades whether in harness or in his free time, and he snarled if anyone happened to stumble over him. He growled also at the black crows when they came too near him and wanted to make off with the bits left over after his meals. He did not like it when we were in a hurry and didn’t care to go at a rate of more than six or seven miles an hour at the outside. One of his ears hung down as the result of a fight. Opala was a very big and powerful dog which we bought to replace another which hurt its leg at the beginning of the journey. He worked very badly indeed. I never won his confidence and after I had had him a fortnight he managed to get free, bolted off ahead of the sledge, and disappeared. I never saw him again and it was a good riddance. His post remained vacant for another fortnight, when he was replaced by Karnauschka, a big, thoroughly satisfactory dog who worked well.

The last pair of all were Pjostri and Captain. The former was good at first, but after a fight in which he got bitten in his leg he was no longer up to much. He did not hear well and he was the only dog in the team who never displayed any affection. He even tried to bite me on two occasions. Captain the reader knows already. He showed a peculiar interest in hare-tracks and had often to be called to order for nosing after them instead of doing his duty.

As I myself had the driving of the dogs throughout our journey I had plenty of opportunities for studying them. It was interesting to note that none of all the ten resembled any of the others. They were as different as human beings in all their ways and habits.

Sledge-dogs are always placed on the principle that the best go in front and the worst nearest the sledge. To be near the sledge is never to the dogs’ liking, and if any of the front dogs try to shirk they are put farther back, where the driver has more control over them and is better able to keep them up to the mark.
The traces of each couple are attached to the main trace at intervals of two yards. The main trace is ten yards long therefore.

My plan now was to take the village of Kosyrevsk as our starting-point for the mountains and the abodes of the nomads, but we had a good way to go first. Kosyrevsk is more than three hundred miles distant from Petropavlovsk.
In the village of Natchika we were held up an entire week by a snowstorm. As soon as it was over the weather became fine but bitterly cold.

Near the village lay a warm spring by which the Kamchadals had built a little shed. We drove out there one day to bathe. We found two dog-sledges halted there already. The little Arctic bath-house was covered with snow and ice and looked anything but warm. We went in. A little stove stood in one corner. There was a fire in it and a tea-kettle was boiling. Some clothes lay on a bench. Two Kamchadals were bathing outside in the pool.

When I went into the water a little later the temperature was 31° F. in the air and 102° F. in the water. It was a delightful feeling to get into the warm water. When one had been lying in it for a good while one felt so warmed through and through that one could stand naked in the biting frost without shivering. But one has to avoid wetting one’s head, for then one’s hair gets frozen into lumps of ice. While undressing and dressing it was very pleasant to have the fire burning in the stove.

The Kamchadals are very fond of these warm springs, which are reputed to be most health-giving. There is a spring at Semljatchik which is reputed to cure syphilis. Except for these warm springs, which are by way of curing all maladies, the Kamchadals, indeed, have no kind of remedies at their disposal except those offered by some quacks. If you have a sore on your body, or have cut your leg, you go to the Warm springs just as you would for rheumatism. But it is for rheumatism that they are in most request. All Kamchadals, men and women alike, suffer from rheumatism. The men lay themselves open to it, as already mentioned, during the winter hunting months ; the women become liable to it through not being able to keep the houses at an even temperature.

March and September are said to be the months when the water in the warm springs is most efficacious. If in either of these months you have a cut finger you have only to put it down into the water for a while, they declare, for it to be healed; but I never saw this miracle accomplished. In March, while it is still winter, the Kamchadals will journey therefore in their dog-sledges to these springs. They generally lie at a distance of several days’ journey from the nearest village. They put up their tents on the snow close to the spring and stay two or three weeks at a stretch to bathe. They spend a good part of the day in the warm water and during the night, when the temperature is often extremely cold, they sleep in their tents. I suspect that they get back during the cold night the rheumatism they get rid of during the day, but you will hear every Kamchadal tell how he himself, or some member of his family, has been cured of some dreadful malady in an incredibly short time by one of these springs.

The evening before we left Natchika a whole procession of dog-sledges arrived in the village from the Kamchatka river valley en route for Petropavlovsk. Suddenly, who should appear but Malaise! We had not met since we parted at Tchapina five months before. He had allowed his hair and beard to grow and presented a very wild appearance, but we recognized him at once, and the pleasure at seeing each other again was mutual. We had only the one night together and we had a lot to tell each other, so we did not get much sleep. Since we had last met, Malaise had been to the great Lake Kronoki. After that he had been up to the pine-forests in the upper region of the Kamchatka river valley. Now he was on his way home to Petropavlovsk with two hired sledges which were laden with valuable collections, among them a pair of unique birds, a sable which he had caught himself, an otter, and a lot of other things, all in a frozen condition.
Next morning we said good-bye to each other for another long period. Malaise set out with his companions for Petropavlovsk, we in the opposite direction,

After driving for nearly an hour I espied an animal about a mile ahead of us. With my field-glasses I thought I could identify it as a wolverine. He was nosing about after the tracks of the sledge-dogs. When we had got to within half-a-mile of him he and our dogs became aware of each other. The wolverine bolted for dear life and I can promise you the dogs put on speed. They completely forgot that they had a heavy sledge behind them with two persons in it, and they tore along

helter-skelter in pursuit. I gave them a free rein as the way was open and level. We appeared to be gaining on the wolverine, which found it necessary to put forth all its powers. The chase continued for two thrilling minutes, but then we came to a river which was unfrozen along the bank. The wolverine rushed across over an ice-bridge and the dogs would fain have followed him. It was with the greatest difficulty that I managed to hold them back so that we could look about and find a safe spot for our crossing. Meanwhile the wolverine got right away and disappeared in a wood and we had to give up the hunt.

After this exhilarating intermezzo we had traversed a hilly birch-wood and so came to another reach of the river with swans and ducks on it. Here we had a pleasant and much-needed halt for tea, while the snow came down thickly, but for once in a way softly. The snowfall on the sledge while we were drinking our tea was four inches deep.

When evening was coming on the dogs lost the tracks owing to the newly fallen snow, and for some hours we wandered about in the darkness without being able to find them again; but at last, a little before midnight, we heard to our delight the barking of dogs in the village of Malka, and following the sound we contrived to get there.

The dogs, who were the only inhabitants of the village awake when we arrived, barked us their noisy welcome. We made for the house of the Caucasian, Afaj Alexandrovitch, who had entertained us the previous winter, and we succeeded in waking up a Tartar who worked for him. Afaj himself happened to be away. The last time we were in the house there had been four calves in the dining-room. Now these were gone but the room was full of cats. The Tartar never ventured to let them out for fear of the dogs, so there was a dreadful smell of cat indoors.

The following night we spent in a comfortable little jurta in which we met three Kamchadal sable-hunters. They had with them a sable which they had shot that day and which was now in a frozen state. We had a very pleasant evening together and when we awoke next day it was Christmas Eve. The Kamchadals took themselves off to the woods and we proceeded to the village of Ganala, situated on the south side of the Ganal marshland.

Soon afterwards there arrived no fewer than fifteen dog-sledges, all of them driven by traders who were beginning their first long winter round. Their sledges were laden to the utmost with their wares. There were Russians, Tartars, Chinese and Koreans.

We had intended to celebrate our Christmas very simply. We had with us in the sledge a bagful of nuts and raisins—a gift from some Swedish sailors who had touched at Petropavlovsk in their schooner. But ten of the traders found their way to the same house as ourselves, and as all had brought some spirits with them on their journey, in order to ingratiate themselves with their hosts and predispose them to do business, the conditions for our little festivities became very bad ;

So we put aside our Christmas box, comforting ourselves with the thought that we should be spending our next Christmas in Sweden—we little guessed that we should spend it, instead; on the Suez Canal! That night we were packed as closely as we had been in the foxhunter’s jurta the previous winter. Our thoughts kept going back alternately to Sweden and to our preceding Christmas at Ust-Kamchatsk. We wondered also how things were with our comrades at Petropavlovsk.

The Kamchadal with whom we were staying had, counting us, twelve guests, with a hundred and ten dogs, to entertain. The remaining five traders put up in other huts in the village. Our host had the best house there and prided himself on looking after his guests and their dogs better than anyone else, and his house was a regular inn. While we were there a hundred and ten salmon a day had to be given to the dogs. But at least he had something to be proud of.

Next day our Zeiss field-glasses scored a veritable triumph in the village. Ganala is surrounded by a high and steep mountain range. I went out with my glasses, through which about fifty mountain sheep (Ovis nivicola) could be made out distinctly against the white mantle of snow, although quite invisible to the naked eye. All the Kamchadals came congregating round me wanting to look, and my glasses went the round of them. It impressed them much to be able to see the sheep from the doors of their own houses. “ We ought to have glasses like that,” was the general feeling. Both the traders and the natives wanted to buy mine. It would have been the right moment to sell them had I not needed them myself.

From Christmas onwards we made better and better progress. I had succeeded in establishing excellent relations with the dogs, which had moreover got rid of the excess of flesh they had put on in the summer and had got their muscles into good condition. We crossed the Ganalska tundra successfully, greeting our old acquaintances in the various villages; went over the unfrozen river at Verchne Kamchatsk with our sledge and the dogs on two canoes fastened together, and on a bitterly cold day arrived at the big village of Milkova, greeted by the barking of innumerable dogs.

After we had tied up the dogs we made our way to the house of the Kamchadal tradesman, Korschunoff, with whom we had stayed on our journey south the previous winter, and were welcomed by his wife as old acquaintances and friends. She told us that he himself would soon be in and that they had plenty of jukkola for the dogs. “ Just you take off your furs and come in and have some tea,” she said. “ Terribly cold it is, isn’t it?’’ A thickly built grey-haired man who had just come in listened a moment to my wife and me as we exchanged a word or two and then exclaimed in our own language: ‘‘ What in the name of the devil do I hear? Why, you are talking Swedish?” “ Are you from Sweden?’’ I asked. Yes, indeed; he was, he declared. “‘ Born at Gnesta and by name Jansson! ”

Whereupon we began a great talk over our tea, and Jansson told us his whole story and explained how he had happened to come to this village. It was a chequered Story, as may easily be imagined. Jansson was well known all over Kamchatka. If we had not heard of him before, that was because no one thought of him as a Swede—everyone took him for an American. He had been a resident in Petropavlovsk for more than twenty years. During part of that time he had been a baker, for the rest of the time a tavern-keeper. It was in the latter capacity that he became known and esteemed over the greater portion of the country, for Jansson was a generous soul. He had earned quite a good income at one time, but then he went and married a Russian, which he ought never to have done. “ If you weren’t married,” he said to me, “‘I would give you a piece of good advice: never marry a Russian | That’s the end to all things.” In the course of time, however, he got a divorce, and had then been to America for some years, after which he went back to life on the sea. He had come over as cook on one of Swenson’s schooners on its last voyage, when’she took fire and was burnt out at sea (a new cinematograph equipment of ours was on board her). He had saved his life but lost all he possessed. ‘Together with others who were saved he returned to America. Presently he came over again on another of Swenson’s schooners to Ust-Kamchatsk. Here he bought a sledge and a team of eight dogs and he was now on his way to the west coast of the peninsula to settle down alongside Karlsson—an old friend and compatriot of his, who had lived in Kamchatka for more than thirty years. He was now going to pay only a short visit to Petropavlovsk before proceeding on to the west coast. ;

Jansson was a man of over fifty, who evidently had experienced a lot of ill-fortune in the course of his life. He looked forward to ending his days in Kamchatka— where he escaped taxation and other evils. “ Besides, I’m cracked about salted salmon!” he declared. He had never been back to Sweden since his young days and he did not think he would ever see the country. again. ‘‘ But,’ he added, with a touch of sadness, “ I no longer have any acquaintances at home, and I should not know myself now at Gnesta. However, give my greetings to dear old Sweden when you get back!”

Jansson took messages to my colleagues with him to Petropavlovsk, where I guaranteed him a cordial reception in the house occupied by the Expedition. As it was part of our plan to look in on Karlsson on the west coast some time in the early spring, we said good-bye only till then, and so our ways parted.

We were anxious to reach the village of Tolbatchik, where there is a church, in time for the celebration of the Kamchadal Christmas, which was four days off. In Kamchatka the old Russian calendar—thirteen days behind ours—is still followed. ‘The journey would take four whole days if the weather were fine.

The dogs were in first-rate condition. They made seven miles an hour easily, although the sledge was weighted with two hundred pounds of goods, in addition to my wife and myself. We passed the villages of Kirganik, Maschura and Tchapina without any

Between Maschura and Tchapina we came upon a party of sixteen sledges at an earth-hut. They were on their way to Milkova to celebrate Christmas there. There were entire families with children. The women and children, as is usual, were buried in furs to such an extent that they could scarcely move. On almost every sledge there was a keg of spirits.

We reached Tchapina late in the evening, just as the snowy weather had begun. The snow came down all night and the prospects in the morning were not bright. The whole place lay covered with snow and it was still falling. Our host advised us not to proceed farther, but we were eager to get to Tolbatchik at any price and we started off. It was very heavy going and my wife had to plough a way for us on skis. About midday we came to Nikolke, where we had encamped during the summer in a wood. The beautiful river was unfrozen, as it remains throughout the winter, but the Kamchadals have laid a bridge over it. When we got to Nikolke, both we ourselves and the dogs were tired out and a somewhat long rest was necessary. We were now convinced that we could not reach Tolbatchik that evening, but we hoped to be there before noon next day.
We lit a fire on the site of our summer camp and made some coffee for the first time since we left Petropavlovsk, a month before. It tasted indescribably

good! The snow was still falling densely and softly, and the neighbouring pines drooped under its weight. The only sound which disturbed the silence in the wood was when a little avalanche of snow came toppling down from some overburdened branch.

The short winter day soon drew to a close, and as there were now no tracks to be seen, and both the dogs and we were tired out, there was nothing for it but to find a suitable spot on which to spend the night, and we found one quickly enough.

EXT day, the Kamchatkan Christmas Eve, we N= Tolbatchik early enough to rest a little before the festivities commenced. There were a lot of people in the village. Many had come from other villages and there were visitors in every house. The Kamchadals like to congregate at Christmas in the villages which have churches, and such villages are not very numerous. All the hunters were back from the forests and many furs had been bartered for spirits—for this was Christmas time and a time for festivity !. When we entered the home of Ivan Viktorevitch, a good old Kamchadal, all the people in the house were putting on their best clothes to go to church. The women donned their brightly coloured silk dresses, and replaced their home-made reindeer-hide boots with soles of bear-hide by high-heeled shoes purchased from traders, which, one felt; they must have found very painful to walk in. Some of them even wore patent-leather shoes. The men wore jackets mostly, some of them frock-coats. The most dandified among them put on celluloid collars with bright-coloured rosettes attached to them which never would keep 163 properly in their place. Most of them wore purchased leather boots instead of their home-made ones. Over those the veritable ‘‘toffs”’ put on slimy rubber goloshes—and yet you will hear people say that the Kamchadals have no care for their appearance !

Presently we heard the church bells ringing. Having put the last touch to themselves, the entire population, men, women and children, began to stream out from their houses. Even infants in arms were taken and only the calves were left in the huts. The little timbered church, which naturally had no seats in it, soon became packed with people. Wax candles, placed high up, were burning, and the whole church reeked with smoke. The church was plentifully ornamented with statues and all kinds of decorations. The priest, a Kamchadal himself, and just returned from hunting—for he had no salary and had to provide for himself—stood before the altar attired in vestments richly adorned in the Catholic style.

The service lasted several hours, and was of little interest to an outsider: for the Kamchadal congregation, one felt that it must have had less interest still, and they could not possibly have understood what it | all meant. Like the service which we attended in Nischne Kamchatsk the previous year, it consisted of the priest’s reading at a bewildering rate out of a book. He gabbled away so fast that his purpose might have been really to prevent anybody from understanding a word. ‘The congregation kept making the sign of the cross continually. A psalm-singer (psalomchik)

chanted a little now and again and read bits at the same breakneck speed as the priest. Occasionally the priest went down among the congregation and swung an incense-burner, while they took part in an antiphony.
_ This was the Christmas Eve service. When it was over, at last, everyone returned home to supper and went early to bed, for there were to be Christmas Matins next morning at seven.

The people began to get up as early as five a.m. in our house, and to dress themselves with the same care as on the previous evening ; and after we had all had tea with specially good bread we went again to the church. The service turned out to be an exact copy of the previous one—and of all the other services at which I assisted in Kamchatka. After it there was more teadrinking at home.

It is the priest’s duty on Christmas Day to go round, accompanied by the psalomchik, to every house in the village, carrying his cross, and, having placed himself in front of the statues which are to be seen in every house, to read out some prayers, always at the same rapid speed, while the psa/omchik chants now and again. While this is in progress a wax candle is lit and the whole family stands behind the priest.

This service takes at the utmost five minutes. After it, the correct thing is to offer the priest something to eat and drink. The results are that both the priest and his companion, who are not accustomed to waste their opportunities, hurry through with the service all the quicker in order to reach the refreshment stage. They

must not display too much eagerness, however, but must allow themselves to be pressed by their host and hostess—who often protest that the liquor is not strong enough. This friendliness is met by the priest’s emptying the glass and assuring them that it was perfectly all right. With the liquor is taken a little meat or salted _ fish, and after any amount of pressing and thanking and bowing the priest and the psalomchik make their way out of the house ceremoniously, and the whole _ performance is gone through again in the next house. As a village consists of from fifteen or twenty to seventy or eighty houses, the reader can imagine for himself the results of all this !

When the priest came to our house he had already been to about ten. With studiously preserved dignity of bearing he stepped in and placed himself before the ikon. The psalomchik followed in his tracks, obviously a little shaky on his legs, but managing to keep erect. While the priest was still going through with his gabbling the psa/omchik began chanting, but the priest did not pay any attention to this and did not attempt to stop it. When he himself began to chant, however, the psalomchik began to titter, and things looked bad; but the ceremony was got through without any greater scandal, and both the priest and his assistant proceeded to empty their glasses quite without regard to the fact that they had still many houses to go to. When at last they left, I noticed that the priest also had some difficulty in maintaining his balance and in holding up the cross steadily. At this stage of the proceedings, by the way, it is etiquette for the host to fire off some shots.

An hour later I went out to have a look at my dogs. The priest and his assistant were just staggering out of another house, but now their round was at an end. They still had a number of houses to visit, but they were not able to get to them, for suddenly the psa/omchik was standing on his head in a snowdrift! He tried to get out of it, but went rolling about until, at last, when he emerged from it, his face was all covered with snow. After moving along a bit on all-fours he finally managed to get on his legs again. Then the priest and he made good their retreat, each to his own dwelling.
Shortly afterwards there was issued a message to the effect that the evening service would not be held. No reason was given.

The rest of Christmas Day is devoted to visiting neighbours: but this is for the men only. They wear their rubber goloshes and long coats and look tremendous swells. In every house there is a table spread with food of various descriptions. You will, however, look in vain there for jukko/a or putrid salmon. What you will see is mountain sheep, capercailzie, salmon trout, and other such delicacies, together with spirits, which are of Japanese origin and contain 96 per cent alcohol, diluted with water. When everyone has had all he wants of these viands then the tea-drinking begins, with fresh rolls; and after that sweets are offered. The sweets are of the same sort in all the houses— indeed it may be said that everything is the same in all the houses. No one likes not to do things as well as his neighbours. Throughout the whole day there is a steady stream in and out of the houses. The talk, for the most part, consists of saying what houses you have been in already, and of telling who were there and where they were going. This terrible conversation 1s punctuated by the efforts of the host and hostess to press upon their guests as much food and spirits as possible. There is no parsimony, and everyone eats and drinks until he can eat and drink no more. And woe betide the man who overlooks one house! He will not be allowed to forget it for long afterwards. The consequence is that on the evening of Christmas Day a great many of the men are “‘ piano,” as the Russians say—in other words, drunk. Even before the afternoon is out not a few of them withdraw into their sleeping-sacks.

On the following day it is the women’s turn to pay visits. The tables are still spread with delicacies and there is incessant tea-drinking. The talk is of the same kind as that of the day before, but in addition there are questions as to where you bought your silk gown and your shoes, and what they cost, etc.; and, naturally, the guests declare how good the food is, and the hostesses lament that it is so poor. As the reader will have observed, there is a certain resemblance be- _ tween civilized society and these dressed-up denizens of the wilds.
But Christmas is not yet over. On the third day comes the greatest spectacle of all. People disguise
