As a rule it is the young people who now take the lead, going about in twos and threes from house to house. When inside, they sit down and do not utter a word. It is now for the people of the house to guess who they are. Usually the young men are dressed as young women and vice versa. If the people of the house cannot guess who they are they go on to the next house, but if they do guess there is great jubilation. They take off their cloth face-coverings and are made to drink tea and eat sweets.

The whole of the third day is taken up with this function and in the evening, as a rule, there is vetjorka (dancing) in some of the houses. As many people as possible are assembled in the one room and the atmosphere could almost be cut with a knife. An outworn gramophone rasps out a tune, or else a fiddler has been brought along from some neighbouring village, should the village itself not boast one. A little space is kept open in the centre of the room, and on it the dancers perform. Several Russian dances are inaugurated and the young people keep at it until the morning. The heat in the room is tropical and the dancers sweat profusely—but that does not matter. Now and again a door is opened for a few seconds and a little fresh air is let in at a temperature of sixty or seventy degrees of frost.

The official Christmas programme is now over, and people can do what they like after this. There are dances, generally, every night until the New Year. The New Year is welcomed in with gun-shots. The festivities continue for several days longer, and it is not until a week after New Year’s Day that the sable-hunters get back to work and life resumes its normal aspects.

After the three days of the Christmas festivities we left Tolbatchik early in the morning on our fifty miles’ journey to the village of Kosyrevsk—which was to be our starting-point for the fjells. That day there began the coldest spell we encountered during the entire period of our expedition. My thermometer had just had an accident. In Tolbatchik, however, I had managed to borrow a quicksilver thermometer from a Russian and this showed that we started at 22° F. The sun was shining and it was a splendid winter’s day. We travelled through beautiful larch-forests, white from hoarfrost. According as the sun sank the temperature went down, and in the course of the afternoon the quicksilver became frozen. When the cold is intense, the snow is no longer katka—i.e. it has become difficult for the sledge to glide over. The runners creak and grate and the dogs have to work twice as hard.

Our hope was to reach a jurta situated about thirty miles from Tolbatchik. But darkness was already coming on when, owing to the intense cold, the dogs had become thoroughly worn out. We ourselves had had continually to get out of the sledge and run alongside it in order to keep warm. We were most anxious, however, not to have to spend the night out-of-doors, so we drove on and on. While we were having a rest we gave the dogs a ration of fish to encourage them, and when at last the moon rose they “ bucked up ” and we went along well. Late in the evening we did at last reach the jurta. No palace could have been more welcome to our eyes.

We were frozen to the bone, so the first thing to be done was to get wood for a fire. It was no easy matter in the moonlight to find the kind of dry wood needed, but we did not require a great deal at the start. What was important was to secure enough to enable us to boil the kettle. We made some coffee and I remember we drank immense quantities of it. Then we felt ourselves again and were able to go off in quest of some more wood.

We sat as near the stove as possible and made our entries for the day, delighting in the warmth, which was heavenly. The poor dogs, as usual, had to remain out in the cold. The lot of a sledge-dog in Kamchatka is certainly an unenviable one. He never in all his life is allowed inside a house: no matter how severe the snowstorm may be, or how biting the frost, he must always remain outside—yet he seldom loses courage.

At midnight we crept into our sleeping-sacks and slept. Our fatigue was so intense that it overcame even the effects of the strong coffee: but after a couple of hours we awoke. It was so terribly cold that further sleep was impossible. ‘The mercury in the thermometer which we had with us in the hut was frozen, and the coffee in the coffee-pot, which was standing near the hearth, was frozen solid. We could not lie still.

There was nothing for it but for me to go out into the moonlight again and get some more wood—one of the toughest jobs I ever tackled in my life! The dogs lifted their heads to look at me, astonished, when they saw me coming out of the hut in the middle of the night. Probably they were startled by the fear that they were going to be disturbed and put into harness again already. "They were accustomed to being never able to know when their “ boss”’ might not be making a start.

We drank two more mugs of coffee each, after which it was useless to think of trying to get to sleep again; so we sat by the fire and talked until daylight began to appear. Then we harnessed the dogs: we harnessed them a couple at a time, returning to the hut between whiles so that our fingers should not get frozen.

We had only about twenty miles still to cover before getting to Kosyrevsk, but it was to prove a hard day. The weather was as clear and fine as the day before, and I could never have believed that a larch-forest covered with rime-frost could look so lovely. When we emerged from it on to a tundra we had before our eyes a marvellous panoramic view over a snowclad volcano world—we agreed it was the most beautiful sight we had yet witnessed in all Kamchatka. Five volcanoes raised their heads before us, and in the middle of them stood the mightiest of all, Klutchefskaja, which we were now approaching. We decided to try to take some photographs so as to have a souvenir, however faint, of this magnificent spectacle, but the camera shutter refused to work. Whenever the temperature was very low it always worked badly, and sometimes it would not work at all. The compound shutter on the second camera, also, was not working normally ; but it did work.
While we were busy with the two cameras my wife’s fingers became quite white. I kneaded them with snow and got them right, but my own fingers very nearly became frozen while I was doing so.

The moon had already been shining a long time when at last we reached the village, almost frozen to death. Some hot tea brought us to our senses again. We both realized that it might have been the end of us if we had had to spend that night out in the open.

The intense cold lasted two more days. There was not a breath of wind and everything was bathed in a kind of mist. Carrion-crows and magpies, which always frequent the villages during the winter, sat about rolled up into balls, with their feathers all on end and their feet covered by their thick feathery dress. All the dogs of the village lay about rolled up into balls and not moving. When I went out to feed my own they did not jump up and bark as was their wont, but lay quite still until I threw them their rations. No one in the village could recall such cold weather. All work was suspended, and everyone just sat and waited for the weather to change. The thermometers in the possession of the Russians in the village were all frozen. Two days later the change came. A lot of snow fell, however, and all progress was made impossible.
We had now reached the starting-point for our

expedition to the region of the nomads, and all we had to do was to get into touch with our friend, Savonoh, who was to be our guide. He had spent his Christmas in Klutchi and had not yet returned. But one day, when I was out on an excursion on skis in the outskirts of the village, I suddenly met five sledges coming from the north. The first was driven by Savonoh, the others by two Koryaks and two Lamuts. They were having a difficult time of it in the deep snow and the dogs were panting from their exertions; but Savonoh was his old self—the same glittering black eyes and the same smile. After his dogs had had a day’s rest he was ready to accompany us.

HEN at last we were ready to start the caravan consisted of no fewer than seventeen dog-sledges—for a number of other traders in furs followed the Ainu’s tracks. They knew that by so doing they would find the right way.

It was quite an international company which fared out that January morning from Kosyrevsk towards the mountains in the west. Only one person drove in each sledge, except for ours. The eighteen of us represented no fewer then eight races: there were Russians, Kamchadals, Koreans, Lamuts, Koryaks, Tartars, Ainus and Swedes. It may be regarded as a piece of pure bad luck that there were no Chinese—they are apt to be found everywhere. Every sledge was drawn by dogs, and the noise became deafening when all the hundred and seventy began to bark together.
In the far distance loomed the fjells, and the snowclad Anaunga volcano rose up from among them as though mounting guard.

Our dogs were in excellent condition after their rest in the village, and they were in all the better humour for having so many companions. Sledge-dogs always work better when there are a number of sledges travelling together. But the snow was lying loose and deep on the sandra over which we had to go after getting free of the woods. The first team of dogs, who had to plough a way for themselves, had the stiffest task, and we had to take it in turn to go first. When we came to the wooded region again we called a halt, as the dogs had become too tired to be able to go forward in the deep snow.

Towards the evening the woods grew more and more primeval in their nature. It became a fearful job to make any progress over the rough and rather hilly ground ; it made one perspire so that one had to take

_off one’s furs despite the frosty weather. One’s arms and legs were in dire peril as the sledge darted in and out between the trees; very often, indeed, one had to turn with lightning-like quickness to avoid colliding with the trunk of a tree.

The long procession swung forward through the dense woodland until it became so dark that it was impossible to see whither we were going. Suddenly there flashed out in front of us between the tree-trunks the flame of a fire. The sledges with the best teams of dogs had gone on ahead of us and had, it seemed, discovered a suitable spot to camp-out in for the night. It was in a grove of tall larches by the bank of a little river, and a big log fire had been lit. Round this we all took up our position. On every sledge there was an axe, and soon the air rang out with the sound of axes striking the dry trunks of the larches. Soon another splendid log-fire was ablaze not far from the first. In

order to avoid having to melt snow for our water a hole was made through the ice on the river—ice nearly two feet in thickness—and soon any number of teakettles were boiling over the two camp-fires.

We had a delightful evening sitting round those fires. We told each other funny stories and shouts of laughter went up. Savonoh, as usual, was the leader in all this, and he narrated in his extraordinarily funny Russian the most astonishing tales concerning his adventures, while we drank our tea and ate our jukkola and dried our. clothes, made damp by perspiration.

The sky was starlit, which boded well for next day’s weather: consequently we did not trouble to set up our tent, but just camped-out in a way which my wife and I practised afterwards throughout the rest of the winter. We merely spread a few branches and twigs on the snow by the fire and then laid out our sleepingsacks on them. The entire company now ranged itself radii-like in a circle round both the fires and went off to sleep in their sleeping-sacks.

Well into the night we were awakened by the concerted barking of all the hundred and seventy dogs. Kamchatkan dogs have a unique faculty for barking musically, so to speak. ‘Their barking is almost like a kind of singing, and when one begins all the others lift up their snouts in the air like wolves and join in the concert. The tone is always plaintive and melancholy, and if you are out in the wilds, and are awakened by this long-drawn barking, you are apt to become perturbed. In the chant-like sounds given out by the sledge-dogs in the wilds, especially on cold moonlight nights, I imagined sometimes I heard the well-founded plaints of generations of the breed against their human masters in respect to ill-treatment, mismanagement and neglect.

Already before daybreak the earliest risers among us were up and busy over the getting of firewood. A certain strength of character is needed to enable you to abandon your sleeping-sack in a biting frost, especially before it is light. It is a great temptation to linger on a bit, so as a rule one takes turn about to rise first and light the fire. When the fire is lit there is no trouble about emerging from one’s sack.

We had radiant sunshine to gladden us that morning, but on the other hand it was bitterly cold. The sledges had to be doctored a little. They were turned over on the side so that the runners could be rubbed over with warm water applied with a bit of hair-covered skin. The runners are made as hard as glass by the water, which becomes frozen while it is being applied. The difference in the running makes itself felt at once.

The rise of the ground on the next stage of our journey soon made progress very difficult, while the density of the wood and the number of branches blown down made matters worse. What was worst of all, however, was the regular race which now began between the various sledges. ‘The company consisted mostly, as I have said, of fur-traders and the natives whom they brought with them to help to carry their wares. It was the object of each and all of them to arrive at the first Lamut jurta so as to have the best chance of securing sables. But after the race had continued for a great portion of the day Savonoh declared that for his part he did not mind whether he arrived first or last: he would get the same number of sables either way—he knew his haunts.

Many guileful tricks were resorted to by the participators in the race. One of the most successful and most unscrupulous was, for the one who had got a little way ahead to break into small pieces a couple of dried salmon and to drop them on the ground at suitable intervals. The next team of dogs would unfailingly detect these bits of salmon and there would be fights for them, the competing animals getting into a regular scrimmage and entangling themselves in the traces, so that the driver must stop and get them into proper order again. After they have gone on a bit the same thing happens again—the fur-trader affected becoming angrier and angrier. Perhaps he may take his revenge on another occasion by rubbing bear’s grease on the runners of his rival’s sledge. ‘That is apt to be equally effective.

The higher we got the more difficult things became for us. Once IJ very nearly had my foot crushed against a tree. My wife also had a narrow escape of a serious injury—a nasty cut just above her right eye. It looked like a bad wound. Her eye became full of blood and we had to melt some snow to wash the blood away. Had the branch struck her a fraction of an inch lower, she would have lost her eye.

While we halted for tea I discovered to my alarm that one of my sledge-runners was damaged. It proved to be only cracked, however, and there seemed ground for hope that it would last all right until the evening, so that I should not have to waste time mending it during the daytime. I drove as carefully as possible, afterwards, and the runner did last until the evening, when, with the help of Savonoh, an axe and a knife, | contrived to mend it after a fashion.

That night we encamped in a declivity of the fjell in the same fashion as on the night before, and before the next morning’s sun was high in the heavens we were well on our way again, toiling up and tearing down one mountain ridge after another.

We were now right in the middle of the fjell region. Twice in the course of the morning we had to fix the dogs’ iron chains round the sledge-runners and unharness the dogs and hold them in leash behind the sledge in order to manage the descent at specially steep points. Several men had to lend a hand in dealing with each sledge.

At one point suddenly the dogs began to increase their pace tremendously. They became absolutely wild, barking frantically as they dashed along. We guessed that we must be coming close to the reindeer, and before long we saw two small black dots moving far away in the distance. With my field-glasses I discovered that they were two reindeer-sledges, which were coming in our direction. The dogs had not seen them yet but had got wind of them. Soon the drivers of the sledges perceived us, and we saw them make a great swerve to one side. A reindeer-sledge and a dogsledge must never meet. If they did; all that would remain of the reindeer would be a pool of blood and some horns and bones and bits of skin. The nomads hesitated to draw near to our caravan and we continued to advance, but now it was almost impossible to keep the dogs in order. Their blood was up and they kept excitedly on the alert for signs of their quarry, but they did not see the reindeer this time.

On every one of the longer descents we had narrow escapes of our lives, and we wondered several times whether we should reach one of the jurtas undamaged. The dogs had become disregardful of words of command: they were obsessed with their desire to get ahead. We were driven up against tree-trunks, knocking our legs and arms, while applying the brake for all we were worth. Although it was very cold, and I drove in an ordinary short double-breasted jacket and wore no cap, I sweated as though we were in the tropics. My hair was white from the frost and my right arm, which I used for holding the brake, ached all over.

At last we came out on a high plateau where the air was delightfully fresh. Here one could take it easy, no longer applying the brake, and letting the dogs go as fast as they liked. But we soon came to steep declivities again. On one I had for the first time to abandon all control of the dogs, in order to save my wife’s life and my own. I saw that we should be dashed against a big tree-trunk and it was out of the question to steer the sledge wide of it at the rate at which we were going. My wife and I both slipped off the sledge, she on her side, I on mine, and went whirling about in the snow. The sledge went against the tree—not absolutely straight, however, but a little to the side. The front bow broke and the sledge was overturned, with the runners in the air. This impeded its advance. Had the dogs and the sledge proceeded a couple of hundred yards farther all would have been destroyed, for there was an abyss gaping below. Cold shivers went down my back when, presently, I looked down over the precipice and saw what would have happened to them had the sledge not capsized.

After we had pulled ourselves together a bit I proceeded to amuse myself by mending the sledge. Savonoh helped me as usual. We had to provide a new front bow. We cut down a sufficiently thick birchtree, made up a fire and put on the tea-kettle—but not to make tea this time. The stem of the birch was made pliable by being held over the fire and bent into the shape of a U. Then some hard, undressed strips of sealskin were taken out of the sledge and placed in the hot water in the kettle, where they soon became quite soft. With a sharp-pointed knife the necessary holes were made in the bow, which was then made fast, in the place of the old one, with the securest possible knots, and so fixed as to be capable of holding out against fresh collisions.

The jurta, we felt, could not now be very far off, and sure enough very soon the dogs, who had calmed down a bit, began to bark again and to tear along at full speed. They had got wind of the herd of reindeer. The route was clear now, so I could let the dogs go as fast as they liked. Before very long we saw a little jurta, made of hides and most beautifully placed beside a river. An instant later we found ourselves in the first of the Lamut encampments, after a month and a half’s journey from Petropavlovsk. I was completely worn out and my whole body ached after the exertions of the previous few hours.

UT of the low juria there streamed a number () of fur-clad human beings, big and little, all with the same strongly marked Mongolian features. All were clad in shaggy furs-and gazed curiously at us out of their narrow eye-slits. The coats of the women were studded with pearl embroideries and hung with metal ornaments, sledge-bells and small bells of other kinds, which tinkled at every step they took.
While the dogs continued to bark energetically the Lamuts invited us, in their halting Russian, to step in and drink tea.

In the dim light within, the natives sat in the middle of the jurta, both the men and the women smoking | pipes. We exchanged greetings with them and accepted their invitation to sit down on the reindeer-hides stretched out on the ground like a carpet.

They all kept their eyes on us curiously. My wife, especially, attracted the attention of the female section of the group. They told us that only once before had a woman paid them a visit. The men talked Russian quite well, but the women, as a rule, knew only a few words of it. Savonoh introduced me in the following words: “ Fevo ni kommersant, jevo Expedizia, jevo jurta schipka daljoko xa more” (‘Fe is not a trader, he is Expedition, his jurta lies a terribly long way off, on the other side of the sea’),
made of reindeer-hides. The number of these inner tents depends upon the size of the family. Each family has its own. During the day the front coverings of these inner tents are drawn up.

The hostess in the inner tent in which we sat took out a dirty-looking little wooden box, in which some cups and glasses and bowls were packed together in an almost black rag, which once upon a time had been white. She placed these on a tray, and poured out tea from an enormous copper kettle. My wife took some biscuits out of a bag and put them on the tray. In less than a minute they were all gone. From every part of the jurta there was a rush for them !

After we had drunk several cups of tea the women offered us dry reindeer-hide shoes so that we should not continue to sit in our own, which were wet. This custom of offering dry shoes to guests we met with in almost all the Lamut jurias.

After a little while we were invited to partake of a meal, The Lamuts’ food is the same morning, noon and night—namely, boiled reindeer. Pieces of the meat are served on a wooden tray and fingers serve as forks —sheath-knives being used to cut up the bits. The Lamuts cook always without using salt : every traveller, therefore, carries with him his own little tin of salt, into which he sticks the pieces before eating them.

Our travelling companions had already begun their business negotiations in regard to the sables; and in the jurta we could see how the sable-skins were produced; and how the bargaining proceeded. The prices varied from one hundred and fifty to two hundred Japanese yen—that is to say, from about sixteen to twenty-two pounds: the payments were all made in kind, never in money. So that the Lamuts should not get it into their heads that they were not being paid enough for their skins, the traders would sometimes give more than they were asked, but they increased the prices of their own goods accordingly: they put on a charge of some shillings a pound merely to cover the cost of carriage over the fjells. Tea and tobacco were the most important items in the merchandise. Strips of sealskin available for making into lassos, reins, etc., were also in great request. The Lamuts buy, too, a good deal of flour, with which to make cakes, as well as biscuits and sweets. Like other primitive races they are also greatly addicted to spirits. One of the traders had forty spirit bottles on his sledge.

In the evening the outer coverings of the inner tents were lowered and each family went into its own compartment. A candle, bought by the Lamuts from one of the traders, was lit, and my wife and I sat and talked with our host and hostess. But before I could get them to answer my questions properly I had to tell them a lot about ourselves and about Sweden, and what life there was like. They were tremendously interested, and they wanted above all to know what kind of animals we hunted there, etc. They bombarded us with all sorts of questions, and their eyes opened wide when I told them that we also had a race very like the Lamuts in the northern portion of our country—a race who made their living out of reindeer, and who had jurtalike homes. I had to tell them a lot about the Lapps, and when I showed them a coloured post card with a picture of Lapp huts and sledges on it they were hugely excited, and asked any number of questions. The Lapp sledges did not meet with their approval. They compared them to the Kamchatkan canoes, and asked whether it was possible to get anywhere in such a trough. They begged me to show the Lapps, when I got back to Sweden, what the Lamut sledges were like, so that they might learn to make them. And then the Lapp clothes! The women wore no pearls. Perhaps there were no sables to sellin Lapland? They indulged in many other such comments and reflections. We became very good friends, and the suspicious attitude which they had shown at first disappeared completely and entirely. Now they were ready to tell me anything I asked.

We spent the night in the inner compartment of the tent, where we were all very closely packed together. The Lamuts began to get up before daybreak, and at a very early hour we were all drinking our morning tea.

The jurta was situated in a valley. All around we saw the snowclad fjells with their slopes: on these mountains the reindeer were grazing. Immediately we had finished drinking tea two of the Lamuts put on their skis—shorter still than the skis used by the Kamchadals, and with underneath them the shorthaired hide from the reindeer’s lee—and made their way up into the mountains to drive the horde down to the jurta. Very soon we could see against the snow-white mountain-sides a dark swaying mass which moved in our direction. With my field-glasses I could see to the side of this two small black marks—the two Lamuts. The Lamuts never use their dogs to help them in managing their herds, as do the Lapps. This surprised me the more as in every Lamut hut there are a number of hunting dogs, which have a great reputation for their intelligence; but so it is, neither the Lamuts nor the Koryaks ever use their dogs in dealing with their reindeer.

While we awaited the coming of the herd we went back into the jurta and warmed ourselves at the fire. Suddenly we heard the tinkling of bells—it sounded very melodious in the frosty air. There they came, streaming down toward us, a thousand of them, fine animals, notably larger than our Lapland reindeer. Most of them were grey-coloured, some very light in colouring, others snowy white, a few spotted.

The sledge-dogs, which were tied up to the trees and bushes all around, began to bark and tear at their chains—especially my dogs, who now saw reindeer for the first time. The wolf in them asserted itself, and they would certainly have thrown themselves on one of the reindeer had they broken loose.

The reindeer did not pay much attention to the dogs——they were accustomed to the sound of their barking—but the Lamuts asked me to make sure that my dogs were securely tied. ‘The herd were now spread over the whole neighbourhood of the jurta and they displayed remarkably little fear—one could even stroke some of them with one’s hands. When I photographed them some of them came up and began nosing about the camera. A good many of them went right up to the jurta, looking out for places where the Lamuts had cast their water, and they ate with relish the snow where this had been done. Often several would engage in a sort of scrimmage to get near such spots. When they began to snatch at the covering of the tent, and at the provision stores packed away outside, the Lamuts drove them away, but they kept coming back.

There was now the question of picking out and catching hold of a number of reindeer to drive and ride, for some of the Lamuts were off to another jurta at a distance. All the male Lamuts in the jurta busied themselves over this. Some of them drove the reindeer to and fro, while others with lassos captured those which were marked out. With wonderful adroitness they slung the twenty-yard lassos round the horns of these animals. It took them only half-an-hour to capture them all.

Then the reindeer-sledges were brought forward. The Lamuts’ reindeer-sledges are veritable works of art. [hey are slender and elegant and wonderfully strong, and are made entirely of birch. As with the Kamchadal dog-sledges, you will look in vain for a

single nail or screw. All the joints in their case also are kept together by straps, not of sealskin—like those of the dog-sledges—but of narrow, undressed reindeerhide. The sledge thus is kept pliable and supple and, despite its slenderness, incredibly strong ; and like the dog-sledges it can be mended anywhere out in the forest.

Two reindeer are harnessed to the sledge side by side. The harness is very simple, consisting merely of a large loop made of a broad band of sealskin, which is hung round the neck and between the forelegs. Reins are attached to the head of every animal in the team and by means of them you can steer in any direction. The whip consists of a long thin stick with a sharp bone button at the end of it, and the brake is made of a piece of reindeer horn, with an iron top to it, which is attached to the outside of the right-hand runner, just where you place your foot. It is so contrived that you only need to press your foot against it to make the iron-shod point press down into the snow and act as a brake.

After the sledge had been got ready two riding animals were brought forward and the neatest little saddles of reindeer-hide laid on them. The Lamuts use reindeer to ride on—a practice which is very unusual among reindeer-breeding peoples and which, except among other Tungus tribes, is only to be met with among Karagos and the Soyots in the Sayansk Mountains in Central Asia. The saddles are placed much more forward on the reindeer than on a horse.

One sits almost above the fore-legs, and one guides the animal with a rein. There are no stirrups. In order to help the rider to preserve his balance a long staff is often carried, especially by women. One rides at a walking or trotting pace, never at a gallop. Reindeer are not equal to the strain involved in galloping. But in other respects they make very serviceable mounts. They will cover thirty miles with a ridef and not be any the worse. My wife and I made the experiment of riding on reindeer, but only for short distances round the jurias. ‘The Lamuts did not much care for us to use their reindeer for longer rides, as they thought we were too heavy for them.
When all the reindeer required had been caught, and harnessed and saddled, the herd was driven back from the jurta and placed out again on the fjells until a fresh lot should be wanted.

It was in our programme not to make a long stay anywhere until we got to the next jurta, which had several others near it. We made up our minds, therefore, to set forth at once in the company of these Lamuts and in the same direction. Now when reindeersledges and dog-sledges are to travel the same way, the dog-sledges have to go first and the reindeersledges have to follow at a good distance behind. If the reindeer were to go first the result would be that the dogs would be excited by their tracks and would be trying excitedly all the time to chase them.
Laden with quite a large quantity of ethnographical material which we had acquired by barter in the jurta,

we started off in the company of my faithful friend Savonoh, who sat and hummed to himself in his delight over the successful business he had done in respect to sables, whereas several of the other traders had not got a single skin. His face shone with pleasure and his black eyes gleamed as he told me how envious of him the others were. ‘To tease them still more he would take up a sable-skin and wave it about in the air, calling out to the dogs: ‘‘ Look at this, dogs! See what a fine sable looks like!’ But he would do this only when his rivals were near enough to see and hear him! But this was only during the earlier portion of the day, for soon we had other things to think about. Savonoh had already encouraged me by announcing in the morning that the ground we had coped with yesterday was a tundra compared with what we were to encounter to-day. Our hearts would be in a state of palpitation, he declared, we should have to put out such efforts. 3 Twice we had to unharness the dogs, fix their chains under the runners, and, combining together, lower the sledges one by one down steep declivities; but now we came to the most formidable height we had yet encountered. When we stood at the foot of it I thought it would not be possible to get the sledges up such an incline. We all concentrated on getting one sledge up at atime. ‘The dogs, admirable beasts that they were, tugged and tugged. ‘Their tongues hung out of their mouths and they puffed and blew like bellows. We got along yard by yard. When anyone let go his hold for

a second the sledge slipped back. When at last we had got the first two sledges to the top we were as weak as rags, and our hearts were going pit-a-pat ; but we had no time to rest. The dogs were tied up, the sledges turned over on one side, and we had to make our way down again in order to lend a hand with the next sledge.

At last we had them all up. The view from the top was magnificent. Wherever we turned our gaze we saw snow-white fjells and volcanoes bathed in sunshine ; the atmosphere up there was delicious. In the overheated condition into which we had worked ourselves the icy cold wind was as agreeable as the softest summer breeze could be in other circumstances. What one most needed was something to cool one, and I ate snow unceasingly. It was the only way to get cool apart from washing one’s face in snow. We did this also repeatedly. I went about bare-headed after this sweat-bath. My hair, being wet through with perspiration, became white and stiff from the frost.

Suddenly Savonoh damaged his sledge. So as not to have to make a second halt we now took our rest for tea, although it was difficult to get wood for the fire. Before we had finished, the Lamuts who were following us came in sight. The dogs got wind of them first and wanted to be off after them: we had to tie them up firmly and threaten them with strong words. The Lamuts pulled up a couple of hundred yards behind us, tethered the reindeer and joined us at our teadrinking.

In the dusk we reached the River Bistraja, on the bank of which was situated the jurta for which we were making, but when we got there I was feeling more utterly tired out than ever before. My whole body was shaking, and I had only just enough energy left to tie up the dogs. Then we went in—my wife was almost as tired out as I was—and sat ourselves down among a new lot of Lamuts, as friendly and hospitable as the other. For some hours I was unable to eat anything, and I still remember how difficult I found it to summon up all my remaining energies to go out to feed the dogs. The poor animals were in a sorry state also; they lay quite still until I placed the fish in front of them—some of them did not eat up all their ration. I may mention here that, like all my travelling companions, I had taken with me enough jukkola for a whole week. The Lamuts do not care to give reindeerflesh to the dogs. Some Lamuts have teams of dogs of their own, and in these cases as a rule they have jukkola, but not in great quantities, so it is well to take with one as much as one has room for in the sledge.

Although many subsequent days were difficult, that day remains in my memory as the most exhausting of any throughout the whole expedition. During the night I could get only a couple of hours’ sleep. But now we had reached a spot which we thought of making our headquarters for a while, and that was a good thing.

We had scarcely entered the jurta before the Lamuts in chorus begged to see the picture post card with the Lapp scene on it. Rumours of it had got there before us; and in all the other jurtas we visited it was the same thing—the akja called forth always the same disapproval. “ And they look so poor, with no beads on them,” the Lamuts would add.

Later in the evening Savonoh persuaded the Lamuts to dance their national dance (Norgai). Himself a master of the art, he managed to assemble them all in the jurta, and in the firelight we were now to be witnesses of this singular dance, which is performed in this way: the Lamuts, both men and women, having taken up their positions in a circle round the fire, swing first in this direction, then in that, discharging at each other a kind of animal-like, snarling sound, while they alternately wink and grimace. The dance, if so it may be called, is not beautiful, nor is there any variety in it— it is merely strange. It is inconceivable how they can keep it up so long without becoming hoarse. Norgali is a form of amusement much enjoyed by the Lamuts.

Next morning the traders proceeded to other jurtas. Soon after their departure began the wildest drinkingbout imaginable. All the traders had paid for their furs partly in spirits, and now the spirits began to disappear. Within half-an-hour all the men in the jurta were completely intoxicated—some of them in the violent fashion, some going off quietly into a drunken sleep. One old man was a very bad case. He began to fight with the others, drew his knife, and regularly ran amuck. He foamed at the mouth and went tearing about like a wild animal. Suddenly he went bang into the fire. We all rushed forward and pulled him out.

After this the women, and such of the men as were not entirely bereft of their senses, brought out some stout straps made of sealskin and bound him hand and foot so that he could not move. Presently he fell asleep and lay there like a log.

My wife and I spent a good portion of the day on a skiing excursion to a neighbouring jurta, while our hosts slept themselves sober. When we got back in the afternoon most of them were recovering. One of the older men, who was of a quiet disposition, was beating his drum and chanting monotonous Lamut melodies. He kept at it all the rest of the day and half the night without stopping. Strictly speaking, the Lamuts have no right toa “magic” drum. They are nominally Christians and belong officially to the Greek Catholic religion. In every jurta there hangs an ikon, and they often make the sign of the cross in front of it. But in their heart and soul they cling to their old Shamanism—that is to say, the art of changing the course of events with the help of guardian spirits, and the principal instrument they resort to for this is the “magic” drum. With its help they call forth the spirits.

The old man became more and more exalted the longer he played. At last he put on his special Shaman dress. This consists of a special Shaman fur with many beads on it and much embroidered, as well as a fur cap or cowl, hung round with long bead-sprinkled leather tufts which prevent the wearer from seeing anything. As he was nominally a Christian, he felt a little constrained over the notion of calling forth spirits in our presence, and he declared more than twenty times that it was really only in former times that they used to beat the drum in this way. Now it was only the old men who did so, he said, adding candidly: “And only when they are drunk!’’ Our hostess in the inner compartment of the tent was also much concerned over the old man, and kept repeating that they had been given the “‘ magic”’ drum by Koryaks, and that it was precisely the same thing as the Russian ba/alajka.

After a couple of days we went on with two Lamuts to another jurta. It lay in a glen about half-a-day’s journey from the encampment at Bistraja, with fascinating vistas in every direction. Here we met the most sympathetic Lamut family of all those we came across up in the fjells, and here also we spent several days. Rumours about us had reached our hosts long before, and they said they had been looking out for days past for the arrival of the travellers from afar.

Our arrival at the jurta, as it happened, was not of a very dignified nature, for when I was negotiating the last bit of the slope down to it we made a sudden curve, and made something like a somersault in sight of everyone. The dogs had no thoughts for anything but reindeer, and paid no attention to my efforts to pull up. However, we were none the less heartily welcomed. In the inner compartment of the jurta, into which we now made our way, dwelt the Lamut, Ivan Petrovitch, and his wife, Maura, and their little five-year-old son, Ilja. Even before we had drunk our first cup of tea they wanted to see the famous Lapp picture post
card. This had come to serve as a sort of letter of introduction !

I think it is at once pitiful and absurd that these poor skin-clad children of the wilds should have been forced to let themselves be baptized by the caricatures of priests who are to be found here in the villages, and who are in no respects their superiors. Why should not the Lamuts be suffered to cling to their “‘ magic’ drums as did their ancestors from time immemorial, and why should they not keep to their old names, which smack of the wilderness, instead of having to be christened under such names as “ Ivan Petrovitch’’—names that are better suited to gentlemen in long frock-coats and indiarubber goloshes? I admit that the missionaries have done good in many regions, but up here in these fjells they have not been a success. When the representatives of the new creeds are of so low a type as those in Kamchatka generally are, they can inspire no respect among their proselytes. They should convert themselves before they try converting others.

Well, this Ivan Petrovitch was in any case an interesting and sympathetic man, and for three whole days I plied him with questions regarding the life of the Lamuts and their methods of dealing with the reindeer. My wife; who won the hearts of the women everywhere, got them to tell her all about their hard lives, their joys and sorrows, their marriage and funeral customs. Maura was not only the best-looking but also the most sympathetic of all the Lamut women we met. She was still in the bloom of youth and had not yet acquired the wrinkles which the hardness of the life soon sets upon the faces of denizens of this region.

We had many noteworthy experiences while in that jurta, ‘Ne got a glimpse into the daily life of a Lamut family, and we had rides on reindeer-back, and accompanied our host and hostess in their sledge on visits to the neighbouring jurtas. We got a strong impression of the peacefulness and happiness of their existence. They possess everything they need.

The herd of reindeer, of course, is their chief possession, but unlike their Koryak neighbours they do not depend exclusively on it. Hunting is an important source of livelihood for them also; and they divide their energies between this and the minding of the reindeer; consequently they cannot go in for such large herds of reindeer as the Koryaks,; who live by them exclusively and who hunt only now and again for pleasure. Neither the Lamuts nor the Koryaks milk the reindeer as do the Lapps. When I questioned them about this it evoked both astonishment and amusement. The whole jurta went off into roars of laughter, and they wondered how I could suppose that they would drink up the milk intended for the calves.

As the Lamuts do not keep large herds—generally speaking, each jurta has from a couple of hundred to at most a thousand animals—they do not like to spoil or slaughter more of them than is absolutely necessary. If, therefore, the Lamuts happen to live near a rich Koryak who is able to keep several thousand herd, they generally prefer to go to him and beg for some of his instead, and the good-natured Koryaks, who take pride in their wealth, go out and bring in as many animals as the Lamuts want. These transactions take place in the most friendly way; and it is to be presumed that the Lamuts make some return to the Koryaks, although this has never come before me. But the Koryaks often said to me after the Lamuts had been to them on such missions: “‘ Well, you know, these Lamuts are impossible people! They keep coming to us all the winter after reindeer. They won’t kill a single deer of their own, just because we give them all they need. Really we ought not to give them a single one; they might learn then to look after their own a bit better instead of wandering about after sable.” But the next time the Lamuts came they would be as hospitably received as ever, entertained to tea and a meat meal, and return with their sledges full of reindeerflesh. The Lamuts put the matter to me then: “‘ Those dirty Koryaks have such a lot of reindeer that we should be fools if we killed our own.”’ Both races talked ill of each other to me, and I got the impression that the friendly formalities in practice between them were of the same sort as the protestations of mutual cordiality with which the sharpest diplomatic communications invariably end.

The day’s happenings in the jurta are quite uniform. They get up early, as a rule before it is quite light, so that the stars are to be seen through the smoke-vent if the atmosphere is clear. The first thing to be done is to light the fire. There is always a supply of wood

ready indoors for this of a morning. Then the teakettle is boiled and they all warm themselves by drinking their tea, and those of them who are so inclined —and they are not so many—wash theniselves. They do so in this fashion. They put the spout of the big tea-kettle in their mouths and suck until their mouths are full of water. Then they spit out the water on their open hands and wash their faces with it a bit. When my wife and I saw for the first time how they wash their children we could not stop laughing. The mother filled her mouth with the water and then squirted out a jet of it right in the face of the bawling infant, and proceeded to rub it with a wad of moss. As a towel she used a very fine and soft wood-wool, which the Lamut women prepare by scraping, with a sharp knife, long thin chips of newly cut sallow-wood. This is also used to clean the teacups.
Some of the men go out at once on their skis to tend the herd, and drive them home to the jurta if any of the animals are wanted.

The women, as a rule, set to work preparing skins —a task they were generally engaged on whenever we paid a visit. They also make all their own clothes as well as those of their men, and this is work which occupies a great deal of their time. All their clothes are made of skins, and, except for their caps and a number of trimmings, only reindeer-skin is used. The caps are often of wolf- or dog-skin, and when they are to be particularly fine, of otter-skin. The summer clothes are made of chamois-skin, which is so treated as to be made quite soft. The Lamuts, in contrast with the Koryaks, wear their coats open.

The preparation of the skins is carried out in various fashions, according to the use to which they are to be put. But all the tanning is begun in the same way. The dried skin is scraped on the flesh side until it is free of all fat and tissues. Then the flesh side is rubbed —according to one method in frequent use—with a decoction of alder-bark and urine, after which it is folded up and must lie in some warm place over the night. Next day it is again thoroughly scraped and then kneaded until it becomes as soft as cloth and is ready for use.
All clothes are sewn with sinews instead of with thread, and with triangular needles. Ordinary round sewing-needles are very unsuitable for sewing skins.

The innumerable glass beads on the Lamuts’ gar-. ments are greatly prized. In every jurta we visited the women asked us for beads. The little store we brought with us had a brisk sale, and we often regretted that we had not brought a bigger supply with us from Sweden. Beads were absolutely the best articles to barter with. They are strung together in long rows on sinews which are sewn fast to the clothes. When a dress is worn out the beads are transferred to a new one.

The Lamuts are very clever at dyeing the skins they use for clothes. The women’s dresses, over and above the beads, are always adorned with a great number of small borders of differently coloured bits of skin. A beautiful red colour is got by dyeing with whortleberry juice; another is got with alder-bark. The fringes of the Shaman’s cap, for instance, consist of tassels made out of the skin of unborn seals dyed in whortleberry juice.

When the Lamuts journey down to the villages dressed in their handsome fur caps, coats and boots the Kamchadals and Russians always try to beg these from them, and sometimes are dishonest enough to make them drunk and then steal their fine clothes, which they replace with worn-out and ragged skins. The Lamuts often complained to us about this, and declared that they would in future put on the worst clothes they had when visiting Russians and Kamchadals.

All the women in Ivan Petrovitch’s jurta smoked. The women use special pipes, different from those of the men. Every pipe has a cleaner, which usually is hung on to the tobacco-pouch by a strap. This is often inlaid with copper and, like the pipe, made by the Lamuts themselves. Side by side with this pipe-cleaner there is often attached to the men’s tobacco-pouch a little pincers-like apparatus, which also is inlaid. This is used with which to pull out hairs. The Lamuts, like the Koryaks, have very scanty beards. They do not like beards and they pull out the hairs of their beards with these pincers.

When I asked for one of these pincers, meaning to add to my ethnographical collections, its owner remarked that it would be a mistake for me to begin pulling out my own beard—it hurt so much, he said, that I would do better to let my beard grow. One had to begin earlier. And in order to enforce his warning he offered to pull out a hair for me, so that I could tell how it felt.

The tobacco-pouch was often handsomely embroidered with beads. To make the tobacco last longer the Lamuts scrape off shavings from a certain kind of dwarf fir-tree. These are cut into small bits and mixed with it. Almost all the Lamuts took snuff. To make the snuff stronger they mixed it with ashes from birch-funguses, which they collected in the woods. Often when out with a Lamut I would suddenly see him stop his sledge and climb up a tree after such a fungus.

It was entertaining to see how the children amused themselves outside the jurta. A very popular diversion was to slide on their knees. Like their elders; the children wore boots made of the skin of the reindeer leg—its fur is short, glossy and extremely durable. It was funny to see the little skin-covered bundles take a short run and then throw themselves on their knees down a little incline. They slid down swiftly, and it often ended in their going head over heels. They evidently got a lot of fun out of it.

Another amusement, which involved more in the way of direct training for the future, was that of throwing a lasso. Sometimes one small boy would run to and fro with a reindeer horn in his hand while another would try to throw the lasso over it; but ordinarily a staff was set up with a long band fastened to the top. At the lower end of the band hung a piece of wood and the band would be sent swinging round in a circle. Several boys at once could try their hand at throwing their lasso over the flying bit of wood.

Ivan Petrovitch liked to sit and talk about his little boy, Ilja; who was only five years old, but who could ride like a grown-up man, and who already helped to look after the herd. He had even begun to set traps and had caught two ermine—he had bartered one of them for a tea-mug and the other for a bell for his riding-reindeer. In his father’s company during the preceding summer he had had his first glimpse of a bear out in the woods. Next winter he was to begin accompanying his father a little on his sable-hunting expeditions —so Ivan Petrovitch declared proudly. But little Ilja was an exception. Other boys did not begin to ride until they were seven years old.

Ivan was given to boasting a little about himself as well as about his son. Among other things he declared that there was no Lamut, and only one Koryak, who could drink as muchas he and not be “ piano.” He could drink three bottles of spirits, undiluted, one after another, and walk steadily on his legs afterwards. It was only after he had had five or six bottles that he became drunk and lay like a sack. ‘‘ Other Lamuts get drunk after a couple of glasses,” he said contemptuously.

In the evening we had supper with him and his wife. It consisted of bits of reindeer-flesh cut up and boiled in water without salt. It was served in a bowl, out of which it was the custom for all to eat direct. One is free to use a receptacle of one’s own and to eat by oneself, but both Lamuts and Koryaks get offended by this and break off their friendly relations with their guests. If one wants to get into intimate touch with them one must live exactly as they do and put aside all civilized customs.

While we were satisfying our hunger out of the bowl; a dog came hopping in on three legs. One of his fore-legs was tied to his collar. The dog presented a pathetic appearance, but he wandered round quite at his ease. This was a thing I came across afterwards in almost all the jurias. The dogs have one of their forelegs tied to their collar so that they shall not be able to run and hunt the reindeer. In all the jurtas, by the way, there were numbers of small rough-looking puppies, with which everyone was friendly. The children played with them, and I never saw anybody kick or beat them as the Kamchadals are always doing.

Now and then, while Ivan Petrovitch and I sat and talked; his wife would come and offer us delicacies, in the shape of raw marrow and reindeer-fat. My wife became very friendly with her and the other female occupants of the jurta, and we became the possessors of quite a lot of new ethnographical items for our collection.

One of the older women, who was named Matrona, had, as a child, paid a visit to the Russian Governor of Petropavlovsk, together with her father and some other Lamuts. She spoke excellent Russian and told us a lot about the life and habits of her race.
The Lamuts, as I have said, are nominally Greek

Catholics. Once a year, at oftenest, a priest—usually from Klutchi or from the west coast—makes a tour round the fjells in his official capacity. On these occasions he baptizes, marries and buries for the whole year, being paid in the currency of the country—sableskins. A Kamchadal priest does not do anything for nothing.

But when two Lamuts want to marry they usually prefer to travel themselves to the priest. Often they go to the large village of Tigil, in northern Kamchatka. Many relatives and friends accompany them. They go partly riding, partly by sledge, and they take with them a big hawser. They cannot go into the village itself for fear of the dogs, but have to encamp at a spot some distance from it. Here they set up a large jurta which they have brought with them packed on their sledges. Many ikons are hung up inside. The wedding is celebrated in the village church, but the festivities take place in the jurta. There are tremendous goingson, and they last for three days and three nights, during which no one has time to sleep. Good care has been taken that there shall be no lack of food or strong liquor. But now there is no question of eating only plain reindeer-flesh. Besides reindeer-tongues, marrowbones, etc., there are other delicacies, which have been placed in store for a long time past so that everyone may have as much as he can eat.

All are dressed in their finest Sunday clothes, heavy with beads and metal ornaments of every description —from great emblems wrought in copper to empty cartridge-cases, padlocks and dog-leashes. The guests indulge in all kinds of diversions, from jumping over — the fire and dancing the Norga/i, to wrestling-matches and sledge-races, and the ‘‘ magic”’ drum is beaten day and night. 3
When the festivities are over the jurta is packed ;; up again, with all its accessories, and the whole long — procession returns to the fjells once more.

When the time came for us to make a fresh start, and Ivan Petrovitch heard that we thought of going on to the west coast later in the winter, he told us that he had often been there and knew the villages there well. The smells were so dreadful in the Kamchadal huts, he went on to say, that he thought it would be impossible for us to sleep in them. The Lamuts being accustomed to fresh air get headaches when they are confined in the dirty huts of the Kamchadals. He advised us to stay with a friend of his named Kosigin, in the village of Chairusovo. It was the only house in the village, he declared, in which one could breathe.

And so we took farewell of our friends in the jurta by the Elorman river, harnessed our dogs and set ” out alone on a new and arduous journey over the fjells to another jurta—as to its situation we were given detailed particulars.

We started early in the morning and hoped to reach our destination in good time before darkness set in. The ground we travelled over was much as usual— down one hill and up another, sometimes a precipitous ravine by way of encouragement. But Savonoh had

taught me a trick worth knowing in connexion with the descent into ravines and declivities. It was as simple as possible, but with a touch of genius in it— namely, to tie up a fore-leg of every dog in his collar on these occasions. If one did this, and fastened a couple of dog-chains round the runners, one found one could descend any ravine whatever in perfect safety. The dogs went limping down on their three legs without any power in them for dragging the sledge. Where the snow lay about loose they could hardly manage to get clear themselves. In this way one was relieved of the necessity of tying them up behind the sledge. It was very quaint to see the ten dogs limping down the slopes like so many cripples. On the first occasion when Savonoh gave us a demonstration of the _ efficacy of his plan, we ourselves and others who were looking on all burst out laughing, but the method : proved a success right to the end. I used it throughout the whole winter and it was often our saving in very difficult situations.

In the middle of our day’s journey one of the runners became broken. It took me several hours to mend it, and by the time I had got it right, darkness had begun to draw its veil over the wilderness. According to our calculations we could not be a long distance from the juria, but the dogs had not yet got scent of the reindeer and the situation began to look black, especially as we had no food ‘either for ourselves or for the dogs. We drove on, therefore, as fast as we could, and it was not yet absolutely dark when we got over the last ridge and

made our descent into the valley in which we reckoned we should find the jurta; yet we saw no sign of one, although the snow had been trampled on all over by reindeer. Instead we found a spot on which a jurta had recently stood. There were still some skin-sacks there and a couple of bearskins.

Had we not learnt the fact before this would have brought it home to us, that the Lamuts are nomads. They had simply moved on with their jurta and their herd. But how far had they gone? Well, that did not matter to us for the moment, for neither we nor our dogs were in a condition to proceed farther in the darkness. We were too exhausted, and there were, moreover, no tracks for us to follow. The worst of the matter was, we had no food. However, there was nothing for it but to spend the night there. First of all we must contrive to get warm. We made up a fire on the spot where the Lamuts had had theirs, but it was not easy to get any dry wood as, naturally, the Lamuts had used up all that had been available. After great exertions we got together enough on which to boil our kettle. The poor dogs would have to sleep on empty stomachs. Ivan Petrovitch had used up the whole of his store of jukkola and he would not kill one of his reindeer for us. But I promised the dogs that night that as soon as we got among the Koryaks they should eat their fill of warm reindeer-flesh !
We spread out our sleeping-sacks on the bearskins which had been left behind on the site of the jurta and laid ourselves down to sleep with hunger gnawing
our insides. We made up our minds to track down the Lamuts next day by following in the tracks of the reindeer.

It was a cold, starry winter night when we lay down, but when we awoke at dawn the whole sky was overcast, snow was whirling about over us, as fine as flour, and the wind was moaning in the fjells—a nice lookout! If only we knew how far it was to that jurta! Soon the reindeer-tracks would be all covered up.

We did not even allow ourselves time to make tea, but with all possible haste we made everything fast on the sledge. It was not pleasant having to harness the hungry dogs, who looked reproachfully at us, wondering why we did not give them any food. As soon as I had inspected the ground, and discovered the direction in which the Lamuts had gone, we started out in the tracks of the reindeer herd, which were not yet quite obliterated. After several miles we came to a point where the herd had crossed a frozen river, after which they had moved up a fjell slope and then down into a valley. Here the dogs got scent of them, and after another half-hour’s progress we came in sight of a jurta, a great undulating herd, and quite a crowd of people. We drove on full speed and reached the jurta just as a Lamut winter festival had begun.
Be« the Koryaks and the Lamuts have several
festival days during the winter and early spring ;

the reasons for these festivals are many and diverse, but most of them are connected with the reindeer herds and, in the case of the Lamuts, with their hunting also. Thus they celebrate it as a particularly joyous event when calving is over—in the month of April; when the sun begins in the early spring to show itself more frequently; when the first sable of the year is caught, etc.
In March, especially, they indulge in a festival in honour of the approach of spring. ‘This is the festival which was in progress when we reached the Lamuts’ juria.
The ceremonies were just beginning. Many Lamuts had come together for it from different directions, and a number of traders also happened to be there.

When we came driving down the slope all the Lamuts were assembled on the open place in front of the jurta. A little in front of them stood a reindeer, round both of whose hind-legs a lasso was tied. A Lamut had hold of the lasso, but apart from this the reindeer was free. Another Lamut stood a little distance from the animal, with a spear in his hand. It was evident that the reindeer was going to be sacrificed.

We had several acquaintances among the Lamuts’ visitors and these understood that we wanted to witness the act, and therefore arranged that there should be a delay of a few minutes until I could tie up the dogs properly. My wife and J then went forward towards the group of Lamuts, which consisted only of men, and got into position to look on at the spectacle.

Suddenly all the Lamuts made the sign of the cross and bowed their heads. Immediately afterwards the spear was skilfully plunged into the reindeer’s heart. The animal stood still a second, then tottered and fell over on its right side, with its wound uppermost. When the reindeer falls with the wound towards the ground it is regarded as an evil omen. When it had fallen, women came out of the jurta with knives in their hands and began to skin it.

When the skin, together with the head and horns, had been separated from the body, the Lamuts erected a scaffolding, with the help of some stakes, on which ‘the former were hung up. We saw several other such sacrificial erections elsewhere. Once we found one in the interior of a forest. A Lamut who was with us said that it had been put up on the spot where the first sable of the year had been shot. The reindeer is offered up always as a sacrifice so as to ensure the continuance of successful hunting.

When the reindeer had been skinned and cut up the flesh was carried into the jurta and laid in the big copper pots which hung over the fire. When the meat was fully boiled, all assembled in the jurta. An old Lamut took a bowl full of moss, made the sign of the cross, bowed down and moved it to and fro over the fire, to an accompaniment of many strange ceremonies. Then he went round to all of those assembled, presenting the bowl to each of them. All took a bit of the moss and threw it into the fire.

When the pots were empty, and all had eaten their fill, the company went out again into the open air. Then ensued reindeer-sledge races—always a feature of a Lamut winter festival. The herd of reindeer was close at hand, and those animals that were wanted were caught. The visitors—i.e. the traders and my wife and I—were, according to tradition, responsible for awarding prizes. One trader offered a cake of brick-tea ; another, a bag of biscuits; a third, a packet of tobacco. All the prizes were fastened to the top of a long pole. There were no second or third prizes, but whoever came in first won everything.

Seven sledges were to take part in the race, each of them with two reindeer harnessed. Both Koryaks and Lamuts have special racing sledges, which are so light that you can lift them on one finger. The competitors were to get to a place three miles off and back again.. They got into position and they were given the word to start.

Every one of them whipped up his reindeer with his switch as hard as he could. They all went off at a gallop and were soon out of sight on the hilly and wooded course. In about twenty minutes’ time the first sledge was back, swiftly followed by several others. The sledges seemed to fly over the ground, so light were they. The Lamuts were still whipping up their animals, which panted from their exertions and had their tongues hanging out of their mouths. Suddenly one of the sledges got a jolt and went over on its side; the driver went tumbling about on the snow, but recovered himself, managed to get the sledge on to its runners again, and drove on at the same wild pace. The winner of the race lost no time in appropriating the prizes.

The next item on the programme was a wrestling bout. Two young Lamuts threw off their furs, so as to be naked to the waist. The fact that it was extremely cold did not seem to worry either of them. While the others stood round and encouraged them with shouts they gripped each other and began wrestling for all they were worth. They were just about a match and it was uncertain for a long time which would win. But at last, amidst a storm of delighted shouts and cries, one of them succeeded in throwing the other and winning the contest, thereby securing as a prize a box of sweets.

The evening was spent inside the jurta, where the programme consisted of meat-eating and tea-drinking alternately with spirits and sweets, all to the accompaniment of the “magic”? drum, which was played until late in the night. In the firelight the Norga/i was danced also, and so ended the Lamut winter festival.

HE day after that festival a Koryak came to visit the Lamuts.. He had some dogs with him and it was evident that he came only for a talk. When our own dogs gave us warning of his approach, by their excited barking, we went out of the jurta to meet him. His name was Akej, and he was the owner of a large reindeer herd and a jurta in the neighbourhood. He was small and sinewy, his complexion was leather-coloured and his features were not unlike those of an Indian. He was slow and awkward in his movements. When he had tied up his dogs he advanced at a leisurely pace towards the jurta.

“* Prijatel, have you any fly-bane for me?”’ were the first words he uttered, after we had exchanged greetings. Prijatel is the word with which both the Lamuts and the Koryaks address everyone. It means simply “friend.” He evidently thought I was a trader and the traders often have fly-bane with them when they go up into the fjells. It is in great request with both Koryaks and Lamuts as an intoxicant.

TWO LITTLE LAMUT MAIDENS The little Lamut maidens are dressed from top to toe in furs and go bareheaded.
