Koryaks and the Lamuts, but I could not make anything of what he said. However, he seemed to deliver himself of a lot of interesting and surprising observations, for the Koryak every now and again emitted a snarling kind of comment which, so I learned later, was a sort of equivalent to “‘ Well I’m damned!” We had been deliberating for some days past as to when we could betake us to the Koryak regions. We had been finding it hard to procure food for the dogs, and I did not want to have them getting thin, as we had exhausting journeys before us. Now we had this chance of having a Koryak to keep us company. I asked him whether he would have any objection to our going back with him to his jurta and staying some days with him, and above all whether he could undertake to feed our dogs properly with reindeer-flesh. He said he could, and after we had sat and talked for a while he proposed that we should make a start. So we said farewell to the Lamuts—though not for the last time—harnessed our dogs and went off with the Koryak. | Our route lay over one larch-clad height after another. Well on in the day we came to a valley at the bottom of which we saw a round black speck. ‘This was the Koryak’s jurta. A large expanse of ground all about the jurta seemed to be covered with young trees. The Koryak, travelling light, had gone more quickly than we and had disappeared out of sight. Putting a couple of dog-chains under our runners we began the descent into the valley all right, but just as we got toa little elevation at the bottom we turned a somersault— and it was just as well we did, for it brought the sledge toastop. The dogs had become very excited, for the forest of young trees had begun to move! It had changed into an undulating herd of reindeer and the dogs had both scented them and seen them. We were now about seven or eight hundred yards from them and the jurta. The dogs began barking furiously and wanted to go on. I scarcely ventured to give the words to start, as I was not sure that even by exerting myself to the utmost I would be able to hold them in. They were as bloodthirsty as wolves. When at last I did let them start—although my wife and I and our baggage weighed five hundred pounds—they simply flew over the snow and made direct for the herd, emitting one great concerted bark. I applied the brake strongly, and there was a whirl of snow all round us, but it did not help. A crowd of Koryaks who had been standing in front of the jurta had just caught some of the reindeer. They did not wish them to be scattered, so three of them came rushing towards us with lassos in their hands ready to throw. When we had got to within sixty or seventy yards of the nearest reindeer, all three of them flung their lassos at our dogs. The first two were caught in them, all the others were huddled together in a heap and we were brought suddenly to a fullstop. The Koryaks proceeded to help us to unharness the excited dogs and to tie them up.

When that was done we were able to exchange greetings quietly with all the prijate/s who stood in front of the jurta. All of them were astonishingly dirty, and looked very wild in their shaggy skins, with their weather-beaten Indian countenances. Some women and a whole flock of children now came out of the jurta. ‘The children were almost black with dirt and the women were not much better. The latter were all bare-headed and had their hair hanging in two plaits. The men had the front part of their heads shaved. All were friendly and hospitable, and pressed us to step into the jurta and warm ourselves with tea.

But before we crept in we stood and looked at the Koryak’s reindeer—they were really worth looking at. I calculated that they numbered above two thousand, and yet our host declared that only half his herd had been driven down from the fjells. The animals were not exactly like those of the Lamuts; one noticed at once that they were smaller and that on an average they were considerably darker in colouring.
The jurta was also much larger than those of the Lamuts, and one was struck by the great number of sledges which stood outside it.

Presently we crept in through the skin hangings, but, blinded as we were by the sun and the snow, it took us some time to distinguish anything in the dim light within. Both the Lamuts and the Koryaks allow daylight into their jurtas only through the smokehole. Everything was on a larger scale than in the Lamuts’ jurtas: in the inner compartment one could stand quite erect without touching the ceiling; but there was no difference in other respects.

A couple of enormous saucepans hung by two chains over the fire, and big bits of meat stuck up out of them. Some elderly women sat and scraped skins near the fireplace and put the scrapings into their mouths. They were so dreadfully dirty that my wife shuddered when she looked at them. The jurta was full of small shaggy puppies and indescribably dirty half-naked children. The latter played with the dogs, and also with two big pieces of meat, which I was afraid we were going to have for dinner. Although we had been quite hungry our appetites completely left us as soon as we entered the jurta.

In the inner compartment we sat ourselves down on reindeer-skins and awaited the inevitable tea. We were glad that the Koryaks did not take bread with their tea, for what would it have looked like? The worst of it was that they were all so tremendously friendly and benevolent we had not the heart to go out to our sledge and fetch our own cooking-pots and mugs. When one does that, as I have already mentioned, it is taken so ill that one might just as well take oneself off at once.

Both Russians, Kamchadals and Lamuts had assured us that the Koryaks never washed from the cradle to the grave. Now we no longer doubted the truth of that assertion. When I was bold enough later to question our Koryak friend and host, Akej; on this delicate subject, he declared it might happen that, on some occasions in the summer, when the sun was shining and they were perspiring; they might bathe their faces in some river. “But there isn’t anything so remarkable in the fact that the Koryaks never wash,” he went on; “you should see the Kamchadals on the west coast. They feed their dogs on kis/a, and if they do not happen to have a pitchfork in their hands they take the kis/a with their hands. A Koryak would never do that,”’ he ended proudly.

Soon the tea was ready and all the occupants of the jurta—children and puppies included—assembled in Akej’s inner compartment where we were sitting. Fach of the matrons had with her a little wooden box, out of which she slowly drew some teacups. They lay wrapped up in rags. The cups were placed on a large tray and one of the women poured out tea. Before filling the two cups which were meant for us, our hostess gave them a wipe with a wad of moss which lay in a corner of the box. This made them, if possible, dirtier than before. We had a bag of sweets and biscuits with us and my wife put some of them on the tray. We thought they had disappeared quickly with the Lamuts, but that was nothing to what happened now. Before one could have counted ten the tray was empty. Not only did they put both the sweets and the biscuits into their mouths at once, but they made away with the rest. Two of the children fell out over their share of the booty, and their contest ended in piercing yells. When I myself had finished my first cup of tea the cup was comparatively clean, so that I could enjoy my second cup better.

While we sat over the teacups we had an pe ie Among the Koryaks opportunity of admiring an exhibition which might well make schoolboys green with envy. The male Koryaks were past-masters in the art of accurate spitting. Quite suddenly, as one sat talking with them, a jet of saliva would go flying past one’s ear or one’s teacup and fall in the neighbourhood of the fire. They did not move their lips, but spat without altering a feature. At first one ducked one’s head, fearing to get a charge full in the face, but there proved to be no danger of this.

The adult Koryaks drank as a rule four or five cups of tea. When the tea-drinking was over the cups were put back in their boxes. Our hostess displayed her respect for us again by drying our cups with the same piece of moss as before. Savonoh had warned us that they would clean the cups by spitting in them and then drying them with moss, but I never saw this done. This uncivilized way of cleaning I have come upon only once—in a fashionable hotel at Port Said! One of the black waiters had been ordered to clean a silver spoon which was dirty. He took it, went into a corner of the elegant dining-room, then spat on the spoon and wiped it with the napkin he carried over his arm: after which he hurried back and handed it to the fastidious diner.

It was difficult to carry on conversation with the Koryaks in this jurta as only two of them knew any Russian, and those two very little. Like the Lamuts, they were very curious about our family history. They wanted to know whether our parents were alive, whether we had any brothers and sisters, what their names were, whether they had reindeer or hunted sable, or were traders, etc. They wanted to know also whether there were any Koryaks in our country, how many bottles of spirits were paid for a sable there, and whether we were Christians or heathens.

All the Koryaks, men and women alike, had snuffboxes ornamented with beads, and one often saw them put a plug of snuff into their mouths. Snuff, however, is an expensive article, and they observed economy in their use of it, never spitting out the roll when tired of chewing it, but taking it in their fingers placed it behind an ear, just as a clerk does with his pen. After a time they put it back in their mouths and begin chewing it again. Frequently one would see a mother offer her quite young daughters a plug. The boys very soon become owners of snuff-boxes, and I never saw ~a male Koryak without one. To be the owner of a handsome snuff-box is a distinction. The snuff is made from Manchurian leaf-tobacco, mixed with ashes.

After tea lasked Akej to let me buy a reindeer as food for the dogs. The herd was still alongside the jurta and he went out with his lasso and caught one animal. It was killed in the usual way, by being pierced to the heart with a knife, having previously been thrown on its side and its legs tied together. Two Koryaks skinned it in a very few minutes and cut it up in ten pieces; which we then gave to my dogs. Inside the skin were the larve of an insect—the reindeer gadfly —which lays its eggs in the skin. These wormlike. larve the Koryaks picked out eagerly and put in their mouths, declaring that they tasted as good as our sweets. Sometimes they took them home to their children.

It was a satisfaction to note the zest with which the dogs ate their meat, which was still warm. Perhaps they had never had such good food before, but from this point onwards they were to have it often. In less than five minutes there was not a morsel of reindeerflesh left. The dogs were really contented and licked my hands gratefully while I stood and talked to them. As payment for the reindeer I gave two boxes of tobacco to Akej, who was so delighted that he went about showing them to everybody. I do not know which he appreciated the more, the boxes or the tobacco.

The reindeer herd was now driven up into the encircling fjells and we went back into the jurta, where we were at once asked to sit down to supper. Like the Lamuts, the Koryaks have boiled reindeer-flesh for all their meals. We had our salt-box with us and now we had the new experience of eating half-boiled meat. The Koryaks cook their meat only for a short time. A wooden tray with big steaming pieces of flesh on it was brought in and each person took out his sheath-knife and extracted a piece of the meat with his finger. With his knife he would then cut off one slice after another from the bone and put it into his mouth. The meat was tough and in the middle quite raw. When the Koryaks got their teeth into the red slices of it drops of blood dripped down from the corners of their mouths. But it is marvellous how soon one gets used to things! After some days we ate the half-raw flesh with quite a good appetite, and we suffered no ill consequences from it during the whole of our stay among these folk.

The existence of the Koryaks, as I have said, is bound up with their herds to a greater degree than is that of the Lamuts. They devote all their energies to the reindeer and always have large herds of them. They give away their surplus stock lavishly, in exchange for a trifle, to anyone who needs them. All the neighbouring people keep going to the Koryaks unceasingly throughout the winter for reindeer-flesh. ‘There are Russians and Chinese also who trade in reindeer-flesh. They are continually coming to the Koryaks to buy it, and they proceed to sell it in the larger villages, where there are always a great many inhabitants who cannot venture on the long and dangerous journey up to the fjells.

Brick-tea is often used in barter for it, but it is paid for more usually in spirits. In return for a bottle of spirits the Koryaks are quite willing to slaughter several reindeer. The Koryaks are greatly addicted to spirits, and are accustomed to this commodity being brought them by all who visit them. They were therefore quite disappointed when they found that I had broken with this tradition and failed to help them to get drunk. An old Koryak said once to me after he had sat expectantly a long time: “‘ You who are young ought to know what an old man needs. I can’t live without spirits.”
When the Koryaks move from one spot to another,

with their herds and their jurtas, they form a big caravan, comprising a large number of sledges. They use their reindeer only to draw the sledges, never to ride or as beasts of burden. They think it a real sin to ride a reindeer, and in fact their animals, being smaller than those of the Lamuts, are not so well fitted for riding.

Outside every Koryak jurta one sees a great number of sledges of different kinds. Two kinds of them are quite identical with those of the Lamuts—namely, the ordinary hunting or visiting sledge, and the racing sledge. But the Koryaks have large sledges for carrying goods, some with bars, as on a haycart, some without. They have also covered sledges, in which they put their children in snowy weather, and a number of other kinds. All are made of birch-wood and fastened together with thongs. ‘They are made very cleverly and are sometimes almost works of art.

A large number of the sledges are always filled with clothes and household utensils which are not used every day. When they are needed, the Koryaks just go out and bring them in with them, thus avoiding the necessity of encumbering the jurtas with them. In the sledges left outside are kept also a supply of burialclothes.

The number of flittings depends chiefly upon the supply of grazing-land for the herds. Reindeer, as is known, live in the winter on lichens which they kick up under the snow. Usually in the winter the jurtas are set up in some valley or on some tundra. The reindeer avoid the very high fjells where the winds and frosts are most severe. During the summer there are incredibly large swarms of mosquitoes on the tandras and in the valleys; and they give the animals no rest, so they are then taken up to the higher fjells. But in summer the Koryaks have to flit more frequently, and they cannot take with them all their baggage when there is no sledge-way ; therefore all the older people and the children spend the summer by the banks of some river and live principally on fish. Only some of the young men and young women accompany the herd. The Lamuts have the same custom.

After spending two days in Akej’s jurta we journeyed on to that of his father, Ikava, a very old and rich Koryak, who lived not far off. As a parting gift we received from Akej some frozen reindeer-tongues to eat on the way, as well as a lot of sinews and skins of reindeer-legs with which to mend our skin shoes in case of need.

Ikava received us in a somewhat reserved manner. He may have suspected some guileful purpose in our visit. His jurta was still larger than Akej’s and housed four large families, but it was also considerably dirtier than Akej’s. The women in it were sitting about as usual scraping skins and putting the scrapings in their mouths. One of them was lying on her stomach and sewing beads on to a cap. They were all very dirty and made a disagreeable impression. Pots containing meat hung over the fire, and the tea-kettle, of course, came into play at once.

I asked the old man his age. He declared he was nearly a hundred, but he certainly exaggerated by at least twenty-five years. The Koryaks never keep account of their age, and they can remember the age of their children only while these are still quite small.

We were given almost black brick-tea and halfboiled reindeer-flesh, and sat there talking with our host and his family; while they chewed their plugs of snuff and spat with the same astonishing proficiency which we had witnessed at his son’s. Ikava told us how in earlier days he used to wander with his herds round Tigil in northern Kamchatka, but had fallen out with his neighbours and had come south. He had a brother up there, and bade me tell him if I should meet him that he, Ikava, had his jurta by the River Bistraja and that all his family were well.

Ikava was one of the few Koryaks I met who spoke Russian comparatively well, but he was evidently not at all delighted over our visit, and he put all possible difficulties in the way of its being prolonged. For instance, when I said I wanted to buy a reindeer, he declared that he had no one to send after the herd, and it was with the greatest difficulty that I secured a reindeer’s stomach filled with blood. Naturally it was frozen and as hard as a stone, and I could only just manage to get my axe into it when I wanted to cut it up for the dogs.

All the people in this jurta were suspicious and unsympathetic, so we made up our minds to proceed on our journey the following day. Afterwards, in another jurta, we were to learn the reason for this suspicion.

Old Ikava had had a superstitious dread of my seeing his reindeer and photographing them. He was afraid of that Satanic apparatus in my possession, and believed that it would bring bad luck down upon his herd.

Our plan now was to cross the central mountain ridge and betake us to the west coast. But first we were to visit the village of Klutchi, where we had a lot of things to do, and where we proposed to deposit the collections which we had made. These had already been sent on ahead on different sledges to the village of Kosyrevsk.

Early on the following morning, then, we took farewell of the Koryaks for the time being; and set out for a Lamut jurta in which we intended to spend the night, and try to find some travelling companions to Kosyrevsk.

We reached the jurza all right, but there was no one there who had occasion to go on with us. If I were willing to wait a couple of days, I was told, I could have company. But we had no time to spare, so we had to decide to proceed at once. This decision was the more imperative in that I could not get food for the dogs, and it might take us three days to reach Kosyrevsk even in good weather. I had; indeed, a reserve store of fifteen fish, but even on half-rations they would last for at most a three days’ journey—so off we must go. We were a little anxious at not having any companion, as we were going over a particularly difficult stretch of country, over which I had driven only once before. Should there be a snowstorm, and should all tracks be obliterated, J was afraid we might miss the way. But there was no choice. The sky that morning was overcast, and it was snowing quite heavily, but a trader had just arrived from Kosyrevsk and we hoped to have his tracks to guide us.

When we started the snow on the ground was a couple of inches deep. By midday it was a foot! We exerted ourselves to the very utmost in ascending and descending the heights, and did not stop for tea until the afternoon, when we had got through the worst part of the hilly region and had reached a larch-forest. Here our course was almost entirely downhill, less snow had fallen and the sledge-tracks were still quite visible, but our advance was much impeded by broken branches blown down by the wind. However, we made quicker progress than we hoped, and even when darkness came on we felt impelled to continue. The dogs were in a particularly good mood, although they had begun work very early that day. They were manifestly glad to be free of the unpleasant hilly region, where they had had a bad time, and often had fared ill as regards their food—otherwise they would not have been pulling with such a will with so heavy a load behind them. The moon rose above the tree-tops and this cheered them up still more.

We drove on, hour after hour, until about midnight the dogs suddenly came to a standstill. We glanced round in the moonlight and found we were on the spot where we had encamped for the night for the first time on our way up to the fjells. It really looked as though the dogs had made up their minds to reach this particular spot. Although much snow had fallen they certainly recognized it at once. We ourselves were much pleased with our day’s driving, which gave us hopes of reaching Kosyrevsk the following evening.

The snow had ceased and the stars had come out in the sky. It was a cold February night. As soon as I had tied up the dogs I took out my axe and started out to get some wood. I found a dry larch-tree quite near and began cutting it down, but at the very first stroke the handle went smash! Here was a nice state of things! We had been looking forward to warming ourselves at a regular log fire, whereas now I had to be content with gathering together as many dry branches as I could, so that we could at least make up a fire on which to boil our kettle.

We kicked away some of the snow, spread out a carpet of twigs and branches, and laid down our sleeping-sacks on top of them. Our bodies ached after our day’s exertions in the hilly region, and it was a long time before we were able to get to sleep.

Next morning the weather was bitterly cold. My jacket, which on the previous evening had been wet through with perspiration, had been left in the sledge during the night. It was now frozen and as hard as a rock. I had to hold it before the fire for quite a long time before I could put it on. It seemed scarcely worth while drying it, for I soon had it wet through again.

We had now several small sundras to drive over. Here we could see no tracks and it was very difficult to plough our way through the loose snow. On several occasions when we ourselves were not certain about our route we let the leader dog go in any direction he thought fit, and generally he was right.

It became colder and colder towards the evening, and at sunset the temperature approached 60° F. On the last extensive tundra we had to walk alongside the sledge, as the snow was so loose and so deep. Soon we could see the Klutchefskaja volcano once more, with its gigantic plume of fire. It looked very strange and fantastic in the darkness and the cold winter landscape. At last we got into the larch-woods again. Here we came across some newly made tracks of a sledge which had travelled between Kosyrevsk and Tolbatchik. This told us that we were about five miles from our destination. But the going was very difficult and slow. ‘The cold was increasing, so we had to run every now and again to warm ourselves, and it was not until late in the evening that we reached Kosyrevsk, where we put up in the house of a Russian, who had understanding enough to offer us coffee instead of tea.

The practice of taking snuff mentioned on page 223 and elsewhere differs in the manner of taking it from that which obtains in the British Isles. The tobacco is not ground toa fine powder as with us. A pinch of it is inserted between the teeth and the lower lip, and after a time acquires such a consistency that it may be taken out of the mouth and stuck behind the ear and, from time to time, replaced in the mouth. Tobacco-leaf is used in the same fashion.
OVER THE JELOVKA PASS TO THE WEST COAST

AVING arranged for the dispatch of our He to Klutchi we started ourselves for that place next day, taking the villages of Uschki and Kresti ex route. Three days later we ar- _ rived at the home of our friend Persson, a Swede, with whom we had got acquainted on one of Swenson’s schooners and who was now Swenson’s principal representative in Kamchatka, and had the management of his fur business throughout a large portion of the country.

Persson had long before invited us to come to stay with him, and now we were received by him with open arms. He immediately arranged for us to have a bath —which was a great luxury after our stay in the wilds, all the more so as we had scarcely been out of our clothes since we had bathed in the warm spring at Natchika two months before.

Persson’s house was extremely snug and comfortable. Naturally he began by giving us coffee. After that I smoked a good cigar and we sat talking and listening to a gramophone. Persson was from Norrk6ping, and as both my wife and I had lived there for a number of years we had many mutual acquaintances to talk about.

We had a delightful time of it at Persson’s, and he entertained us in princely fashion. Every evening we feasted on Californian fruit, chocolate and other good things, and we felt we were in heaven. Persson saw to it also that I had no need to worry over food for my dogs.

But we had things to do and we could not idle there. We had our collections to pack up and photograph plates to develop; and I had to study the bird-life on some of the unfrozen rivers of the districts. In addition we had to look about for someone who could guide us over the famous Jelovka Pass to the west coast.

The Jelovka Pass is the only point in the whole of this part of northern Kamchatka at which one can get over the great mountain range that separates the west coast region from the east, but it is little known and it is notorious for its snowstorms, which sometimes continue for whole weeks unceasingly. The outstanding difficulty about it is that it is in the best of weathers a four days’ journey from the last human dwelling-place on the one side to the first on the other. I had much talk on the subject with the village folk, who were all against my venturing to traverse the pass, but one man who knew the way promised to accompany us for sixty pounds. Another said he would come if he might have my double-barrelled gun in payment. I was prepared to give one of my pairs of Zeiss fieldglasses, but beyond that I would not go. At last I got hold of a Kamchadal who agreed to accompany us for a reasonable price.

After we had made all our preparations, and said good-bye to Persson, from whose hospitable dwelling we took with us pleasant memories of the blessings of civilization, we set forth for the village of Jelovka, fifty-six miles away, which was to be our starting-point for the journey over the pass. Two other Kamchadals and a Siberian from Yakutsk availed themselves of the opportunity of following in our tracks. They also were bound for the west coast.

A cold north wind was blowing when, at early dawn two days later, we quitted the dilapidated little village of Jelovka. Our caravan consisted of fifty-two dogs harnessed to five sledges, driven by me and the four men already mentioned. We covered up our faces as much as possible in our shaggy fur caps to protect them against the wind and the frost.

On every sledge we had packed away as much food for the dogs as possible. On this stage of our journey —i.e. from Klutchi to the great Russian-Kamchadal village of Tigil on the west coast, a distance of about one hundred and ninety miles—we could not hope to make any addition to our store of fodder. Owing to the difficulty of the ground, and to the fact that we had to carry so much other baggage, we could not take with us more than half the supply of fish we really needed, so, as always, the poor dogs would have to be * contented with half-rations while putting forth double their exertions. But they had had good food and a good rest at Persson’s and were now in brilliant condition.

On the first day we met with no adventures. We travelled through birch- and larch-woods, and when the sun began to set we had reached the foot of the fjells, where we encamped under a birch-tree in a hollow. We set up a screen-tent and made ourselves very comfortable sitting round a log fire.

Before daybreak we crept out of our sleeping-sacks into the biting cold, and the rising sun saw us speeding along hollow and ravine and gradually getting on to higher and higher ground. The dogs toiled and panted. We had to keep shouting to them to urge them forward at the worst bits.

The ground became steeper and stiffer all the time until at last we reached a high plateau named Stolbovaja Tundra. It is very precipitous on every side. Only at two points can one ascend and descend it. The Kamchadals had often told me how dangerous it was in snowstorms: the storm might be so violent as to sweep sledges away like pieces of paper, blowing them right off the plateau and down into the abyss underneath.

But we were favoured by the sun and the atmosphere was very clear. We spent some time up on the summit. The view was so magnificent that I felt it surpassed anything we had yet seen in Kamchatka. To the southeast there rose a line of big volcanoes glittering in the snow. One of them towered above all the others and sent up a pillar of smoke, which floated towards the south—this was Klutchefskaja, the pride of Kamchatka. To the east we could see the moribund volcano of Schiveljutch with its irregular outlines. All the volcanoes to this side were old acquaintances of ours, both from our winter and our summer journeys; but to the west, near at hand, rose another many-peaked mountain over which we should be faring the following day by the Jelovka Pass.

That evening we struck camp in a wild-looking hollow at the foot of this western range. We had caught sight, as we advanced, of a little wooden hut which had been built as a protection for travellers against snowstorms, but on coming to it we found that there was nothing left of it but a few half-rotten stakes. The rest of it had been cut to pieces for use as firewood.

Sitting round our camp-fire we discussed the pro- -posals for the next day’s journey while we ate our dinner of dried salmon and tea. The oldest of the Kamchadals sat for a long time gazing up at the starry sky. At last he remarked: ‘‘ Poslesaftra budjet purga”’ (“The day after to-morrow there will be a snowstorm’’). He could see that by the stars, he declared. So we laid out our sleeping-sacks and went to sleep in good able hopes of fine weather next day, when we should be able-to get over the pass.

At noon next day we stood on the highest point of the pass, close by the cross with the ikon on it—shown in the photograph. We were worn out with our exertions during the hours it took us to get up. It seemed a wonderful thing to see a cross with a gilt ikon in the midst of this wilderness. It is a cross famous throughout Kamchatka. It was put up after a terrible snowstorm in which a Russian and his party narrowly escaped destruction: after three days and three nights of it they escaped with their lives. ‘The cross was raised afterwards to protect other travellers against the storms.
Our companions left their sledges and, going up to the cross, knelt down before it and made the sign of the cross repeatedly—a strange sight this also.

After we had loitered a little and gazed admiringly at the mountains all around we continued our journey. We had now about fifty-six miles to cover before reaching any human habitations, but there were no more uphill roads to be encountered. The snow up on the pass had been frozen so hard that it was more like ice than snow.

We went down the other side of the fjell at a tremendous rate. I had to put on the brake to the utmost and to do all I could to steer clear of boulders. When at last, after a wild rush down and several upsets, we found ourselves once again on level ground, my arm ached badly from the strain put on it by holding the brake.

But now we were over our worst dangers for the present, and on the west coast of the peninsula, and if we were a long way from the sea at least the route henceforth would be over level ground. We made our tea in happy mood, in the midst of a birch-wood, and then went on again until darkness fell. We were anxious to make as much progress as possible before the night, as there was an ominous roaring sound up in the fjells—premonitions of the dreaded purga.
Finally we encamped for the night on a tundra with sparse-growing osiers. It turned out to be one of the fiercest winter nights we ever experienced in Kamchatka.

The snowstorm began about midnight. There was a tremendous roaring all round us and the snow whirled about in dense clouds. We had laid ourselves down on the snow and soon we were almost buried by drifts. The snow made its way into our sleeping-sacks and became piled up everywhere. Further sleep was out of the question and in the cold black darkness there was nothing we could do to improve our position. It was impossible to get up. The storm would blow us off our legs. We just had to lie quiet until daybreak and keep the mouths of our sleeping-sacks as much closed as possible. Yes, that was indeed a dreadful night. We thought it would never come to an end.

As soon as daybreak began, we raised ourselves a little and looked around us. The Kamchadals were absolutely snowed under—all of them— in their sleepingsacks. One received a buffet in the face from the snow the moment one raised one’s head.

The wind blew in the direction of Sedanka—our next destination. Having with difficulty managed to get up, we decided to try to get on before the snow got any deeper. Shivering from the cold, and with our furs all drenched by the snow, we got up the poor dogs, who now had been living for six whole days on halfrations and who were wild with hunger. It was out of the question to think of making tea, and like the dogs we had to begin that horrible day on empty stomachs.

We drove off in an almost unbroken line, just as near each other as possible. I admired the faculty, alike of the Kamchadals and of the dogs, of discovering the way in such circumstances. Presently we came to a frozen river. It made a curve so that the sledges were caught broadside by the storm. Both the dogs and the sledges were driven towards the bank. The snowstorm kept intensifying and abating turn about. If one faced the wind one could not breathe. Sometimes the snow was so thick that one could not see farther than the nearest dogs. For hours together we sat cowering and unable to look up, trusting to the dogs to follow the sledge in front of us. I admired the trusty animals and felt glad to think that I should be able to give them as much food as they could desire in the first village in which there was fish to be had.

We kept on the move all day. In the evening we held a council of war. We were all afraid of the effects of another night out in the open with our clothes and sleeping-sacks all wet with the snow. We decided to urge on the dogs for all we were worth on the chance of reaching Sedanka. Darkness was falling. We came out on a wide-stretching ¢uzdra. Our hopes of getting to the village became weaker the darker it became. The dogs were tired to death and we were not much better, having had no sleep during the night and nothing to eat all day, and being, in addition, chilled to the bone.

Suddenly they all gave a start. They had cocked their ears and were listening. ‘They had heard something and they at once began to pull harder. We could scarcely trust our own ears for joy when in another few moments we ourselves heard the barking of dogs ahead of us. A light now shone out. We had reached the village and were saved. Never had we been : SO delighted to see the lights of a village.

We were kindly welcomed into the house to which ‘we went. The whole building was creaking in the wind and we were happy to find refuge in it, but I was sorry for the poor dogs. That night one of the dogs relieved the pangs of hunger by gnawing away at his harness—for there was not a bit of fish in the village to give them.

Sedanka was the first west-coast village we made acquaintance with. It was quite unlike all the villages of the east coast. For the first time we now heard Kamchadals talking their own language. As I have mentioned before, those living on the east coast all talk Russian.

All the people were friendly and helpful and they made a considerably more sympathetic impression on us than the people of the east coast. That is due for the most part to the fact that they very seldom receive a visit from strangers in their out-of-the-way homes, and are therefore rejoiced when any come.

In Sedanka we heard a big piece of news. The Bolsheviks—who shortly before our departure from Petropavlovsk had been driven out of the town by the whites and who had sought refuge in the woods—had occupied the village of Natchika, cut off the telephone wires to Petropavlovsk, and were now in possession of both the telephone lines which ran to the Kamchatkan valley and to the west coast. They had sent messages

to all the villages announcing that they controlled the country, and urging all the inhabitants to proceed to Petropavlovsk and drive out the white robber-bands who hung on in the town and whose only objects in life were to get as many sable-skins as possible in return for strychnine and spirits. This communication had been sent forth two days before like a flash of lightning to all the villages and it had been the subject of lively discussion ever since.
Sedanka is a very primitive village. It lies sixty miles from the sea and is very seldom visited. It was obvious from their faces that the inhabitants had very little Russian blood in them.

During the days we spent in the village I made it known that we were anxious to obtain examples of the arts and crafts of the village, and that I would give, among other things, sweets in exchange. One after another they came to our quarters with different objects, mostly made out of birch-bark, with or without ornaments. In addition there were fire-making boxes, oillamps, models of canoes, models of fishing implements, etc. There was a constant stream of visitors, mostly children. They received one or two handfuls of sweets in brightly coloured paper bags for each thing we bought. But we did not merely sit at home and receive visitors. We visited every hut, and when we left Sedanka we were in possession of more than fifty ethnographical specimens. I had to hire an extra sledge to transport them to the big village of Tigil, which was our next destination, and where we were going to deposit our things, to be shipped afterwards for Petropavlovsk.

As a parting present we received a reindeer-tongue or two from almost every hut in the village. We thus acquired more than twenty frozen reindeer-tongues. It was obvious from what we saw in the village that the inhabitants practically lived upon the Koryaks. They ate nothing but reindeer-flesh, and all their clothes were made of skins supplied by the Koryaks. Even the dogs were fed on reindeer-flesh which the Koryaks must have provided. There had been a shortage of fish throughout the whole of the preceding summer. When the salmon traps were arranged across the river the water had risen to such a height that they had been washed away. The whole village had been swamped and communication between the houses had to be by canoes. }

Following the course of the Sedanka and Tigil rivers, we came to the large village of Tigil, the most northern place we visited during the whole expedition. Here we added considerably to our ethnographical collections.
THROUGH MORIBUND REGIONS ALONG THE OKOTSK SHORE

ROM Tigil we had a journey of about six | ee miles to Petropavlovsk. The greater part of it was over one continuous tundra. On this tundra lie eighteen Kamchadal villages situated at distances of from thirteen to fifty miles from each other. A great portion of the tundra is as level as the sea. You can see no end to it. Here and there stretch small birch-woods, which are indescribably welcome to travellers in the winter. At other points its uniformity is broken by somewhat rough ground. Low hills and valleys alternate. The rivers which run through the tundra are bordered by a streak of salix vegetation. The tundra extends some twenty or thirty miles inland - from the sea and is bordered on the east by a mountain range.

The people who dwell in this God-forsaken region belong probably to the most pitiable in the whole world, | and a journey through it is depressing in the extreme., Here live the last remnants of a race which will soon be : wiped off the face of the earth. In all the other parts | of Kamchatka the natives have become so intermingled | with the Russians that they have forgotten how to talk ;

their own language, whereas in some of the west-coast villages—ten or twelve of them—there has been only a little intermingling, and the Kamchadal language is still in use. But even here civilization has set its mark on what is left of the inhabitants, for every one of them—men, women and children—suffer from hereditary syphilis introduced long ago by Russians. This malady has raged appallingly in these wildernesses where no kind of medical assistance is available. In addition, the Japanese and Chinese and Russians vie with each other in drenching the degenerate villagers in spirits, which, in their miserable condition, they value above all else.

The consequences are that the west coast of Kamchatka furnishes a terrible example of what can happen when a civilized nation takes control of a primitive race and sends its worst representatives to rule over it.

This was the tract through which we were now to travel. It was not an agreeable prospect, especially as we were to be absolutely dependent on these villages for our provisions. We decided that as soon as we -eached the village of Chairusovo, situated one hundred ind twenty miles south of Tigil, we should leave the Kamchadals for a time and betake us up into the fjells igain to continue our studies of the Lamuts and the Koryaks.

With this plan fixed upon we duly set forth from Tigil where we had been most hospitably entertained yy Mr Pimenoff, the agent of the Hudson Bay Company. ‘rom him we had directions as to the houses in the
various villages in which it would be least unpleasant to spend the night.

The first village on our way was Napana—a cluster of grey-hued, tumble-down huts standing in the midst of the tundra, and looking as though they had been dumped down there by chance. We reached it in the afternoon. Our dogs got scent of its putrid fish from afar, and when we got near it we were greeted as usual by the barking of the village dogs. The inhabitants, clad in garments of skin acquired from the Koryaks, hurried out of their huts to peer at us inquisitively. As soon as we had tied up the dogs, placing one of them by the sledge on guard, I sought out the man in whose dwelling we were to spend the night, and he conducted us to it through the ramshackle village, which consisted of about ten huts in all.

When we went in through the door such an appalling stink reached our nostrils that we nearly fell backwards. The hut consisted of only one room. There was no furniture whatever except a table. A couple of boxes did service as seats—on one of them one could read ‘* California Fruits,” on another some Japanese words. On the ground, in a corner, lay heaped up together a lot of dirty-looking ragged clothes, reindeer-skins and a damaged gramophone. A couple of natives, who were evidently ill and hardly able to rise, lay covered up with rags in another corner. Some half-naked children were playing on the floor with a piece of meat. Near ' the fireplace lay the entire frozen carcass of a reindeer,, ready to be cut up. The woman of the house came!
forward shyly, greeted us, and then went back to the chimney-corner, where she began to busy herself with a samovar. A Kamchatkan hut never lacks a samovar even if it should lack everything else.
In these surroundings we accepted the invitation to sit down on a box at the table and drink tea—bricktea, without sugar, and served in dirty mugs. But we let them serve our tea in our own mugs.

While we were at tea all the dogs in the village suddenly began to bark, which meant that another sledge was arriving. We tried from old habit to look out of the window to see what sort of persons were in the sledge, but we found that the window consisted of fish-skins sewed together. It allowed some light to enter, but one could not see through it. One of the neighbours had a window made of bears’ entrails sewn together, others had windows made of seals’ entrails. But the most common substitute for glass was fish-skins. They serve the purpose not at all badly, but the hut owner has to take the precaution to have the window at such a height that the sledge-dogs cannot get at them, otherwise he would run the risk one fine day of having his window eaten up.

I took a stroll among the huts, trying to procure food for the dogs—often a difficult business. The entire village stank of putrid fish. All the huts were alike— everywhere the same disgusting stink, the same filth, the same misery, the same signs of illness. The Kamchadals are so indolent that they do not trouble in the summer to catch as many fish as they require, although
it sometimes does not take them more than a week’s work to lay in the necessary store.

It was getting dark, so our Kamchadal host lit his schirnik (or lamp), which consisted of an iron bowl, filled with bear’s grease or seal’s grease—a little shred of cloth served as a wick. We sat and talked with him. He talked Russian quite well, but his family could talk only the Kamchadal language. He told us how difficult it was to live in Kamchatka; how one had to toil over the fishing all the summer; how little fish there was now, since the coming of the Japanese; and how hard it was to get any sables in the winter. “ You have sometimes to travel for two or three days from the village,” he said, “ before you get on the tracks of a sable. If only the Koryaks would go away there would be plenty of them—the Koryaks frighten off the sables. But it is true I must go to see the Koryaks again in a few days as I have no food for my dogs. We have run short of fish, and it is still two months to the spring. We never get any rest. How is one to hunt sables when one has to go to get meat every week ?”’

The fact is that these west-coast Kamchadals would starve to death if the Koryaks did not help them. They are unceasingly going to the Koryaks’ jurtas and begging | for reindeer, and the Koryaks, who are too kind-hearted to see their fellow-mortals die of hunger, supply their needs. ‘The Koryak women make clothes out of reindeerskins for Kamchadals, who declare they can’t sew, but who are too lazy to do so.

All the other villages were of the same dreadful along the Okotsk Shore 249 kind. If the weather had not been bad, and hunger had not forced us, we should not have gone into them at all. In some of them we could not bring ourselves to spend the night, but contented ourselves with getting food for the dogs and for ourselves, finding refuge instead in one of the earth-huts, which were generally situated, for the benefit of travellers, about half-way between the villages.
CHAPTER XVII BACK TO THE WILDS

N Chairusovo, one of the largest of the west- [=< villages, we turned aside from our southerly progress and drove eastward towards the fjells to pay a final visit to the Koryaks and the Lamuts. I succeeded in getting a native to guide us up into the mountains by agreeing to photograph him and his family. They had never been photographed before, and they regarded it as some strange form of magic. As a rule the Koryaks are very disinclined to let themselves be photographed and usually refuse. The Lamuts do not object to it, but are not especially pleased. The Kamchadals, on the other hand, are always very keen on having their pictures taken, and would often undertake quite laborious tasks for me on condition I “snapshotted”’ them. Often when they declared to God that they had come to an end of their jukkola my camera was my only means of getting some out of them.

Our Kamchadal guide, whose sledge was empty, took my wife in it as a passenger. I had weighted our sledge with things available for barter which I had bought in the Hudson Bay Company’s store in Chairusovo. The most valuable of my wares was a quite big supply of tobacco. Throughout almost the whole of the west
coast people had run short of tobacco, and the first thing they all did was to ask for some.

The first Koryak we met was a man named Jutta. His jurta lay about thirty miles from the village and we got to it in the evening. His reindeer herd was to be seen in the distance. We were cordially received by the old man, who came forward to meet us. He was tanned and weather-beaten, and clad from top to toe in skins, and he walked with slow, waddling steps. After our experience of the smelly and unwholesome Kamchadals. it was refreshing to come across the Koryaks again, with Geir look of health and strength and general well-being

“This is the first time I have seen you,” he began. “Where have you come from? Have you come to get reindeer-flesh?”’ I explained to him that we had come from “the other side of the sea”—the Koryaks’ term for everything outside of Kamchatka—and that all we wanted was some reindeer-flesh for our dogs and to stay with him for some days if he permitted. “Certainly,” he replied; “I never drive away a stranger, and you need have no anxiety about food for your dogs. You see my herd yonder. But you must tie your dogs up securely, for to-morrow we shall be driving the herd down to the jurta. Go in now and drink some tea, for it is cold out-of-doors to-day.”’ All this was pleasant hearing, and we crept into the jurta under the skin hangings, and made acquaintance with the other members of the family. All were clad in skins, and presented a wild-looking appearance as ane Back to the Wilds they sat there in the glare of the fire which burned in the middle of the jurta.

By the time we had got through with the regular routine of meat-eating and tea-drinking it was already dark. Each branch of the family went into its own compartment and lit its bear’s-grease lamp. We remained with the old man and talked with him. He told us a lot about Koryak habits and customs. It was particularly interesting to hear how the Koryaks behave when one of their family dies. Huis account of what they do on these occasions agreed largely with Jochelson’s description of the Koryaks who dwell to the north of Kamchatka.

When a Koryak dies, his body is wrapped in special burial clothes richly embroidered in skin. These clothes, which with all their adornments it takes an entire winter to make, must be prepared in advance, as otherwise they would not be ready when needed ; but they ought not to be quite ready. That would be considered wrong, and calculated to hasten the death of the person. Therefore a number of small details are left unfinished. The sewing of the burial clothes is done by the women, usually during the night, while the men are asleep. When a Koryak dies the finishing touches are put to the clothes.

As long as the corpse remains in the jurta no one must sleep. The women complete their sewing and the men keep themselves awake by playing cards—an art which they have learned from the Russians. Jochelson tells how the Koryaks farther north, in order to allow
the dead man to take part in the game, sit round the body and use it as a card-table!

When the burial clothes are ready, and the dead man has been clad in them, his own reindeer are attached to the sledge upon which the body has been placed, and one of his nearest relatives drives him to the spot where the funeral pile is to be erected—for the Koryaks burn their dead. Enough wood for this purpose has been collected together in advance. Both the reindeer are sacrificed, so that the dead may have them with him also in the next world. The body in its handsome coverings is placed on the funeral pile, which is set on fire. Alongside the body are placed a number of things of which he was fond—for instance, his pipe and his snuff-box, as well as some delicacies, such as reindeertongues, marrow-bones, etc., for him to have with him on his journey to the other world. Occasionally there are placed beside him also presents for some relatives previously deceased.

The Koryaks are heathen. ‘They believe in good and evil spirits and they practise Shamanism—that is, the art of altering the course of events with the help of guardian spirits. The “ magic” drum is the chief appliance they make use of in this connexion. There is one in every jurta. On festival days—or when someone is sick and needs to be cured, or when something else of importance is afoot—one of them will don his Shaman attire and begin beating on the drum to summon the spirits. Only a few Koryaks are skilful Shamans. Our old host claimed to be one, and at my request put

on his Shaman attire. On his head he placed a hat encircled with a long fringe of beads and skin tassels. A special fur coat with a lot of tassels, beads and bells formed part of the costume. He then began to beat the drum and to sing. He made a tremendous noise, became more and more excited, and at last got into a sort of ecstasy. Suddenly he stopped, quite exhausted. He had put his whole soul into it and was now worn | out. What the spirits had said to him he did not tell us.
It was now late and time for us to go to sleep. We laid ourselves down in our sleeping-sacks, while the wind raged outside and the dogs were sending forth their plaintive sounds.

We spent several days in that jurta. The old man’s talk was very interesting and we were well cared for, and the dogs were fed on reindeer-flesh every day. I became such good friends with the old Koryak that he allowed me to take a photograph of him in his Shaman costume while he beat on the drum. When, a short time before, I had made the same request to another Koryak he was so much annoyed that he would hardly answer me when I spoke to him. He at once put away the drum in its skin case, declaring that it was the Koryaks’ doctor.

I took a photograph also of the interior of the jurta, with our host and hostess and their two sons. It was in the evening and I had to use a flashlight. Just before I produced the flash I asked them not to look in my direction lest they should be blinded by the light. When I had taken the two photographs I wanted, the

elder of the two sons—a jolly youth of twenty—said he would like me to give him a large supply of that powder. He would then go to the nearest Lamut jurta and tell the Lamuts to look straight at it while he produced the flash !
NLY a few miles from Jutta’s dwelling there
(-)::: a Lamut encampment. We heard one day
' that the Lamuts would be moving camp next day if the weather were good. We>were very anxious to take part in their move, so we decided to proceed to their camp next morning.

Lest we should be late we started before dawn, having first had tea and eaten some meat, and taken farewell of our very friendly hosts. The dogs, who had enjoyed their ample fare and who had had a good rest, were in excellent condition, and went at a gallop almost the whole way. We reached our destination in about twenty minutes.

We found the Lamuts on the move. They were just taking down both their jurtas. Everything was put into sacks, which the reindeer were to carry; the jurtastakes were tied together, the sledges drawn up and packed, and all the sacks placed in rows. The children ran about and did mischief and got in the way. The smallest of them, a healthy-looking little Tungus-type of one-and-a-half, had been put into a cradle very finely ornamented with beads and embroideries, and he did not seem at all happy to judge by the expression of sre.
