At last all the sledges had been packed and all the sacks filled. Now the reindeer required had to be caught, and that was not a few. Eighty sacks lay out on the snow: for these alone forty animals were wanted. In addition, fourteen were needed to draw the sledges, and five to ride. The herd were driven up and the capturing of those required took a couple of hours, two other Lamuts who had come over from other jurtas lending a hand. They had their dog-sledges with them, and these also were requisitioned to take some baggage. One of the two had had his face disfigured—his nose and one eye were missing. He had been mauled by a bear which he had wounded.

When finally the necessary reindeer had been caught and laden with their packs, and these had been made fast, the animals which were to be ridden were saddled and the sledges got ready. At last, after much trouble, the whole caravan started. It was a wonderfully fine sight to see it set itself in motion and slowly begin its progress over the zundra, which lay bathed in sunshine.

the reindeer in each group were attached to each other by thongs. The first pack-animal in each group was bound to the riding-reindeer in front. Last of all came the herd. Ordinarily the herd is driven on in front, so as to make a road for the caravan, but now the snow was so hard that it could be counted on to bear both the sledges and the reindeer.

The place where the Lamuts intended to pitch their new camp was not much more than three miles away. We waited until the whole procession had disappeared from sight on the undulating tundra; then I started again and we shot ahead at a tremendous pace, catching up the caravan just before it had reached its destination.
We tied up our dogs near the site on which the new jurta was to be raised and we were now free to look on quietly at the operation, and take photographs of them from time to time.

After the pack-animals had been relieved of their loads, and the other reindeer of their saddles and bundles, they were let loose, and they at once rejoined the rest of the herd, which was busily occupied in kicking up the snow and seeking for lichens on their new and rich grazing ground.

The sites were now chosen for both jurtas, and the work of getting them up began at once. This was the women’s work exclusively. First they cleared away the snow from the ground—the Lamuts have specially made snow-shovels for this purpose. When they had got the snow cleared away three stick stakes were set up in the middle to hold up the outer coverings. Then branches were collected and spread over the ground: after which the whole framework of the tent was put up. All the stakes had been brought along from the previous camping-ground.

_ As may be seen from the illustrations, the roof ends within a yard or so of the ground, on the tops of the stakes which constitute the outer framework. ‘These stakes are bound together in couples with thongs. The roof-coverings, which all reach up to the smoke-hole and are supported by the three stout stakes already mentioned, stretch from the smoke-hole down to these short double stakes all round the structure and are made fast to them. When the entire framework has been made ready it constitutes a remarkably strong—though slender and elegant—structure, of a kind that certainly did not come to perfection all at once. Now a great layer of reindeer-hides sewn together is placed over the roof and sides. They are made fast with thongs here and there. All this continues to be the job of the women. They begin at the bottom and work upwards until the whole jurta is covered. The men sit around and smoke or amuse themselves in some other way. Some of them get together a supply of dry wood, which is a man’s job. Within a couple of hours the jurta had been put up and the inner compartments completed, with reindeer-hides covering the floor and the tea-kettle hanging over the fire. We marvelled at the efficiency with which everything had been done. There had been no hitch of any kind, and it was quite a big piece of work that had been achieved. No fewer than six families had moved house, with all their possessions, animate and inanimate.

It was a very pleasant experience to sit down to tea for the first time in the new jurta. All were delighted to have moved to a new place, and they confessed to us that they thought it monotonous to live for long in any one place. The nomadic spirit is in their blood and keeps them continually on the move.

While we were at tea old Jutta and his two sons came over on three reindeer-sledges. They only came to greet us and drink tea. All the nomads in these fjells are very fond of paying visits in this way, I found. The Koryaks told us that they also had made a move—and yet when I had asked them that very morning when they were going to move they had replied that they did not know exactly! Evidently they had not wished to have us with them while they were doing so.

The Lamuts now decided to pay a return visit, and after several mugs of tea had been consumed two of them went out and got hold of the required number of reindeer. My wife and I wanted to accompany them on the sledges, so I asked our Lamut host to have two sledges made ready for us; but he shook his head and declared that the reindeer were wild and we might easily have our legs broken—in other words, he was not at all keen on our going. But when I had urged that it was our own affair if we broke our legs he went out and got hold of three more animals. These he harnessed — two to one sledge for me, and one to another sledge for my wife. ‘‘ Well, but who is to drive?” Iasked. ‘‘ You will drive yourselves,” he answered. I had contemplated our going only as passengers, and as we had never driven reindeer alone, but had always had a native to drive us, we felt it was a rather risky proceeding. We decided, however, to take the risk. Six other sledges started ahead of us and we whipped up our reindeer and followed.

The Koryaks’ new jurta lay about three miles off. The greater part of our route lay over tundra. The other six sledges were soon out of sight. Our companions were singularly off-hand and did not bother themselves in the least about us. Our reindeer behaved well, however. At first they indulged in some curvettings, but soon they got into a trot and kept going steadily in the tracks of the others. Soon the jurta came into sight and outside it we found all the Koryak family assembled in full force together with the Lamut visitors. ‘They watched us curiously, and we did our best to make an effective approach without any somersaults, and, fortunately, we succeeded. It was quite amusing to visit the same family in the same jurta which we had seen that same morning in another region. Our return journey passed off quite all right, but it was wearisome to have to sit astride, as you must do in a reindeer-sledge. Dog-sledges are much more comfortable—in them you can sit as you like.
Next day we spent transacting business with the Lamuts. We purchased some of their riding-saddles, pack-sadddles and packing-sacks. We succeeded in acquiring specimens also of the different kinds of

dresses worn by Lamut women, with their beads and embroideries, as well as of the men’s; of their summer and winter boots, as well as of various sorts of utensils, and a lot of other things. In another jurta I acquired a particularly elegant reindeer-sledge with harness and reins.

The day after that we took farewell of both jurtas and their hospitable inhabitants and continued our journey. We visited two other Lamut jurtas before we returned to Chairusovo, and after that we saw no more Lamuts during our winter journey.
In the village we packed up our collections in boxes, which were deposited in the Hudson Bay Company’s store until they could be shipped to Petropavlovsk.
ALONG THE WEST COAST TO KARLSSON’S
tance with Kamchatka’s oldest inhabitant, a
white-haired old fellow who claimed to be in his one-hundred-and-sixth year, and really he looked that age. He was entirely blind, but he could hear and speak quite well.

He told us stories of times long past, and he could remember well the day when the Kamchadals lived in earth-caves. He declared that there used to be far more sables and bears in the country, and that the supply of salmon also had decreased. ‘The Kamchadals lived better now though, he added. Now they all had good guns, formerly they had only spears to hunt with. Everything had improved since he was a young man, he admitted, but there was not so much peace and quiet.

We now had everything ready for our return to Petropavlovsk—a journey of some five hundred miles. The first portion of it lay along the line of the diseasestricken villages, but a little farther south, on the west coast, we had a peculiarly agreeable change to look forward to—our visit to Mr Karlsson. ‘This Mr Karlsson, already mentioned, had lived for many years in the village of Monomachova. At his house we hoped also to meet again Mr Jansson. But between Karlsson’s home and us there lay two hundred and fifty miles and eight villages.

The first place we passed was Bjelogolovaja, the smallest village we saw in the whole of Kamchatka, consisting as it does of only four huts. It lies in the middle of a tundra and without a tree to protect it. The next village was called Moroschetsnaja—lI think it was the most primitive-looking Kamchadal village we saw. Almost every hut in it had fish-skin or bear-gut windows, and for lighting the inhabitants depended mostly on bear’s-grease or seal-oil lamps. They all spoke the Kamchadal language. Our host there begged us to excuse him for having only Kamchadal bread— that is, dried salmon. Besides jukko/a and tea we were given crake-berries. Almost all the villagers came round to the hut in which we stayed to have a look at us. They peered at us as curiously as though we were wild beasts in a menagerie.

In the village of Sopotschnaja we saw for the first time a dalagan of a type different from those we had previously come across on the west coast. It was one of the most primitive type, which one finds described in the oldest accounts of Kamchatka. The food-store up above the erection of stakes was in pyramidal form and occupied the whole of the structure. The village of Itschik, south of Sopotschnaja, was the last in which we heard the Kamchadal language talked generally.

Gradually we came nearer to the sea, on which we had not set eyes for so long. On the zundras adjoining the coast large herds of reindeer were sometimes to be descried, and now and again a Koryak jurta ; and whenever our dogs got scent of the former they tore along as usual, but here on the level ground it was always a pleasant experience when they did so.

We paid a visit to one Koryak jurta near which we had to pass. It was one of the largest we had seen, and we met a number of Koryaks there. I asked one of them if he knew Karlsson. Yes, indeed, he knew him —Karlsson was his special friend ; and he proceeded to tell us proudly that our friend always came to him when in need of reindeer-flesh. When the Koryak in his turn needed something he always bought it from Karlsson, who never humbugged him as the other traders did. Karlsson was a splendid man, the Koryak declared. He remembered now that Karlsson had told him that he expected to have some countrymen of his on a visit in the early spring. But at the moment he was away from home, he thought.

After we had left Chairusovo the weather had been warm and sunny, the temperature often rising above freezing-point in the middle of the day, with the result that the snow became cloggy and the sledge would not glide over it. At this period of the year it is the custom to put iron steel or whalebone under the runners of the sledge—that is to say, a pair of thin runners of one or other of these materials are screwed under the wooden runners. It is a question whether steel or whalebone is best. Steel glides better on the snow but whalebone glides better on the bare ground, and in spring you often have to drive over bare ground; therefore it is always a great subject of discussion in the spring as to which is best, steel or whalebone—some say the one, some the other. I had had a pair of steel runners screwed under the sledge throughout our journey, but I now unscrewed them and put them in their right place, to the great comfort of the dogs. The sledge went twice as smoothly.

Another article which becomes necessary at this time of the year is snow-spectacles. Especially on the west-coast tundras, where you frequently for long stretches have not a single point on which to rest your eyes, snow-spectacles are absolutely essential. You cannot get on for a day without them. All the natives, whatever class they may belong to, have snowspectacles to put on at this time, and most of the traders have them on sale.

Every day brought us a good stretch farther south, usually about thirty or forty miles. The villages we now passed were all very similar. The only difference between them was the nearer we got to Petropavlovsk the more Russians were to be found in them and the more the Kamchadals showed signs of having Russian blood in them.

One custom which we disapproved of much was as widespread on this coast as we had found it on the other—namely, that of eating supper as late as possible, Throughout the whole of Kamchatka (and it would seem to be the same over the whole of north-eastern

Siberia) the chief meal of the day is eaten in the evening. With the Kamchadals it is etiquette to sup as late as possible. Nine or ten o’clock is thought too early, and if you want to be really distinguished you offer your visitors supper between eleven and twelve. On innumerable occasions we would arrive at a village, worn out, about six or seven o’clock in the evening. As soon as we had been given tea our hostess as a rule would begin at once to busy herself over the supper—which in a well-provided house consisted generally of salmon cooked in bear’s fat, and of soups with big pieces of bear or reindeer or mountain sheep in it. By eight o’clock everything, perhaps, would be ready, and then an appetizing smell would pervade the whole house; but although we were all hungry, and desired nothing better than to be allowed to eat, the woman of the house would deliberately place the meat in a warm oven, where it would remain and get dry, until it was late enough to offer it to us. When one is not allowed to pay for one’s food one cannot very well insist upon it being served at one’s own convenience. Occasionally the hostess will actually, as I have said, keep supper back until midnight, but sometimes she herself becomes so sleepy that she has to take forty winks now and then to keep herself awake, as one might say.
At last, at midnight, yawning and half-asleep, she comes forward and wonders whether you would like a little supper.

Once we arrived at a village about nine in the evening. We were too tired to wait for something to eat, and lay down to sleep. Between midnight and one A.M. we were wakened up and offered a carefully prepared supper.

The nearer we came to Karlsson’s village the longer were our journeys every day, and during the last seven days we did not indulge in any break. As a rule one gives the dogs one complete day’s rest after five working days—but they would be having a really good long rest at Karlsson’s.

At last, on the afternoon of 28th March, we heard the barking of the dogs of the village of Monomachova —Karlsson’s village. Half-an-hour later we reached it. I asked the first villager we met to show me Karlsson’s home, and he directed me to a fine house witha veranda and a flagstaff. Some nice little boys who saw whither we were walking ran forward towards us and called out: ‘‘ Are you coming to Karlsson? He is our father.’ And they proceeded to hang on to the back of the sledge, directing us meanwhile how to go.

There now came out of the house two young men. One was Karlsson’s son, the other his son-in-law. We had been long expected and were given a hearty welcome. We learnt, however, that Karlsson himself and Jansson were not at home, but might be back any day. They had gone some weeks before to the village of Javina, one of the most southerly villages in Kamchatka, where Karlsson had previously lived, and where he still had a good deal of business to transact. It was a great disappointment to us not to meet them, but we were obliged in any case to spend a couple of days at
Monomachova and we hoped that they might return before we left.

Coffee and hot and cold snacks were at once placed before us. Karlsson had evidently given instructions how we were to be received. I found letters awaiting me both from him and Jansson and from my colleagues in Petropavlovsk. Karlsson’s own letter was as brief as it was cordial. It ran:
“Dear Compatriots,—Welcome to my village! If there is anything you want, just tell my son. You need be at no loss for food for your dogs. Yours,
He knew what would be our greatest need. The most difficult thing to manage on a winter journey is the supply of food for one’s dogs, and he was anxious to save us from any anxiety on this head.

Karlsson’s house was not like any other we had seen in Kamchatka. He had one room which might have been in a Swedish farmer’s house. In the centre of it stood a round table with a flowered cloth on it. Above it hung from the ceiling a nice hanging-lamp—the only one of that kind I saw in the country; in the window were pots of fuschia and pelargoniums in full bloom, and against one wall stood a bookcase. The whole room was quite unique in its way in Kamchatka. In the bookcase we found a number of Swedish books.

Karlsson had been married three times, to Kamchatka women, and had had a large number of children. He had lost his third wife and many of his children, but there were still eight of them living. Five of them were _ at home—three quite small, two grown-up, a son and a daughter: both of these looked as Swedish as anyone could desire. There was no trace of Asiatic blood in them.

We stayed in Karlsson’s house two days, but as there was no news from him we could not wait any longer —especially as the ice on the rivers was beginning to break up a little everywhere on account of the warm weather, and we had many to cross. Therefore on the third day we had to say good-bye. We made for the sea-coast, along which we were to drive for some days. Along the coast were a number of Japanese fishing stations here and there. In some of them there was a caretaker who had to watch over them throughout the winter.

When we had travelled more than fifteen miles we came upon the hut of one of these watchmen, outside which there stood a dog-sledge. When we got near this, and our dogs began to bark, a big fellow came out of the house. It was Jansson, and we greeted each other uproariously. ‘‘ But where is Karlsson?” J asked, after we had shaken hands. “Oh, he may be along any moment,” was the reply. ‘‘ Karlsson remained behind in the last village where he had a lot of business to do in the matter of sables,’’ Jansson went on, ‘‘ and I came on ahead. I had heard that you were here and I wanted to try to catch you. Let’s go in and have some tea and Karlsson may turn up.”

Therewith we went into the watchman’s hut. He was an unfortunate Siberian whose sole occupation was to hang about there all the winter and see that everything was all right. He seemed a little off his head, and I was not surprised—for at least eight years he had been ruminating there. Had he been a European he would probably have taken up some kind of handiwork, but it suited him best to do nothing. He preferred to spend the day keeping on the look-out for passing sledges so as to have company at tea.

We sat there talking with Jansson for a couple of hours, but no Karlsson came. Jansson urged us to return so that we could all spend the day together. At last we fell in with this suggestion, although in my mind’s eye I saw before me a whole series of open rivers to be crossed. On the other hand, I felt we could not leave Kamchatka without meeting “‘ Karlsson on the west coast,’’ of whom my colleagues and I had all heard so much, but whom none of us had seen. So we turned back, not indeed to the village but to the mouth of the river where Karlsson had a smaller house and his store, for he was now a large dealer in furs. We had the wind against us all the time but we got there in a couple of hours.
It was a nice, cosy little house. A large corrugatediron storehouse stood alongside it. It was situated not more than one hundred and fifty yards from the sea.

We spent the evening and night there, and next day we kept sweeping the suxdra with our field-glasses, but still no sign of Karlsson, until at last, towards dusk we espied a little black spot on the horizon. It increased gradually in size until at last, when it was only about two miles off, Jansson was able to declare that he recognized Karlsson’s team of dogs. Soon afterwards Karlsson arrived and we went out to greet him. He looked thoroughly Swedish, despite his snow-overall and shaggy Koryak cap of reindeer-skin. As soon as he had tied up his dogs he came in, and we made each other’s acquaintance. After we had all had coffee, Karlsson produced the keys of his storehouse and brought back some suitable preserves, for now we were all to hold festival in honour of the occasion. Never before had a quartette of Swedes assembled there.
Jansson, who, as mentioned already, had been in his time a ship’s cook, knew well how to produce a meal, and set to work on this immediately.

Karlsson told us a lot about his adventures and experiences. He was born in Halmstad, in southern Sweden; he had been round the world as a sailor, and had been wrecked on the west coast of Kamchatka thirty-four years before. With him he had had a Finnish Doctor of Philosophy, Otto Kuorikoski, who for political reasons had fled his country. They had made their way to the village of Javina, near the south of — the peninsula. As they were both of them sportsmen —Karlsson especially—they settled down among the Kamchadals and lived by hunting and fishing, like them. Fifteen years later the Finn died. Karlsson continued to live by hunting and fishing for some years, but gradually began to become a trader in skins. He had himself shot more than one thousand bears. Formerly, he said, there were infinitely more bears in Kamchatka than there were now. At one time they used to make their way right into the villages, and he had shot many from the window of his house in Javina. Once he counted no fewer than thirty-one bears all feasting on the fat of a stranded whale.

In those days, he said, he used to go up the Ozernaja river to the Kuril Lake bear-hunting. He used to shoot a great many of them every year in that region, and when he had finished his hunting he would make himself a boat out of a pair of large skins, with the hair side inwards and the fleshy side out. In this he would place all the other skins and so return down the stream with his booty.

Once he succeeded in capturing a little wolf, which he reared with his sledge-dogs. When it grew up, it mated with some of the latter, and so Karlsson had introduced wolf’s blood into his team. The next generation of the dogs proved strong and hardy, but they had much of the wolf nature in them and it was dangerous to hit them. Once when they were in a wilful mood and Karlsson was hitting them he slipped and fell over. All the dogs had rushed at him and he had had a very narrow escape of his life. He still had scars from their bites.

While Karlsson was relating these things, Jansson had prepared the most splendid supper we had seen for years. It ended with preserved grapes and cheese, all American. Karlsson told us much more that evening, and it was long after midnight when we lay down to sleep.

But next morning we had absolutely to be off. We got up at five o’clock. Jansson gave us coffee and pancakes for breakfast. Before we said good-bye we made both our friends promise to spend Easter with us at Petropavlovsk. And so we waved adieu to them and disappeared from their sight into the distance.

T was our intention on this last stage of our journey not to spend a day anywhere, but to keep on straight ahead, if the weather permitted. We had about two hundred and fifty miles to cover. Of these, one hundred and twenty-five or so were in a southerly direction, and for the most part over zundras. After that we should be swinging off at an angle due east, and crossing the country.

About our route there is not much to say. We drove from morning until late in the evening, spending some nights out in the open, but most of them in villages. When we came to the Bolschaja river at Bolscheredsk it was already full of holes in the ice, and there were unfrozen channels in it. The ice was soft and weak, and it was with really anxious feelings that we guided the dogs out on to the river and drove over it, dodging the holes, to the other bank. Fortune favoured us, for I heard afterwards that the ice on the whole river was broken up next day.

Between the villages of Apatcha and Natchika we were less lucky. Here we had to cross the river several times. At the first place the ice still held, but at the second there was a gap of nearly four yards along the bank. A steep and narrow bank led down to the surface of the river. To judge from tracks, the last sledge that had been that way had tried to get over but had had to turn back and find another crossing-place. I was aware that one could avoid the river by going over a hill, which, however, was very difficult going. We decided to do this; but when we came to the foot of the hill and tried to get up it with our heavily weighted sledge we found it so difficult that we agreed it would be easier to get the sledge over the unfrozen channel of the river, which was only about two feet deep. So we went back and took off our boots and stockings, but, my word, it was cold! We drove the dogs into the water and got them up on the ice beyond. Then we had both of us to go back into the water, and with great difficulty we managed to get the sledge also up on to the ice, having first removed from it our photographic plates and other things that might be damaged if they got wet. When we had got the sledge right across to the other bank, and had fetched over the things we had had to take out of it, we breathed a sigh of relief and put on our stockings and boots again as quickly as ever we could.

After this we proceeded, feeling happy and contented, but within five minutes we were confronted by a new and unpleasant surprise—a great wide raging river, on which the ice had entirely broken up! The one which we had just crossed was a mere streamlet in comparison. We were now caught, as it were, in a rat-trap, with water in every direction. There was nothing for it but to turn round and take off our stockings and boots again. And so back into the water ! But now we had that steep farther bank of the river to get up. The whole business took us over three hours, and when it was over our feet and legs were nearly frozen. Our dogs were as tired as we. The mounting of the steep bank needed the putting forth of all our remaining strength. We managed it before darkness fell, but we did not reach Natchika that evening, as we had calculated. We had to spend the night in the wood. We-were so worn out that we had to let the dogs sleep as best they could where they were, in their harness, while we ourselves just took out our sleepingsacks and lay down to sleep without making tea or eating anything. I felt as weak as a rag, and my heart was palpitating. I could not get any sleep during the night.

Next day we reached Natchika. Ever since we had left Sedanka we had been hearing the wildest tales about the strife between the Whites and the Reds. We had been assured that no one could get through the front of the Reds to Petropavlovsk, that all sledges were examined and that all arms and valuables were confiscated. We took all these rumours with a grain of salt, however, for we knew something about the Russians and the Kamchadals by now. The Bolsheviks had been friendly to us before and we felt sure they would be so again.

According to most of the reports the Red front was at Natchika, but there the only red flag we saw was over the telephone office. We were now told that it was five miles from Petropavlovsk. We neared that point with some curiosity and feeling of suspense. For safety’s sake I had repacked the sledge, putting firearms and field-glasses—its most covetable contents— down in the bottom. We drove along smartly towards the hillock by the side of the road, where according to report the guard was posted. There was no one to be seen there. When we had got half-way up the hill two armed men did suddenly pop up and put field-glasses to their eyes. I slowed down a little to show that I was ready to pull up, and I kept looking in their direction. They did not cry out to us to halt, however, as they had done to all the preceding sledges, but allowed us to pass without hindrance when they saw who we were.

And so we drove past the little village of Avatcha, and out to Avatcha Bay, which was frozen over. Here we steered our course direct for the town, and on 7th April, in the afternoon, we passed the White outposts on the outskirts of Petropavlovsk and ploughed our way along the muddy chief street, being greeted with cries of ‘‘ Welcome back!” by several acquaintances. Thus we arrived at last at our house in Third Street, where we found all at home.
And so our long journey through Kamchatka was brought to a successful close, and our trusty dogs had a well-deserved rest, after taking us a drive of about seventeen hundred miles.

It was certainly a pleasant feeling to be back in possession of our lives and with no ill results from our travels except a touch of rheumatism, from which both of us suffered a little, and this, we agreed, was a small payment for the results of our expedition, which had been better than we had dared to hope for. We had learned to know something of Kamchatkan animal life in the winter and of the human inhabitants of the fjells and the zundras. We had moreover brought back with us the ethnographical collection which now is housed at the State Museum in Stockholm, where the other collections of the expedition are also preserved.
